title: Daily Assessment: Git Architecture & Version Control Concepts
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is the primary architectural purpose of a distributed version control system (DVCS) like Git?
options: A central server stores all code and clients only keep lightweight metadata pointers
It eliminates the need for branches by overwriting files immediately in real time
Source code is compiled directly on a central mainframe before distribution to developers
Every developer clone contains the entire project history and repository mirror locally
questions.explanation: In Git's distributed architecture, every local clone is a full repository backup containing complete commit history, enabling offline operations and decentralized workflows.

questions.question: Which three distinct zones constitute the core local architecture of Git?
options: Feature Branch, Release Tag, and Master Mirror
Working Directory, Staging Area (Index), and Repository (HEAD)
Frontend UI, Backend Controller, and SQL Database
RAM, ROM, and Solid State Drive
questions.explanation: Git manages local changes across three distinct areas: the Working Directory (modified files), the Staging Area / Index (prepared snapshot), and the Repository (committed history in HEAD).

questions.question: What fundamental data structure does Git use internally to represent commit history and object relationships?
options: Singly Linked List with integer auto-incrementing IDs
Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of cryptographically hashed objects
B+ Tree indexed table stored in SQLite
Circular FIFO buffer allocated in cache memory
questions.explanation: Git models commits, trees, and blobs as immutable objects in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), linked together by their SHA-1 cryptographic hashes.

questions.question: In Git object storage, what is a 'blob' (Binary Large Object) responsible for storing?
options: The folder directory hierarchy and file permissions
The active branch pointers and remote URLs
The commit author name, email, and timestamp only
The pure file contents/data without filename or directory metadata
questions.explanation: A blob stores solely raw file contents. Directory structures, filenames, and file modes are stored in 'tree' objects.

questions.question: What is the function of the HEAD pointer in a Git repository?
options: It marks the very first root commit created during repository initialization
It specifies the HTTPS URL of the remote GitHub repository
It points to the current branch reference or the latest commit in your active working tree
It locks files against concurrent edits across the network
questions.explanation: HEAD is a symbolic reference indicating which commit or branch is currently checked out in your local working directory.

questions.question: What scenario causes Git to enter a 'detached HEAD' state?
options: When the local hard drive runs out of disk space during a merge
When two developers commit simultaneously with identical timestamps
Checking out a specific commit SHA, tag, or remote branch directly rather than a local named branch
When the remote GitHub server fails to respond to SSH handshakes
questions.explanation: A detached HEAD occurs when HEAD points directly to a commit SHA rather than a branch ref. Commits made in this state can be lost if not attached to a named branch before switching away.

questions.question: What is the exact purpose of the .gitignore file?
options: To hide sensitive code lines from developers during peer reviews
To define file patterns that Git should intentionally ignore from tracking and staging
To bypass password requirements when pushing to remote servers
To permanently delete binary files from the local file system upon commit
questions.explanation: .gitignore prevents unintended files (such as build artifacts, node_modules, .env secrets, and log files) from being tracked by Git.

questions.question: How does Git guarantee the cryptographic integrity of its object database?
options: By signing every file with a hardware TPM security chip
By using operating system file locking mechanisms
By storing duplicate files across hidden cloud partitions
Every object is addressed and verified by its SHA-1 / SHA-256 content hash
questions.explanation: Git uses content-addressable storage where the identity of any object is the hash of its contents. Modifying even one byte changes the hash and breaks the commit chain.

questions.question: What is stored inside the hidden .git folder in your project root?
options: The entire object database, commit history, refs, configuration, hooks, and staging index
The operating system virtual machine hypervisor configuration
Only compiled binary bytecode and node dependency caches
Temporary scratch files that can be deleted safely at any time
questions.explanation: The `.git` directory contains the complete Git repository engine—including refs, objects, index, config, and commit history.

questions.question: Which command creates a brand new Git repository in your current working folder?
options: git start
git setup
git init
git create
questions.explanation: `git init` creates the `.git` directory and initializes all core metadata structures needed for version tracking.

questions.question: What distinguishes Git from Centralized Version Control Systems (CVCS) like SVN or TFS?
options: Git allows full offline commits, branching, and history inspection without connecting to a central server
Git does not support branching or merging workflows
Git requires constant 24/7 internet connectivity to record file changes
CVCS stores all repositories in local developer RAM while Git uses tape storage
questions.explanation: CVCS requires a continuous connection to a central server for commits and history queries, whereas Git performs virtually all operations locally and instantaneously.

questions.question: Which glob pattern in .gitignore recursively ignores all .env files across the entire project repository?
options: /env-all
ignore .env
*.env
.env::all
questions.explanation: The glob pattern `*.env` matches and ignores any file ending with `.env` in the root directory or any nested subdirectory.

questions.question: What is a 'tree' object in Git's internal architecture?
options: A visualization tool used exclusively in graphical Git user interfaces
A security certificate authorizing SSH connections
An object that represents a directory, mapping filenames to blob SHA hashes and sub-trees
A data compression algorithm used to zip repository downloads
questions.explanation: A tree object corresponds to a directory entry in the filesystem, associating filenames, modes, and SHA hashes of blobs and child trees.

questions.question: What metadata is permanently recorded inside a Git 'commit' object?
options: The full source code of the operating system and BIOS version
Tree hash, parent commit hash(es), author, committer, timestamps, and commit message
The user's GitHub billing account details
The IP addresses of all computers that downloaded the repository
questions.explanation: A commit object captures the top-level tree hash (snapshot of project files), parent commit SHA pointers, author/committer credentials, timestamps, and the log message.

questions.question: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
options: Git and GitHub are identical open-source desktop software packages
Git is a paid enterprise database; GitHub is an open-source text editor
Git is developed for Windows operating systems; GitHub is exclusively for Linux
Git is the version control CLI tool; GitHub is a cloud-based hosting and collaboration platform for Git repositories
questions.explanation: Git is the distributed version control system tool itself. GitHub is an online service that hosts Git repositories and provides pull requests, issues, and CI/CD pipelines.

questions.question: Which command sets your global author email across all Git repositories on your system?
options: git set --email "you@example.com"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git auth --user-email "you@example.com"
git register-email "you@example.com"
questions.explanation: `git config --global user.email "..."` writes your author email to the global `~/.gitconfig` configuration file.

questions.question: What state is a file in after it has been modified in the working directory but not yet staged?
options: Modified (Unstaged)
Committed
Staged
Untracked (New)
questions.explanation: A previously tracked file that contains local edits is in the 'Modified' (unstaged) state until `git add` moves it to the 'Staged' state.

questions.question: What happens when you run git status on a freshly cloned, clean repository?
options: It forces a remote fetch and rebases the current branch
It prints a fatal error requiring repository re-initialization
It reports 'nothing to commit, working tree clean'
It deletes all untracked files automatically
questions.explanation: When no files are modified, staged, or untracked relative to the HEAD commit, `git status` confirms the working tree is clean.

questions.question: Why does Git store file changes as full snapshots rather than delta difference lists?
options: Because snapshots consume zero hard drive storage space
Because Git cannot compute differences between files
Because delta storage is forbidden by open-source licenses
Snapshots allow rapid branch switching and cryptographic integrity verification without recalculating deltas
questions.explanation: Git treats data as a stream of snapshots over time. While packfiles compress identical blobs later, the conceptual snapshot model makes checkouts and history traversal extremely fast.

questions.question: Which command displays the configured Git configuration settings and where they originate?
options: git config --list --show-origin
git inspect-config
git show-config --all
git view --settings
questions.explanation: `git config --list --show-origin` outputs all effective configuration keys alongside the exact file paths (system, global, local) where they are defined.

title: Daily Assessment: Core Git Commands: init, add, commit, push, pull
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI
lessonTitle: Core Git Commands: init, add, commit, push, pull

questions.question: Which command moves all modified and newly created untracked files in the current folder to the staging area?
options: git push --all
git commit --stage
git stage --all-now
git add .
questions.explanation: `git add .` stages all modifications and new untracked files in the current working directory and subdirectories into the index.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to create a commit with an inline descriptive message?
options: git commit --message = "Descriptive commit message"
git record -msg "Descriptive commit message"
git commit -m "Descriptive commit message"
git save -m "Descriptive commit message"
questions.explanation: `git commit -m "message"` records a snapshot of the staged changes with the provided inline log message.

questions.question: What does the command git diff without flags display?
options: A summary list of all commit hashes created in the last 24 hours
Differences between your working directory and the staging area (unstaged changes)
Differences between your local branch and the remote origin master branch
Differences between the staging area and the latest commit in HEAD
questions.explanation: By default, `git diff` shows the unstaged changes currently in your working directory compared to the staging index.

questions.question: Which command compares changes that are currently staged in the index against the last commit in HEAD?
options: git diff --index-all
git diff --staged (or git diff --cached)
git diff --head-only
git diff --ready
questions.explanation: `git diff --staged` (synonym `--cached`) displays the exact diff of changes that have been added to the staging area and will be included in the next commit.

questions.question: How can you stage and commit all modified tracked files in a single shortcut command?
options: git push --commit "Commit message"
git add --commit "Commit message"
git commit -all -save "Commit message"
git commit -am "Commit message"
questions.explanation: `git commit -am "..."` automatically stages all tracked modified files (not untracked files) and commits them in a single step.

questions.question: What does git log --oneline --graph --decorate achieve?
options: A concise, visual ASCII graph of commit history, branches, and tags with one line per commit
A graphical popup window displaying source code syntax highlighting
An automated rollback of the last five commits in history
A direct export of the repository to a PDF report
questions.explanation: `--oneline` truncates commit hashes and shows one line per commit, `--graph` draws an ASCII branch merge graph, and `--decorate` shows branch and tag pointers.

questions.question: Which command connects your local repository to a remote repository hosted on GitHub?
options: git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
git remote set-url new https://github.com/user/repo.git
git connect origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
git link --remote https://github.com/user/repo.git
questions.explanation: `git remote add <name> <url>` registers a new remote repository alias (conventionally named `origin`).

questions.question: What does the -u (or --set-upstream) flag do when running git push -u origin main?
options: It unzips compressed files on the remote server
It pushes the branch and links local main to track remote origin/main for future parameterless pushes
It undoes the previous commit before pushing new files
It unlocks the remote repository for public read access
questions.explanation: The `-u` flag sets the default upstream tracking reference so subsequent pushes and pulls can simply use `git push` or `git pull`.

questions.question: What is the key difference between git fetch and git pull?
options: git fetch deletes local files; git pull restores them from the trash
git fetch downloads remote commits without merging; git pull fetches remote commits and automatically merges them into the active branch
git fetch is an alias for git clone; git pull is an alias for git push
git fetch works with GitHub; git pull only works with GitLab
questions.explanation: `git fetch` safely updates remote tracking branches (`origin/main`) without modifying your local working files. `git pull` is essentially `git fetch` followed by `git merge`.

questions.question: Which command un-stages a file from the staging area while preserving your modifications in the working directory?
options: git delete --staged <file>
git remove --keep <file>
git revert --soft <file>
git restore --staged <file> (or git reset HEAD <file>)
questions.explanation: `git restore --staged <file>` removes the specified file from the staging area without discarding local modifications in your working directory.

questions.question: How can you safely modify the commit message of the most recent commit before pushing?
options: git revert HEAD --edit "Updated commit message"
git update-message "Updated commit message"
git commit --fix-last "Updated commit message"
git commit --amend -m "Updated commit message"
questions.explanation: `git commit --amend` replaces the tip of the current branch with a new commit incorporating any staged changes and/or an updated commit message.

questions.question: Which command completely discards unstaged local modifications in a specific file, reverting it to the HEAD version?
options: git clean -f <file>
git rollback <file>
git restore <file> (or git checkout -- <file>)
git drop <file>
questions.explanation: `git restore <file>` overwrites working tree changes with the version from the staging area or HEAD, permanently discarding uncommitted local edits.

questions.question: What command removes untracked files and directories from the working tree that are not ignored by .gitignore?
options: git clear -untracked
git purge --all
git rm --untracked
git clean -fd
questions.explanation: `git clean -f` forces the deletion of untracked files, and `-d` includes untracked directories.

questions.question: Which command lists all configured remote repository names and their fetch/push URLs?
options: git remotes --show
git remote -v
git remote --list-all
git view --remotes
questions.explanation: `git remote -v` (verbose) outputs the names and corresponding fetch and push URLs for all registered remote repositories.

questions.question: What does git clone <url> do when executed in an empty directory?
options: It deploys the application directly to a live web server
It downloads the remote repository, initializes .git, checks out the default branch, and configures origin
It creates a shallow zip archive without commit history
It copies code to the clipboard without saving files to disk
questions.explanation: `git clone` initializes a new local directory, copies the entire remote repository and history, sets up remote tracking branches, and checks out the default branch.

questions.question: Which command shows the line-by-line author attribution and commit SHA for a specific file?
options: git authors <file>
git audit <file>
git blame <file>
git who <file>
questions.explanation: `git blame <file>` annotates each line of a file with the commit hash, author, and date of the last modification.

questions.question: How do you inspect the full details, diff, and metadata of a specific commit SHA?
options: git view-commit <commit-sha>
git log --commit=<commit-sha>
git show <commit-sha>
git inspect <commit-sha>
questions.explanation: `git show <commit-sha>` displays the commit metadata, author information, log message, and the unified diff of changes introduced by that commit.

questions.question: What does git rm <file> do compared to deleting the file using standard OS commands?
options: It deletes the file from the filesystem and stages the deletion in Git index automatically
It deletes the file from remote GitHub but keeps it locally
It creates a backup copy of the file in the root directory
It encrypts the file so other developers cannot read it
questions.explanation: `git rm <file>` removes the file from both the working directory and stages the removal in the index, ready for the next commit.

questions.question: Which command limits the output of git log to the 5 most recent commits?
options: git log --top 5
git log -n 5 (or git log -5)
git log --limit 5
git log --count 5
questions.explanation: `git log -n 5` or `git log -5` limits the commit history output to the specified number of recent commits.

questions.question: What happens when you run git push origin main and remote main contains commits you do not have locally?
options: Git automatically deletes all remote commits to prioritize your local code
Git creates a duplicate hidden repository on GitHub
Git crashes the remote GitHub server
Git rejects the push with a non-fast-forward error, requiring you to pull/merge remote updates first
questions.explanation: Git enforces non-fast-forward protection. You must fetch and integrate remote changes (`git pull`) before your push will be accepted.

title: Daily Assessment: Branching Strategy & Merge Conflicts
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is a branch in Git from an architectural standpoint?
options: A physical hardware partition on the developer's storage drive
A database table containing locked rows
A complete duplicate copy of all project files in a separate folder
A lightweight, movable pointer (40-byte file) referencing a specific commit SHA
questions.explanation: In Git, a branch is merely a lightweight pointer containing the 40-character SHA of its latest commit. Creating a branch is virtually instantaneous and consumes only 41 bytes.

questions.question: Which modern Git command creates a new branch named feature-login and switches to it immediately?
options: git move -b feature-login
git branch --create-and-move feature-login
git switch -c feature-login (or git checkout -b feature-login)
git new-branch feature-login
questions.explanation: `git switch -c <name>` (introduced in Git 2.23) or `git checkout -b <name>` creates a new branch and checks it out simultaneously.

questions.question: Which command lists all local and remote branches in the repository?
options: git list --branches
git view-branches -v
git branch -a
git branch --show-all-remotes
questions.explanation: `git branch -a` (all) lists both local branches and remote-tracking branches (prefixed with `remotes/origin/`).

questions.question: What is a 'Fast-Forward' merge in Git?
options: A merge executed using multiple CPU threads simultaneously
A merge that forces remote repository overwrites without checking conflicts
A merge where the target branch pointer is simply advanced directly forward to the source commit without creating a merge commit
A merge that skips automated tests to complete faster
questions.explanation: A fast-forward merge occurs when no divergent commits exist on the base branch; Git simply moves the base branch pointer forward to match the feature branch.

questions.question: Which flag forces Git to create a dedicated merge commit even if a fast-forward merge is possible?
options: git merge --force-commit <branch>
git merge --create-node <branch>
git merge --always-commit <branch>
git merge --no-ff <branch>
questions.explanation: `git merge --no-ff` preserves the historical existence of the feature branch in the graph by generating a merge commit even when fast-forward is possible.

questions.question: Under what exact condition does a Git merge conflict occur?
options: Whenever a merge involves more than 10 files simultaneously
Whenever code comments contain special punctuation characters
When developers commit from different operating systems (Windows vs macOS)
When two branches modify the exact same lines of the same file differently since their common ancestor
questions.explanation: Merge conflicts happen when Git encounters competing changes to the same lines of code in the same file and cannot automatically determine which version is correct.

questions.question: In a conflicted file, what does the marker <<<<<<< HEAD denote?
options: The code that will be automatically deleted by Git
A fatal syntax error reported by the compiler
The start of the incoming changes from the branch being merged
The beginning of the changes present in your currently checked-out active branch
questions.explanation: `<<<<<<< HEAD` marks the start of the code version from the current branch. `=======` separates the conflicting versions, and `>>>>>>> <branch>` marks the end of incoming changes.

questions.question: What are the correct steps to resolve and finalize a merge conflict?
options: Delete the repository and clone it again from GitHub
Run git push --force to override the conflict markers
Edit the conflicted file to resolve differences, remove conflict markers, run git add <file>, and execute git commit
Rename the file and delete the other branch immediately
questions.explanation: To resolve a conflict: manually edit the file to the desired state, remove the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers, stage the resolved file (`git add`), and finalize with `git commit`.

questions.question: Which command aborts an ongoing merge and returns your working tree to the pre-merge state?
options: git stop-merge
git merge --abort
git rollback --merge
git merge --cancel
questions.explanation: `git merge --abort` halts the merge process and restores the working directory and HEAD to the state before `git merge` was executed.

questions.question: How do you safely delete a local branch that has already been merged into main?
options: git delete-branch <branch-name>
git remove-branch <branch-name>
git branch -d <branch-name>
git branch -D <branch-name>
questions.explanation: `git branch -d` (lowercase) deletes a branch only if it has been fully merged into its upstream, preventing accidental loss of unmerged work.

questions.question: Which command force-deletes a local branch containing unmerged changes?
options: git branch -force-del <branch-name>
git branch --kill <branch-name>
git branch -D <branch-name>
git drop-branch <branch-name>
questions.explanation: `git branch -D` (uppercase, shortcut for `--delete --force`) deletes a branch regardless of its merge status.

questions.question: How do you delete a remote branch named feature-cart from GitHub?
options: git remove origin/feature-cart
git push origin --delete feature-cart (or git push origin :feature-cart)
git delete remote feature-cart
git remote branch --delete feature-cart
questions.explanation: `git push origin --delete <branch>` sends a request to the remote server to delete the specified branch ref.

questions.question: What is the Gitflow branching model standard for staging and releasing production code?
options: main contains production releases, develop contains integrated features, and short-lived feature/* branches branch off develop
develop is deployed to production and main is used for testing
Every developer maintains a completely separate repository with no shared branches
All developers commit directly to main without creating branches
questions.explanation: Gitflow uses `main` for stable production releases, `develop` for integration, `feature/*` for new capabilities, `release/*` for pre-prod hardening, and `hotfix/*` for urgent patches.

questions.question: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
options: git rebase deletes all commit messages permanently while git merge preserves them
git rebase is an irreversible command that destroys code
git merge preserves complete history with a merge commit; git rebase re-applies commits on top of another base, creating a linear history
git merge is only for local branches; git rebase is only for GitHub
questions.explanation: `git merge` creates a new merge commit combining two histories. `git rebase` moves the base of your feature branch to the tip of target branch, rewriting commit SHAs to produce a clean linear history.

questions.question: Why should you avoid running git rebase on shared public branches (like main)?
options: Rebasing rewrites commit SHA hashes, which desynchronizes the commit history for all other collaborating developers
Because Git will automatically delete the repository from GitHub
Because GitHub forbids rebase operations on paid accounts
Because rebasing on public branches causes CPU hardware overheating
questions.explanation: The Golden Rule of Rebasing: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a public/shared repository, as rewriting public history breaks tracking for team members.

questions.question: Which command allows you to temporarily shelve (stash) uncommitted modifications without committing them?
options: git stash
git pause
git temporary-save
git hold
questions.explanation: `git stash` saves your modified working directory and staged changes to a temporary storage stack and reverts your working tree to match the HEAD commit.

questions.question: How do you re-apply your most recently stashed changes and remove them from the stash stack?
options: git stash pop
git stash apply --clean
git stash restore
git stash extract
questions.explanation: `git stash pop` applies the modifications from the top of the stash stack (`stash@{0}`) back to your working directory and removes them from the stash list.

questions.question: Which command shows the list of all currently saved stash entries?
options: git stash --show-all
git stash view
git stash list
git list-stashes
questions.explanation: `git stash list` outputs all saved stash references (`stash@{0}`, `stash@{1}`, etc.) along with the branch and commit where they were created.

questions.question: What does git cherry-pick <commit-sha> do?
options: Applies the exact changes introduced by a specific commit from another branch onto your currently checked-out branch
Replaces the current branch with a random commit
Deletes a specific commit from history across all branches
Picks the top 5 highest rated commits on GitHub
questions.explanation: `git cherry-pick <commit-sha>` copies the diff of a specific existing commit and commits it cleanly onto the current branch as a new commit.

questions.question: Which command displays which branches contain a specific commit SHA?
options: git whereis <commit-sha>
git branch --contains <commit-sha>
git find-commit <commit-sha>
git branch --has <commit-sha>
questions.explanation: `git branch --contains <commit-sha>` lists all local branches that have the specified commit in their direct ancestor history.

title: Daily Assessment: GitHub Pull Requests & Collaboration Workflows
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is a Pull Request (PR) in modern software engineering workflows?
options: A mechanism to lock all developers out of a repository
A formal proposal on a platform like GitHub to review, discuss, and merge code changes from a feature branch into a target branch
A command that pulls binary dependencies from the npm registry
A request to purchase additional cloud server memory
questions.explanation: A Pull Request (or Merge Request in GitLab) is a collaborative review mechanism where developers submit code changes for automated testing, peer review, and approval before merging.

questions.question: In open-source workflows on GitHub, what is a 'Fork'?
options: A command that terminates a repository connection
A hardware server rack used to host Git repositories
A personal, independent copy of another user's repository hosted under your own GitHub account
A software tool used to split commit messages into multiple lines
questions.explanation: A Fork creates a distinct copy of an upstream repository under your GitHub account, allowing you to freely experiment and submit pull requests without write access to the original project.

questions.question: What is the standard convention for configuring remotes in a forked repository workflow?
options: origin points to your personal fork; upstream points to the original central repository
remote1 points to production; remote2 points to staging
origin points to the local folder; upstream points to Google Drive
master points to your fork; main points to the original repository
questions.explanation: Conventionally, `origin` references your personal fork on GitHub where you push feature branches, and `upstream` references the parent open-source project from which you pull upstream updates.

questions.question: How do you synchronize your local master branch with the latest changes from the original upstream repository?
options: git fetch upstream && git checkout main && git merge upstream/main
git push upstream main --force
git download upstream/main
git sync --all-remotes
questions.explanation: Syncing a fork requires fetching commits from the upstream remote (`git fetch upstream`) and merging `upstream/main` into your local `main` branch.

questions.question: What role do Branch Protection Rules play on GitHub?
options: They restrict repository access to a single computer IP address
They automatically delete branches after 7 days of inactivity
They enforce safeguards such as requiring peer PR approvals, passing CI checks, and preventing direct force-pushes to main
They encrypt repository files using user passwords
questions.explanation: Branch protection rules protect critical branches (like `main`) by requiring code reviews, passing CI/CD status checks, preventing deletions, and blocking direct `git push --force`.

questions.question: What is Continuous Integration (CI) in the context of GitHub Pull Requests?
options: An automated bot that answers student questions in chat
A billing system that charges for each line of code written
Automated pipelines that build, lint, and run test suites against every PR commit to detect bugs before merging
A system that automatically commits code every 5 minutes
questions.explanation: CI (e.g., GitHub Actions) automatically triggers automated test runners, linters, and security vulnerability scanners whenever code is pushed or a PR is opened.

questions.question: Which merge strategy on GitHub combines all commits in a PR into a single unified commit on the target branch?
options: Squash and Merge
Standard Create Merge Commit
Direct Mirror Push
Rebase and Fast-Forward
questions.explanation: 'Squash and Merge' condenses all individual WIP commits from the feature branch into a single clean commit with a consolidated message on the base branch.

questions.question: How does a developer leave an inline comment on a specific line of code during a GitHub PR review?
options: By committing a text file containing the feedback to the branch
By writing the comment inside .gitignore
By navigating to the 'Files changed' tab, hovering over the target code line, and clicking the '+' icon
By sending an email with the line number to the repository owner
questions.explanation: In GitHub's 'Files changed' diff viewer, reviewers click the '+' on any modified line to start an inline discussion thread, request changes, or suggest code replacements.

questions.question: What keyword in a PR description automatically closes linked issue #42 when the PR is merged into the default branch?
options: Link #42
Relates #42
See #42
Fixes #42 (or Closes #42, Resolves #42)
questions.explanation: GitHub recognizes keywords like `Closes #42`, `Fixes #42`, or `Resolves #42` in the PR body and automatically closes the referenced issue upon merging.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a README.md file in a GitHub repository?
options: It stores the billing history of the repository
It contains encrypted database passwords for production deployment
It instructs the Git compiler how to build binary executables
It serves as the landing page documentation explaining the project's purpose, setup instructions, usage, and architecture
questions.explanation: `README.md` is written in Markdown and renders automatically on the repository root page to guide developers on installation, prerequisites, and features.

questions.question: What file defines automated CI/CD workflows using GitHub Actions?
options: YAML files stored in the .github/workflows/ directory
XML files defined in public/workflows/
Python scripts located in ~/.git/actions/
JSON files stored in the root/config/ directory
questions.explanation: GitHub Actions automatically discovers and executes workflow pipelines defined as `.yml` or `.yaml` files inside `.github/workflows/`.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of using SSH keys rather than Personal Access Tokens for Git authentication?
options: Public-key cryptography provides secure, password-less authentication without exposing credentials in command history
SSH keys allow access to private repositories without owner permission
SSH keys increase download speeds by 500%
SSH keys eliminate the need to run git commit
questions.explanation: SSH keys (like ed25519) use asymmetric cryptography to authenticate your local machine securely and permanently with GitHub without re-entering tokens.

questions.question: What does a 'Draft Pull Request' indicate on GitHub?
options: Work is in progress and open for discussion, but not yet ready for formal review or merging
The PR has been permanently rejected by the maintainers
The PR has failed automated unit test validation
The PR can only be viewed by GitHub employees
questions.explanation: Draft PRs allow developers to share work-in-progress code and trigger CI pipelines while signaling to the team that the branch is not yet ready for final review.

questions.question: Which file format and location is used to provide an issue or PR template for contributors?
options: Text files in templates/git/
HTML files in public/templates/
Python files in backend/templates/
Markdown files in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/ or .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md
questions.explanation: Placing `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` or markdown files in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` pre-populates standardized contribution forms when developers open PRs or issues.

questions.question: How do you update an existing open Pull Request after making changes based on reviewer feedback?
options: Delete the remote branch and recreate it from scratch
Commit your changes locally and run git push origin <feature-branch>—the PR updates automatically
Close the current PR and open a brand new PR with the new code
Email the updated file attachments directly to the reviewer
questions.explanation: A Pull Request tracks the branch head. Pushing new commits to the remote feature branch automatically updates the PR diff, discussion timeline, and triggers CI checks.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the CODEOWNERS file in a repository?
options: It automatically assigns designated individuals or teams as mandatory reviewers when files they own are modified in a PR
It lists the copyright ownership and licensing terms of the codebase
It grants root access to server infrastructure
It restricts who can clone the repository from GitHub
questions.explanation: The `.github/CODEOWNERS` file defines patterns matching files and directories to specific GitHub users or teams who are automatically requested for review on relevant PRs.

questions.question: What does the GitHub 'Rebase and Merge' option do when merging a PR?
options: It deletes all commit authors and replaces them with the repository owner
It re-applies the PR commits individually on top of the base branch without a merge commit, maintaining individual commit granularity
It squashes all commits into a single commit
It creates an octopus merge with all historical branches
questions.explanation: 'Rebase and Merge' appends each individual commit from the PR branch onto the tip of the base branch linearly without creating a merge commit.

questions.question: Which command generates a new high-security Ed25519 SSH key pair on your machine?
options: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
ssh-auth --generate-key ed25519
github-keys generate --email "..."
git create-ssh --type ed25519
questions.explanation: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "email"` generates a modern, cryptographically secure Ed25519 SSH public/private key pair.

questions.question: What does a green checkmark next to a commit on GitHub signify?
options: The commit was created by an automated bot
The commit contains zero lines of code modifications
The commit was approved by GitHub legal compliance
All automated CI/CD checks, unit tests, and linters associated with the commit passed successfully
questions.explanation: Status badges (green checkmarks, yellow dots, or red crosses) reflect the live build and test results reported by CI/CD integrations like GitHub Actions.

questions.question: What is the ultimate professional outcome of enforcing structured Git collaboration workflows?
options: High code quality, regression prevention, clear audit trails, and seamless multi-developer team velocity
Preventing developers from writing Python code
Eliminating the need to write unit tests or documentation
Restricting code releases to once every five years
questions.explanation: Structured Git workflows with feature branches, code reviews, automated CI, and branch protection enable teams to deploy software rapidly and reliably with complete auditability.

title: Daily Assessment: Web Architecture & Client-Server Communication Model
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is the primary role of a DNS (Domain Name System) server in web architecture?
options: Rendering DOM trees and executing JavaScript code on client machines
Storing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript source files directly on edge web servers
Translating human-readable domain names (e.g., example.com) into numerical IP addresses
Encrypting HTTP request payloads before transmission over the public Internet
questions.explanation: DNS acts as the Internet's address book, translating domain names like 'google.com' into machine-routable IP addresses like '142.250.190.46'.

questions.question: Which default TCP port numbers are standard for unencrypted HTTP and encrypted HTTPS traffic, respectively?
options: Port 22 for HTTP and Port 80 for HTTPS
Port 80 for HTTP and Port 443 for HTTPS
Port 21 for HTTP and Port 443 for HTTPS
Port 8080 for HTTP and Port 8443 for HTTPS
questions.explanation: Standard web protocols use TCP port 80 for standard HTTP traffic and port 443 for SSL/TLS encrypted HTTPS traffic.

questions.question: In the TCP 3-way handshake used to establish a reliable connection between client and server, what is the exact order of packet flags sent?
options: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
PING -> PONG -> ACK
ACK -> SYN -> SYN-ACK
SYN -> ACK -> FIN
questions.explanation: The TCP handshake begins with the client sending a SYN packet, the server replying with SYN-ACK, and the client confirming with an ACK packet before data transmission begins.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is considered both safe (does not alter server state) and idempotent (multiple identical requests yield the same outcome)?
options: GET
POST
CONNECT
PATCH
questions.explanation: GET and HEAD are both safe and idempotent because retrieving a resource does not modify server state and calling it repeatedly produces identical results without side effects.

questions.question: What does the HTTP status code 304 'Not Modified' indicate to the client?
options: The server encountered a temporary internal error and cannot process the request
The client is unauthorized and must provide valid authentication credentials
The requested resource has not changed since the version specified in the client's cache headers (e.g., If-None-Match / ETag), so the browser should use its cached copy
The requested URL has permanently moved to a new destination URI
questions.explanation: Status code 304 informs the browser that its cached copy of the resource is still fresh based on validation headers (like ETag or If-Modified-Since), saving bandwidth by not resending the response body.

questions.question: Why is HTTP described as a 'stateless' protocol?
options: The protocol cannot send binary data such as images or video streams
Servers are legally prohibited from caching user data across sessions
Each request from a client is treated as completely independent, with the server retaining no memory of past requests by default
Clients must re-establish a brand new TCP connection for every single asset requested
questions.explanation: Statelessness means the server does not retain session context between transactions; state must be maintained explicitly using cookies, tokens, or sessions.

questions.question: Which sequence accurately depicts the Critical Rendering Path executed by a web browser?
options: DOM Construction -> Paint -> Layout -> CSSOM Construction -> Compositing
CSSOM Construction -> Paint -> Render Tree -> Layout -> DOM Construction
HTML parsing -> DOM Construction + CSSOM Construction -> Render Tree -> Layout (Reflow) -> Paint -> Compositing
JavaScript Execution -> Layout -> DOM Construction -> Paint -> CSSOM Construction
questions.explanation: The browser parses HTML to build the DOM and CSS to build the CSSOM, combines them into a Render Tree, computes exact positions in Layout, paints pixels, and composites layers onto screen.

questions.question: What is the key difference between loading an external script with 'async' versus 'defer' in HTML5?
options: 'async' scripts execute as soon as they finish downloading (interrupting HTML parsing), while 'defer' scripts execute only after the entire HTML document is parsed, in order
'defer' executes immediately when encountered, whereas 'async' waits for user interaction
'async' scripts only work for inline scripts, whereas 'defer' is required for external URLs
'defer' scripts block HTML parsing during download, whereas 'async' scripts never download in parallel
questions.explanation: Both attributes download scripts asynchronously in the background, but 'async' runs immediately upon download (potentially blocking parsing), while 'defer' guarantees execution in source order after DOM parsing finishes.

questions.question: What is the primary function of a Reverse Proxy (e.g., Nginx, HAProxy) in web architecture?
options: To inspect and filter outgoing traffic initiated by internal employees within a corporate intranet
To sit in front of web/application servers to handle load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and routing client requests
To compile JavaScript code into native machine code directly on client devices
To replace relational database storage engines with file system caches
questions.explanation: A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers to intercept incoming client requests, performing load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and security filtering.

questions.question: When a browser makes a cross-origin HTTP request with custom headers or methods other than GET/POST/HEAD, what does it send first?
options: A TCP RESET packet to test if the remote firewall is open
A WebSocket upgrade handshake request to verify network latency
A preliminary GET request containing the user's plain-text session cookie
A Preflight request using the HTTP 'OPTIONS' method to check server CORS permissions
questions.explanation: The browser issues a preflight OPTIONS request containing Origin and Access-Control headers to verify if the server permits the cross-origin operation before sending the actual request.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code series represents Client Errors, such as malformed requests, unauthorized access, or non-existent routes?
questions.explanation: 4xx status codes indicate client-side errors (e.g., 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found).

questions.question: What is the key advantage of WebSockets over traditional HTTP polling for real-time bidirectional applications?
options: WebSockets maintain a persistent, full-duplex TCP connection with minimal frame overhead after an initial HTTP handshake
WebSockets do not require any network ports or TCP connections
WebSockets automatically encrypt all data without needing TLS certificates
WebSockets guarantee zero packet loss over unreliable cellular networks
questions.explanation: WebSockets upgrade an HTTP connection to a persistent, bi-directional, full-duplex TCP channel, eliminating the latency and overhead of continuous HTTP request/response cycles.

questions.question: What HTTP header does a server send to tell the browser not to cache a response under any circumstances?
options: Cache-Control: no-store
Cache-Control: max-age=0
Pragma: public
Cache-Control: no-cache
questions.explanation: 'no-store' directs the browser and intermediate proxies never to store any version of the response in cache. 'no-cache' allows caching but forces revalidation before reuse.

questions.question: In the URL 'https://api.example.com:8080/v1/users?role=admin#section2', which component represents the query parameters?
options: api.example.com
role=admin
#section2
questions.explanation: In a URL, the query string follows the '?' symbol (here 'role=admin'), while '#section2' is the fragment/hash identifier.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 regarding request handling?
options: HTTP/2 only supports plain text payloads and disallows binary file transfers
HTTP/2 introduces binary framing and multiplexing, allowing multiple bidirectional streams over a single TCP connection without Head-of-Line blocking at the application layer
HTTP/2 abandons TCP completely and runs exclusively over UDP
HTTP/2 eliminates all request headers to reduce bandwidth consumption
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple requests and responses over a single TCP connection using binary frames, solving HTTP/1.1's application-layer Head-of-Line blocking.

questions.question: What is the role of a Content Delivery Network (CDN) in modern web architecture?
options: Compiling Python or Java backend code into executable binaries on the fly
Preventing all client-side JavaScript execution to enhance security
Managing database transactions and enforcing ACID compliance
Distributing cached static assets across geographically dispersed edge servers to reduce latency and origin server load
questions.explanation: CDNs store static assets (images, stylesheets, scripts) on edge servers located geographically close to users, drastically cutting latency and reducing origin server load.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the difference between an Application Server (e.g., Gunicorn, Uvicorn, Node.js) and a Web Server (e.g., Nginx, Apache)?
options: There is no difference; both terms refer to the exact same software component
Web servers parse SQL queries directly, while application servers handle DNS routing
Application servers only run on mobile phones, whereas web servers only run in physical cloud datacenters
Web servers specialize in serving static files and routing traffic, whereas application servers execute dynamic server-side application logic and database interactions
questions.explanation: Web servers (Nginx/Apache) handle static files, SSL termination, and reverse proxy routing, while application servers execute dynamic programming logic (Python/Django/Node.js).

questions.question: Which HTTP status code is returned when a server acting as a gateway or proxy receives an invalid or no response from an upstream server?
options: 504 Gateway Timeout
502 Bad Gateway
500 Internal Server Error
404 Not Found
questions.explanation: 502 Bad Gateway occurs when an intermediary proxy (like Nginx) receives an invalid or dropped response from the upstream application server (like Gunicorn/Node).

questions.question: What is the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) enforced by modern web browsers?
options: A rule that forces every web server to share its database credentials with clients
A network restriction preventing a computer from opening multiple browser tabs simultaneously
A core security mechanism that restricts scripts on one origin from accessing or reading sensitive DOM/data on a different origin (protocol, domain, or port mismatch)
A policy requiring all web pages to use the same CSS styling framework
questions.explanation: Same-Origin Policy isolates potentially malicious documents, preventing scripts on `site-a.com` from reading cookies or DOM data belonging to `site-b.com`.

questions.question: How does Server-Side Rendering (SSR) differ from a Client-Side Rendered Single Page Application (SPA)?
options: SSR does not allow the use of any CSS or styling on web pages
SSR runs exclusively on client web browsers without needing any server hardware
SPAs cannot communicate with backend APIs or databases
SSR generates the complete HTML page on the server for each request, whereas SPAs deliver a minimal HTML shell and render UI components dynamically in the browser via JavaScript
questions.explanation: SSR builds full HTML markup on the server before sending it to the client (improving initial page load and SEO), while SPAs download a bundle and build the DOM in the browser via JS.

title: Daily Assessment: HTML5 Document Structure & Semantic Elements
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration at the beginning of an HTML file?
options: To allocate memory in the browser's JavaScript engine before page load
To specify the server-side database schema for web form submissions
To inform the browser that the document is written in HTML5 and ensure standard rendering mode rather than quirks mode
To link external CSS and JavaScript files to the document automatically
questions.explanation: The `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration is a document type declaration that tells modern browsers to render the webpage in standards-compliant mode rather than legacy quirks mode.

questions.question: Which `<meta>` tag is essential inside `<head>` to ensure proper scaling and responsive rendering on mobile devices?
options: <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="mobile=1">
<meta name="responsive" content="true">
<meta name="screen-size" content="device-width">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
questions.explanation: The viewport meta tag instructs mobile browsers to set the viewport width to the device screen width and establish an initial 1:1 zoom ratio.

questions.question: Why should web developers use semantic HTML tags (e.g., `<article>`, `<nav>`, `<header>`) instead of generic `<div>` tags everywhere?
options: Semantic tags encrypt all textual content to prevent web scraping
Semantic tags convey structural meaning to search engines, assistive technologies (screen readers), and improve code maintainability
Semantic tags automatically apply modern CSS grid styling without writing any CSS
Browsers execute JavaScript 50% faster when semantic elements are present
questions.explanation: Semantic HTML provides contextual meaning to both search engines (SEO) and accessibility tools (screen readers), making pages accessible and structured.

questions.question: According to HTML5 specifications, how many `<main>` elements should be visible and unique within a single document?
options: As many as desired, with one inside every `<section>` and `<article>`
Exactly one `<main>` element representing the dominant central content of the document
At least two: one for desktop view and one for mobile view
Zero, because `<main>` has been deprecated in HTML5 in favor of `<div id='main'>`
questions.explanation: The `<main>` element represents the dominant content unique to that document and must not be duplicated or nested inside `<article>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>`, `<header>`, or `<nav>`.

questions.question: What is the primary semantic distinction between the `<article>` and `<section>` elements in HTML5?
options: `<article>` is meant for self-contained, independently distributable content (e.g., a blog post or tweet), whereas `<section>` groups thematic content typically with a heading
`<article>` can only contain plain text, whereas `<section>` can only contain images
`<article>` creates a sidebar layout, whereas `<section>` creates full-width containers
`<section>` is used exclusively for page headers, whereas `<article>` is used exclusively for footers
questions.explanation: An `<article>` represents an independent, reusable composition (like a blog post, comment, or product card), whereas a `<section>` represents a standalone generic section of a document grouped by theme.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is most appropriate for sidebar content, callout boxes, or related links that are tangentially related to the surrounding content?
options: <aside>
<appendix>
<sidebar>
<section type='side'>
questions.explanation: The `<aside>` element represents content tangentially related to the main content around it, such as sidebars, pull quotes, or advertising units.

questions.question: Which element pair is semantically designed to group an illustrative image or code snippet together with its descriptive caption?
options: and
<media> and <caption>
<figure> and <figcaption>
<picture> and <label>
questions.explanation: The `<figure>` element encapsulates self-contained content (like diagrams, photos, or code snippets), and `<figcaption>` provides its associated caption.

questions.question: What is the difference in semantic meaning between `<strong>` vs `<b>`, and `<em>` vs `<i>`?
options: There is no difference in semantics or accessibility between these pairs
`<strong>` and `<em>` convey importance and linguistic emphasis (read with stress by screen readers), while `<b>` and `<i>` represent stylistic bolding/italics without extra semantic importance
`<strong>` and `<em>` are deprecated legacy tags, whereas `<b>` and `<i>` are modern HTML5 elements
`<b>` and `<i>` trigger bold and italic fonts in CSS, while `<strong>` and `<em>` only work in HTML tables
questions.explanation: `<strong>` signifies strong importance/urgency, and `<em>` indicates verbal stress emphasis. `<b>` and `<i>` merely apply typographic style without implying structural weight to assistive tech.

questions.question: When creating external links with `target="_blank"`, why is it a security best practice to add `rel="noopener noreferrer"`?
options: To prevent the newly opened target page from accessing the opening window object via `window.opener` (preventing tabnabbing attacks)
To prevent search engines from indexing the current website
To force the browser to download the linked webpage as a local PDF file
To disable all CSS styling on the linked external webpage
questions.explanation: Without `rel="noopener"`, the destination page gains a reference to `window.opener` and can manipulate the original tab's location (reverse tabnabbing exploit).

questions.question: Which of the following represents a correct, accessible HTML heading hierarchy structure?
questions.explanation: Headings must follow a logical sequential order without skipping levels downward (e.g., from `<h1>` directly to `<h4>`), allowing screen readers to construct a meaningful outline.

questions.question: Which HTML tag structure is used to create a Description List (glossary or key-value list)?
options: <ol type='desc'> containing <item> and <val>
<ul> containing <li> with nested <label> and <text>
<dictionary> containing <key> and <value>
<dl> containing pairs of <dt> (term) and <dd> (description)
questions.explanation: A description list is declared with `<dl>`, enclosing term items (`<dt>`) and their corresponding definitions or descriptions (`<dd>`).

questions.question: Which HTML entity should be used to display the literal character '<' in webpage text without triggering HTML parser tag errors?
options: <
&lessthan;
&
>
questions.explanation: `<` stands for 'less than' (`<`), while `>` is 'greater than' (`>`), and `&` is the ampersand (`&`).

questions.question: What is the proper attribute syntax in HTML5 to store private custom data directly on an HTML element for JavaScript consumption?
options: custom-* (e.g., custom-user-id="42")
meta-* (e.g., meta-user-id="42")
data-* (e.g., data-user-id="42")
var-* (e.g., var-user-id="42")
questions.explanation: HTML5 specifies the `data-*` prefix for embedding custom data attributes on standard elements, accessible via JavaScript's `element.dataset` property.

questions.question: Which boolean HTML5 global attribute completely hides an element from both visual display and screen reader accessibility trees?
options: invisible
display-none
aria-hide
hidden
questions.explanation: The `hidden` attribute specifies that an element is not yet, or is no longer, relevant, hiding it visually and from assistive technologies (similar to `display: none`).

questions.question: What does the `lang="en"` attribute on the root `<html>` element accomplish?
options: It restricts users from typing non-English characters into input forms
It sets the character encoding of the database server to English UTF-8
It automatically translates any foreign words on the webpage into English
It informs browsers, search engines, and screen readers of the primary natural language of the document for correct pronunciation and indexing
questions.explanation: The `lang` attribute declares the base natural language of the text, enabling screen readers to load correct pronunciation engines and assisting search engines.

questions.question: Which element is used to highlight or mark text for reference purposes due to its relevance in another context (e.g., search results)?
options: <spotlight>
<yellow>
<highlight>
<mark>
questions.explanation: The `<mark>` tag represents text marked or highlighted for reference or notation purposes, typically due to its relevance in a search query or user action.

questions.question: Which Open Graph `<meta>` property is used by social platforms (LinkedIn, Facebook, Discord) to display a preview thumbnail when a link is shared?
options: <meta name="preview-img" content="https://example.com/banner.png">
<meta name="thumbnail" content="https://example.com/banner.png">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/banner.png">
<meta property="social:poster" content="https://example.com/banner.png">
questions.explanation: The Open Graph protocol defines `og:image` as the standardized property for social share thumbnail previews.

questions.question: What is the semantic role of the `<time>` element in HTML5?
options: To pause JavaScript execution for a specified number of seconds
To measure the network latency and loading speed of the current webpage
To represent a specific period in time or a timestamp in a machine-readable format using the `datetime` attribute
To display an animated real-time countdown clock in the browser toolbar
questions.explanation: The `<time>` element represents time or date data, providing a machine-readable ISO format via the `datetime` attribute (e.g., `<time datetime="2026-09-11">`).

questions.question: Which of the following is a classic inline element by default in HTML?
options: <span>
<section>
<div>
questions.explanation:
`` is an inline element that only occupies the width necessary for its content and does not break onto a new line, unlike block elements (`
`, `

`, `

`).

questions.question: Which attribute can be added to an HTML element to allow users to directly edit its text content directly in the browser?
options: interactive="text"
contenteditable="true"
allow-input="true"
user-editable="true"
questions.explanation: The global `contenteditable` attribute transforms any HTML element into a rich-text editable region in the browser.

title: Daily Assessment: HTML Forms, Input Types, & Client-Side Validation
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI
lessonTitle: HTML Forms, Input Types, & Client-Side Validation

questions.question: Which `<form>` attribute specifies the MIME type encoding used when submitting forms containing binary files?
options: enctype="binary/octet-stream"
enctype="text/plain"
enctype="application/x-www-form-urlencoded"
enctype="multipart/form-data"
questions.explanation: When uploading files via `<input type="file">`, the form must use `method="POST"` and `enctype="multipart/form-data"` so the browser splits inputs into MIME parts.

questions.question: How do you correctly bind an explicit `<label>` to an `<input>` element for maximum accessibility?
options: Set the `<label>`'s `name` attribute equal to the `<input>`'s `name` attribute
Set the `<label>`'s `for` attribute equal to the `<input>` element's `id` attribute
Set the `<label>`'s `id` attribute equal to the `<input>`'s `placeholder` attribute
Set the `<label>`'s `href` attribute to point to the input's CSS class name
questions.explanation: Binding `label for="xyz"` to `input id="xyz"` ensures screen readers announce the label when the input receives focus, and clicking the label focuses the input.

questions.question: What happens when a form control has the `disabled` attribute compared to the `readonly` attribute upon form submission?
options: Both `disabled` and `readonly` fields are submitted normally with empty values
Fields with `readonly` are omitted from submission, while `disabled` fields are submitted
Fields with `disabled` are omitted from the form submission payload, while fields with `readonly` are included and sent
Neither `disabled` nor `readonly` fields can ever be inspected via JavaScript DOM
questions.explanation: A `disabled` input is ignored during form submission (not submitted in the payload), whereas a `readonly` input prevents user edits but submits its value.

questions.question: Which HTML5 input attribute enforces client-side validation using a regular expression pattern?
options: validate
pattern
regex
match
questions.explanation: The `pattern` attribute accepts a JavaScript regular expression (e.g., `pattern="[0-9]{10}"`) that the input's value must match before submission.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element provides pre-defined autocomplete options for an `<input>` field while still allowing custom user input?
options: <datalist>
<select>
<autocomplete>
<optgroup>
questions.explanation: A `<datalist>` contains a set of `<option>` elements connected to an `<input list="listId">`, offering suggested autocomplete options without restricting custom entries.

questions.question: How do you group multiple radio buttons together so that selecting one automatically deselects the others?
options: Give all radio buttons in the group the exact same `name` attribute
Give all radio buttons the exact same `id` attribute
Wrap each radio button in the same `<fieldset>` without any names
Set their `type` attribute to `type="radio-group"`
questions.explanation: Radio buttons sharing the same `name` attribute belong to a mutual exclusion group where only one radio button can be checked at a time.

questions.question: Which elements are used to semantically group related form controls together with a visible title or caption?
options: <section> and <caption>
<group> and <title>
<fieldset> and <legend>
<formgroup> and <label>
questions.explanation: The `<fieldset>` element groups related controls in a form, and `<legend>` provides an accessible caption for the fieldset container.

questions.question: What is the default `type` attribute of a `<button>` element placed inside a `<form>` if none is specified?
options: type="menu"
type="reset"
type="submit"
type="button"
questions.explanation: By default, standard `<button>` elements inside a form have `type="submit"`. If you want a button to not submit the form, you must explicitly set `type="button"`.

questions.question: Which HTML5 input type provides a slider control for selecting a numerical value within a bounded range?
options: <input type="number-bar">
<input type="scroll">
<input type="range">
<input type="slider">
questions.explanation: `<input type="range">` renders a slider control allowing the user to select an imprecise or bounded numeric value between `min` and `max`.

questions.question: What does the `novalidate` attribute on a `<form>` element do?
options: It converts all POST requests into GET requests automatically
It bypasses the browser's native HTML5 client-side validation constraints upon submission
It disables all server-side validation checks on backend API endpoints
It prevents the user from typing special characters into any text field
questions.explanation: Adding `novalidate` to `<form>` suppresses browser built-in popup constraint validation messages, useful when handling validation entirely through custom JavaScript.

questions.question: Which HTML element is semantically designed to display the calculated result of a user action or form calculation?
options: <output>
<calc>
<computed>
<result>
questions.explanation: The `<output>` element represents the calculation result from script operations or form calculations (e.g., dynamic pricing or range sliders).

questions.question: Which attribute allows an `<input type="file">` element to accept only JPEG and PNG image files?
questions.codeSnippet: <input type="file">
options: extensions=".jpeg, .png"
filter="*.jpg, *.png"
type-restrict="images"
accept="image/jpeg, image/png"
questions.explanation: The `accept` attribute specifies a comma-separated list of allowed file types or MIME types that the operating system file picker will filter.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `step` attribute on numerical and date inputs?
options: It controls the animation speed of form transition effects
It defines how many times a form can be submitted before timing out
It determines the tab order when a user presses the Tab key
It specifies the legal number intervals or increments that the input value can jump by (e.g., step="0.01" for currency)
questions.explanation: The `step` attribute defines valid numeric increments (e.g., `step="5"` allows 0, 5, 10, etc., and `step="0.01"` allows cents in financial inputs).

questions.question: Why is client-side HTML5 form validation alone never sufficient for web application security?
options: Modern web browsers charge licensing fees for verifying form constraints
HTML5 input validation only works when the client is disconnected from the Internet
Client-side validation causes severe memory leaks in the browser's DOM parser
Client-side validation can easily be bypassed, modified, or disabled by attackers using developer tools or direct API requests (e.g., curl/Postman)
questions.explanation: Client validation improves user experience, but server-side validation is strictly mandatory because anyone can send raw HTTP requests directly to backend endpoints.

questions.question: Which JavaScript method on an HTML form element can be called to trigger native constraint validation checks programmatically?
options: checkValidity()
verifyForm()
isFormCorrect()
testValidation()
questions.explanation: The Constraint Validation API method `element.checkValidity()` returns `true` if an element satisfies all its validation constraints, or `false` otherwise.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between `<progress>` and `<meter>` elements?
options: `<progress>` represents task completion progress toward a goal, while `<meter>` represents a scalar measurement within a known range (e.g., disk usage, battery level)
`<progress>` only supports binary yes/no states, while `<meter>` supports text inputs
`<meter>` is used for music volume, while `<progress>` is used exclusively for video streaming
There is no difference; both are interchangeable synonyms in HTML5
questions.explanation: `<progress>` indicates completion percentage of an ongoing task, while `<meter>` represents a scalar gauge measurement within a known range (like disk space or temperature).

questions.question: What autocomplete attribute value is recommended for password fields to assist password managers when a user registers a new account?
options: autocomplete="current-password"
autocomplete="generate"
autocomplete="new-password"
autocomplete="create-pass"
questions.explanation: `autocomplete="new-password"` prompts password managers to generate and store a secure strong password instead of autofilling existing credentials.

questions.question: How are form values transmitted when a `<form>` uses `method="GET"`?
options: Sent over a separate background WebSocket channel
Stored in local browser cookies and never transmitted over the network
Included as an encrypted JSON binary payload in the HTTP request body
Appended directly to the destination URL as URI-encoded key-value query parameters
questions.explanation: Forms with `method="GET"` encode input names and values as query parameters in the URL (e.g., `/search?q=term`), making them bookmarkable but visible in browser history.

questions.question: What is the purpose of including a hidden input field (`<input type="hidden">`) with a CSRF token in server-rendered forms?
questions.codeSnippet: <input type="hidden">
options: To compress images uploaded by the user before network transmission
To protect the application against Cross-Site Request Forgery by ensuring the form submission originated from an authenticated session on the trusted site
To bypass HTTPS encryption overhead on local development servers
To store the user's plain-text credit card number securely in the browser cache
questions.explanation: CSRF tokens stored in hidden inputs validate that the request was generated by the actual authenticated user and not forged by a malicious third-party site.

questions.question: Which attribute can be set on an input to automatically focus it when the webpage finishes loading?
options: auto-select
autofocus
default-focus
active
questions.explanation: The `autofocus` boolean attribute instructs the browser to place keyboard focus on that specific form control upon initial page load.

title: Daily Assessment: HTML Tables, Media Tags & Accessibility
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `scope` attribute on a `<th>` (table header) element?
options: It controls whether a table row is rendered on desktop or mobile devices
It explicitly associates header cells with their corresponding columns (`scope="col"`) or rows (`scope="row"`) for screen readers
It defines the CSS border-radius and background color gradient of the cell
It limits the number of characters that a user can type into table cells
questions.explanation: The `scope` attribute (`col`, `row`, `colgroup`, `rowgroup`) provides clear contextual association between header cells and data cells for assistive technologies.

questions.question: Which HTML attribute is used to make a single table cell span across 3 columns horizontally?
options: span-col="3"
col-width="3"
rowspan="3"
colspan="3"
questions.explanation: `colspan="3"` causes a `<td>` or `<th>` cell to extend across 3 horizontal columns, while `rowspan` merges cells vertically across rows.

questions.question: Which table element pair is used to apply shared styles or attributes to entire columns without repeating classes on every individual `<td>`?
options: <tablegrid> and <gridcol>
<columns> and <column>
<colgroup> and <col>
<thead-cols> and <th-col>
questions.explanation: The `<colgroup>` element and its nested `<col>` child elements allow styling and attribute definitions across vertical table columns.

questions.question: Why should every content image (``) have a descriptive `alt` attribute?
options: To provide alternative text for visually impaired users using screen readers and as a fallback if the image fails to load
To force search engine crawlers to download high-resolution copies of the image
To display an animated tooltip popup when the user hovers their mouse over the image
To prevent unauthorized users from downloading the image via right-click
questions.explanation: The `alt` attribute is vital for accessibility (read aloud by screen readers), SEO indexing, and graceful fallbacks when image requests fail or are slow.

questions.question: What should the `alt` attribute contain for a purely decorative image that conveys no informative meaning (e.g., decorative divider lines)?
options: alt="null"
alt="decorative image"
alt="" (an empty alt attribute)
Omit the alt attribute completely from the tag
questions.explanation: An empty `alt=""` tells screen readers to ignore the decorative image completely. Omitting the `alt` tag entirely is an accessibility error that causes screen readers to announce the raw file URL.

questions.question: Which modern attribute on an `` element enables native browser-level deferred loading until the image is near the viewport?
options: defer="true"
loading="lazy"
fetch="deferred"
preload="none"
questions.explanation: `loading="lazy"` instructs the browser to defer loading images that are below the fold until the user scrolls near them, saving initial bandwidth.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is specifically designed for 'Art Direction' and serving different image sources based on media query conditions?
options: <image-group> with CSS background rules
containing multiple elements and an fallback
<canvas> with WebGL responsive shaders
<svg-responsive> with embedded bitmaps
questions.explanation: The `` element wraps multiple `` tags alongside a fallback ``, allowing developers to serve different crops or formats (e.g., AVIF/WebP) per screen size.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the `<track>` element inside `<video>` or `<audio>` tags?
options: To adjust playback volume and bass equalizer frequencies automatically
To prevent unauthorized video screen recording on client browsers
To track user watch time and send analytics data to marketing platforms
To specify timed text tracks such as subtitles, closed captions, or audio descriptions (using WebVTT format)
questions.explanation: The `<track>` element attaches timed text streams (like `.vtt` subtitles or captions) with attributes like `kind="subtitles"` and `srclang="en"`.

questions.question: Which attribute is required on an `<iframe>` element to ensure screen reader accessibility?
options: title="Descriptive title of frame content"
caption="Summary"
alt="Description"
aria-frame="true"
questions.explanation: WCAG guidelines require every `<iframe>` to have a clear, descriptive `title` attribute so screen reader users understand what content the embedded frame contains before focusing it.

questions.question: What does the `sandbox` attribute on an `<iframe>` element accomplish?
options: It limits the CPU and RAM allocation of the embedded page to exactly 10MB
It renders the embedded webpage in a high-contrast black-and-white theme
It forces the iframe to load only from localhost testing servers
It applies strict security restrictions (disabling scripts, popups, form submissions, and same-origin access) unless explicitly re-enabled with tokens
questions.explanation: The `sandbox` attribute heavily restricts untrusted third-party iframe content by disabling scripts, forms, popups, and same-origin cookies unless explicit exceptions like `allow-scripts` are added.

questions.question: What is the key technical difference between `<svg>` and `<canvas>` in HTML5?
options: `<canvas>` files are stored in XML format, while `<svg>` is rendered strictly with WebGL
`<svg>` cannot be styled with CSS, whereas `<canvas>` styles are written exclusively in CSS
`<svg>` can only be rendered with server-side plugins, while `<canvas>` is supported natively
`<svg>` is vector-based, retains a searchable/styleable DOM node structure, and scales infinitely without pixelation; `<canvas>` is a raster/pixel-based immediate-mode drawing surface
questions.explanation: SVG is an XML-based vector format where every element is part of the DOM tree and scales losslessly. Canvas is a raster surface manipulated via JavaScript pixel drawing APIs.

questions.question: What are the four core accessibility principles defined by the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)?
options: POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust
REST: Representational, Encapsulated, Stateless, Tiered
CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete
FAST: Functional, Accessible, Scalable, Trustworthy
questions.explanation: WCAG is structured around the four foundational POUR principles: Perceivable (users can perceive content), Operable (UI components are operable), Understandable (info is clear), and Robust (content works across tools).

questions.question: What is the foundational 'First Rule of ARIA' in web development?
options: If you can use a native HTML5 element or attribute with the semantics and behavior you require, use it instead of repurposing an element with ARIA
Every single `<div>` must have an ARIA landmark attribute attached
Always add `role="button"` to every `<button>` element to ensure full compatibility
ARIA attributes should only be written in uppercase letters
questions.explanation: The First Rule of ARIA states: If a native HTML element (like `<button>`, `<nav>`, `<dialog>`) already has built-in semantic behavior and keyboard support, never replace it with a `<div>` styled with ARIA roles.

questions.question: What does `aria-hidden="true"` do to an HTML element?
options: It disables all mouse click and hover events on the element
It hides the element and all its children from assistive technologies (screen readers) while keeping it visually visible on screen
It applies CSS `display: none` to hide the element completely from screen and accessibility trees
It encrypts the text content inside the element so search engines ignore it
