questions.explanation: `aria-hidden="true"` strips the element from the accessibility tree (useful for decorative icons accompanying visible text) without affecting visual layout.

questions.question: What is the accessibility impact of assigning `tabindex="0"` to a custom element (like a `<div>`)?
questions.codeSnippet: to a custom element (like a
options: It forces the element to be the very first focused element when the page loads
It turns the element into an automatic submit button for forms
It inserts the element into the natural keyboard tab navigation order and makes it focusable via the Tab key
It permanently removes the element from keyboard navigation entirely
questions.explanation: `tabindex="0"` places an element into the sequential keyboard navigation flow. `tabindex="-1"` makes it focusable only via JavaScript, while positive tabindex values are discouraged as an anti-pattern.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an 'aria-live' region (e.g., `aria-live="polite"`) in dynamic web applications?
options: It instructs screen readers to announce dynamic content updates (like notifications or status messages) without requiring page reloads
It measures the user's typing speed inside form inputs
It streams real-time audio and video directly through the user's microphone
It forces the browser to refresh the webpage every 5 seconds
questions.explanation: An `aria-live` region notifies assistive technologies of live DOM updates. `aria-live="polite"` waits until the user is idle, while `aria-live="assertive"` interrupts current speech.

questions.question: Why is anchor text like 'Click Here' or 'Read More' considered poor for web accessibility?
options: It increases the file size of the HTML document unnecessarily
It prevents search engines from caching the destination URL
It triggers spam filters in modern web browsers
It lacks meaningful context when screen reader users navigate through an extracted list of all links on a page
questions.explanation: Screen reader users frequently navigate pages using link lists out of context; descriptive text (e.g., 'View Python Full Stack Syllabus') clarifies the destination, whereas 'Click here' is meaningless alone.

questions.question: What is the purpose of providing a 'Skip to Content' link at the top of a webpage?
options: To load the page in low-bandwidth mode by omitting all images and videos
To allow keyboard-only and screen reader users to bypass repetitive header navigation menus and jump directly to main content
To close the current browser window quickly using keyboard shortcuts
To automatically skip past all paywalls on news subscription websites
questions.explanation: A skip link allows keyboard and screen reader users to jump over large navigation headers straight to `<main id="main-content">`, saving significant tabbing effort.

questions.question: Which image format is modern, open-source, and provides superior lossless and lossy compression compared to JPEG and PNG for web delivery?
options: ICO
TIFF
AVIF / WebP
BMP
questions.explanation: Modern formats like WebP and AVIF offer 30-50%+ better compression efficiency than legacy JPEG/PNG while supporting alpha transparency and animations.

questions.question: What does the `playsinline` boolean attribute on a mobile `<video>` element do?
options: It restricts playback exclusively to inline CSS keyframe animations
It embeds the video as an inline base64 string inside the HTML document
It allows video to play directly within the webpage layout on mobile devices (e.g., iOS Safari) instead of automatically forcing fullscreen mode
It forces the video to loop indefinitely with subtitles enabled
questions.explanation: `playsinline` tells mobile browsers (notably iOS Safari) to play the video inline inside the document flow rather than automatically launching a fullscreen media player.

title: Daily Assessment: CSS Syntax, Rules, and Element/Class/ID Selectors

lessonTitle: CSS Syntax, Rules, and Element/Class/ID Selectors

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the 4-part specificity weight calculation for standard CSS selectors (Inline, ID, Class/Attribute/Pseudo-class, Element/Pseudo-element)?
options: Universal selector * (1,0,0,0) > ID (0,1,0,0) > Class (0,0,1,0) > Element (0,0,0,1)
Inline styles (1,0,0,0) > ID (#id: 0,1,0,0) > Class/Attribute/Pseudo-class (.class, [attr], :hover: 0,0,1,0) > Element/Pseudo-element (div, ::after: 0,0,0,1)
ID (1,0,0,0) > Inline styles (0,1,0,0) > Element (0,0,1,0) > Class (0,0,0,1)
questions.explanation: CSS Specificity is calculated as a 4-tier vector (a, b, c, d): Inline styles = (1,0,0,0), ID selectors = (0,1,0,0), Classes/Attributes/Pseudo-classes = (0,0,1,0), and Elements/Pseudo-elements = (0,0,0,1).

questions.question: What is the specificity weight of the universal selector (`*`) in CSS?
options: 0,0,0,1 (Equivalent to a standard HTML tag name selector)
0,0,0,0 (Zero specificity, easily overridden by any element, class, or ID selector)
1,0,0,0 (Highest priority across all selectors)
0,1,0,0 (Equivalent to an ID selector)
questions.explanation: The universal selector (`*`) has a specificity value of (0,0,0,0); it matches every element but contributes zero specificity points to the calculation.

questions.question:
Which combinator selector matches only paragraphs (`

`) that are direct, immediate children of a `

` element?
options: div + p
div p
div > p
div ~ p
questions.explanation: The child combinator (`>`) targets direct children only, whereas the descendant combinator (space) targets all descendants regardless of nesting depth.

questions.question: What does the adjacent sibling combinator `h2 + p` select in an HTML document?
options:
A `

` element that is placed immediately after an `

` element sharing the exact same parent

Every `

` element that follows an `

` at any point within the same parent container

Both the `

` and `

` elements merged together into a single flexbox item

All `

` elements located anywhere inside the preceding `

` element
questions.explanation: The adjacent sibling combinator (`+`) matches an element only if it immediately follows the specified element and both share the same parent.

questions.question: Which attribute selector matches elements whose `href` attribute begins exactly with 'https://'?
options: a[href~="https://"]
a[href^="https://"]
a[href$="https://"]
a[href*="https://"]
questions.explanation: `^=` matches values that start with the specified string, `$=` matches values that end with the string, and `*=` matches substrings appearing anywhere.

questions.question: What is the difference between the pseudo-classes `:nth-child(2)` and `:nth-of-type(2)` when applied to `p:nth-child(2)` vs `p:nth-of-type(2)`?
questions.codeSnippet: :nth-of-type(2)
options:
`p:nth-child(2)` selects the element only if it is the 2nd overall child of its parent and is a `

`, whereas `p:nth-of-type(2)` selects the 2nd `

` among all paragraph siblings regardless of other elements
`p:nth-of-type(2)` requires an explicit `class` attribute, whereas `:nth-child(2)` does not
`p:nth-child(2)` only counts even numbered elements, while `p:nth-of-type(2)` counts odd elements
There is no difference; modern CSS treats them as interchangeable aliases
questions.explanation: `:nth-child(n)` checks the element's index among all siblings regardless of tag type, while `:nth-of-type(n)` filters siblings by the specific element tag type first before indexing.

questions.question: Which property is strictly required when declaring pseudo-elements `::before` or `::after` for them to render on the page?
options: visibility
position
content
display
questions.explanation: Pseudo-elements `::before` and `::after` will not render in the document tree unless the `content` property is explicitly defined (even as an empty string `content: '';`).

questions.question: How does the pseudo-class `:is()` differ from `:where()` in modern CSS?
options: `:is()` adopts the specificity of its most specific argument in the selector list, whereas `:where()` always has zero specificity (0,0,0,0)
`:where()` only works on desktop browsers, while `:is()` is mobile-only
`:is()` is strictly case-sensitive, whereas `:where()` ignores letter casing
`:where()` can only contain element selectors, while `:is()` can only contain IDs
questions.explanation: Both `:is()` and `:where()` simplify complex selector lists, but `:where()` always strips specificity to (0,0,0,0), making it ideal for easy CSS resets and base design systems.

questions.question: Which of the following CSS properties is inherited by child elements by default?
options: padding
background-color
border
font-family
questions.explanation: Typography and textual properties (like `color`, `font-family`, `font-size`, `line-height`, `letter-spacing`) inherit automatically, while box model properties (`margin`, `padding`, `border`, `background`) do not.

questions.question: What does setting a CSS property value to `initial` do?
options: It resets the property to the official W3C CSS specification default value, regardless of browser user-agent styles or parent inheritance
It forces the property to take the exact value computed by its immediate parent container
It makes the property inherit values from the `<body>` element only
It restores the value that was saved in the browser's local storage session
questions.explanation: The `initial` keyword sets a property to its default value as defined in the CSS specification (e.g., `color: initial` becomes `black`, `display: initial` becomes `inline`).

questions.question: How do you declare and access a CSS Custom Property (CSS variable) correctly?
options: Declare with `var:` prefix (e.g., `var:brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `#brand-blue;`
Declare with `$` prefix (e.g., `$brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `val($brand-blue);`
Declare with `--` prefix (e.g., `--brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `var(--brand-blue, #000);`
Declare with `@` prefix (e.g., `@brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `get(@brand-blue);`
questions.explanation: CSS variables are defined on any selector (often `:root`) with a `--` prefix and retrieved using the `var(--custom-property-name, fallback)` function.

questions.question: When two CSS rules have identical specificity and target the exact same element, how does the cascade determine which rule applies?
options: The rule that appears last in the stylesheet source order wins (Source Order rule)
The rule with the shorter property name is selected automatically
The browser randomly picks one rule during DOM construction
The rule declared in an external stylesheet always overrides internal styles regardless of order
questions.explanation: In the CSS Cascade algorithm, when origin, importance, and specificity are equal, the declaration appearing last in the stylesheet source order takes precedence.

questions.question: What is the primary performance drawback of using `@import` inside a CSS file compared to `<link rel="stylesheet">` in HTML?
options: `@import` disables all JavaScript execution on modern mobile web browsers
`@import` creates sequential waterfall network requests by waiting for the parent stylesheet to download before initiating child downloads
`@import` converts CSS colors to low-resolution monochrome gradients
`@import` files are completely ignored by search engine indexing bots
questions.explanation: `<link>` tags allow browsers to discover and download stylesheets in parallel, whereas `@import` delays stylesheet downloads by creating a blocking sequential network waterfall.

questions.question: What does the compound selector `.btn.primary` (without any space between classes) select?
options: Any element with class `primary` that is a descendant inside an element with class `btn`
Any HTML element that possesses both the `btn` class AND the `primary` class simultaneously
Only the first child element located inside the `.btn` container
Any element that has either the `btn` class OR the `primary` class
questions.explanation: Chaining classes without a space (`.btn.primary`) creates a compound selector matching elements that have both classes applied at the same time.

questions.question: Why should the `!important` declaration be avoided in general CSS authoring whenever possible?
options: It incurs monetary server hosting charges for each page render
It prevents browsers from caching CSS files in local storage
It causes browser rendering engines to crash when compiling CSSOM trees
It breaks the natural cascading specificity hierarchy and makes debugging and overriding styles difficult in larger codebases
questions.explanation: `!important` overrides normal specificity rules, creating maintenance headaches because the only way to override an `!important` declaration is another `!important` with higher specificity.

questions.question: Which pseudo-class targets an element when it receives focus specifically via keyboard navigation (such as Tab), while suppressing focus outlines on mouse clicks?
options: :focus
:hover
:active
:focus-visible
questions.explanation: `:focus-visible` applies focus indicators only when the user navigates via keyboard or assistive tech, avoiding unwanted focus rings during mouse clicks.

questions.question: What is the effect of the `:focus-within` pseudo-class?
options: It prevents all child elements within a form from receiving focus
It targets only the very first `<input>` inside an active modal dialog
It matches an element if the element itself OR any of its descendant children currently has keyboard/mouse focus
It matches an input field only when the user is actively typing text inside it
questions.explanation: `:focus-within` allows styling a parent container (like highlighting a whole form group or navigation bar) when any child element inside it gains focus.

questions.question: How does the pseudo-class `:not(.active)` behave on a selector `li:not(.active)`?
options: It hides all `<li>` elements that have the `.active` class using `display: none`
It selects all `<li>` elements that do NOT have the `.active` class applied
It selects only disabled button elements inside an inactive list
It removes the `.active` class from all `<li>` elements in the DOM
questions.explanation: The negation pseudo-class `:not(selector)` matches elements that do not match the selector list provided in its parenthesis.

questions.question: What does the `&` symbol represent in modern native CSS Nesting?
options: A command that forces the browser to recompile CSS into WebAssembly
A logical AND operator that requires two stylesheets to load simultaneously
An escape character used for unicode typography symbols
A nesting selector that explicitly references and represents the parent selector rule
questions.explanation: In modern native CSS nesting, `&` represents the parent selector, allowing modifier classes (e.g., `&.is-open`) and pseudo-classes (e.g., `&:hover`) to be nested cleanly.

questions.question: Which of the following styling approaches has the highest natural specificity according to the CSS cascade specification?
options: An external rule selecting multiple elements `header nav ul li a` (0,0,0,5)
An internal `<style>` tag rule combining three classes `.nav.menu.active` (0,0,3,0)
An external stylesheet rule with an ID selector `#main-header` (0,1,0,0)
Inline styles applied via HTML `style="..."` attribute (1,0,0,0)
questions.explanation: Inline styles have a specificity weight of (1,0,0,0), which naturally overrides any external or internal stylesheet selector unless `!important` is used.

title: Daily Assessment: The CSS Box Model: Margin, Padding, Border, & Content
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI
lessonTitle: The CSS Box Model: Margin, Padding, Border, & Content

questions.question: Under the standard default CSS box model (`box-sizing: content-box`), if an element has `width: 200px`, `padding: 20px`, `border: 5px solid black`, and `margin: 15px`, what is its total rendered horizontal space on the page?
options: 200px total occupied space
240px total occupied space
280px total occupied space (Content 200 + Padding Left/Right 40 + Border Left/Right 10 + Margin Left/Right 30)
250px total occupied space
questions.explanation: Under `content-box`, total horizontal space = Content (200px) + Padding (20px * 2 = 40px) + Border (5px * 2 = 10px) + Margin (15px * 2 = 30px) = 280px. Total element width is 250px.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of setting `box-sizing: border-box` across all elements?
options: It eliminates the need for writing media queries on mobile viewport screens
It disables margin collapse across all nested block elements permanently
The specified `width` and `height` include content, padding, and border, making responsive sizing and layout math predictable
It automatically adds rounded corners and drop shadows to all HTML containers
questions.explanation: With `border-box`, setting `width: 300px` guarantees the element's outer border box is exactly 300px, absorbing padding and border inward rather than expanding outward.

questions.question: What is the standard CSS universal reset snippet used by modern developers to enforce consistent border-box sizing across all elements and pseudo-elements?
options: html { border-box: true; }
body { box-sizing: all; }
:root { sizing: border-box !default; }
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
questions.explanation: Targeting `*`, `*::before`, and `*::after` ensures every element and generated pseudo-element adheres to predictable `border-box` calculations.

questions.question: What occurs during 'Margin Collapse' between two adjacent vertical block-level elements?
options: The vertical margins merge into a single margin equal to the largest individual margin value, rather than adding together
The browser throws a CSS parsing warning and disables padding
The two elements are automatically forced onto the same horizontal line
The bottom element's margin is completely erased and set to 0px
questions.explanation: When adjacent block elements meet vertically, their top and bottom margins collapse into a single margin whose size equals the maximum of the two margins.

questions.question: Under what condition will `margin: 0 auto;` successfully center an element horizontally inside its parent container?
options: The element must have `display: inline` and no explicit width defined
The element must have `position: absolute` with `left: 0`
The element must be a block-level container with a specified, constrained `width` (or `max-width`) less than its parent
The parent container must have `overflow: scroll` enabled
questions.explanation: `margin: 0 auto` divides remaining horizontal space equally between left and right margins, which only works if the block element has an explicit width less than 100%.

questions.question: In the 4-value shorthand `margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px;`, which value corresponds to the left margin?
questions.codeSnippet: margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px;
options: 10px (Top)
40px (Clockwise order: Top=10px, Right=20px, Bottom=30px, Left=40px)
20px (Right)
30px (Bottom)
questions.explanation: CSS 4-value box model shorthands follow a clockwise order: Top, Right, Bottom, Left (often remembered by the acronym TRouBLe).

questions.question: What is the key visual and layout difference between `outline` and `border` in CSS?
options: `outline` increases the total computed width of the element in the DOM
`outline` is only supported on SVG elements, whereas `border` is for HTML
`border` cannot have custom colors, whereas `outline` supports gradients
`outline` is drawn outside the element's border box and does NOT occupy space in the layout flow, so toggling it never causes content layout reflow
questions.explanation: Unlike `border`, an `outline` does not take up box model space or affect element dimensions, making it ideal for focus indicators without triggering layout shifts.

questions.question: What is the behavior of vertical margins (`margin-top` and `margin-bottom`) and vertical padding when applied to a pure inline element (like `<span>` or `<a>`)?
options: Vertical margins and padding push all preceding and succeeding text lines upward and downward identically to block elements
Vertical padding visual background renders but does NOT push surrounding line boxes away, and vertical margins have zero effect on layout spacing
Inline elements ignore all horizontal and vertical margins and padding completely
The browser automatically converts the inline element into `display: block`
questions.explanation: Inline elements only respect horizontal margins and padding for layout flow. Vertical padding will visually overlap adjacent lines without pushing them apart, and vertical margins are ignored.

questions.question: How does `display: inline-block` differ from `display: inline`?
options: `inline-block` allows setting explicit `width`, `height`, and respects top/bottom margins and padding while still sitting inline on the same line with adjacent content
`inline-block` forces the element onto its own brand new line like a `<div>`
`inline-block` is deprecated and behaves identically to `display: none`
`inline-block` disables all background colors and text decoration styling
questions.explanation: `inline-block` elements flow inline horizontally like text, but gain full box model capabilities (explicit `width`, `height`, `margin-top/bottom`, `padding-top/bottom`).

questions.question: What is the difference between `overflow: hidden` and `overflow: clip` in modern CSS?
options: `overflow: hidden` only works on images, whereas `overflow: clip` only works on text
`overflow: hidden` creates a scroll container (allowing programmatic scrolling via JS), whereas `overflow: clip` forbids all scrolling and reduces memory overhead
`overflow: clip` adds a visible scrollbar, while `overflow: hidden` hides the scrollbar
There is no difference; `clip` is just a legacy alias for `hidden`
questions.explanation: `overflow: hidden` prevents user scrolling while still allowing programmatic scrolling (creating a scroll container), whereas `overflow: clip` completely disables scrolling in all forms.

questions.question: What is the difference between `em` and `rem` units in CSS sizing?
options: `rem` is always relative to the root `<html>` font size, whereas `em` is relative to the immediate parent element's font size (which can compound with nesting)
`em` is relative to root font size, while `rem` is relative to viewport height
`rem` only applies to margins, while `em` only applies to font sizes
`em` is fixed to 16px forever, while `rem` changes based on device screen resolution
questions.explanation: `rem` (Root EM) scales consistently relative to the root `<html>` element (default 16px), preventing the nested compounding issue seen with `em` units.

questions.question: What does the CSS viewport unit `100dvh` represent compared to `100vh` on mobile web browsers?
options: `dvh` represents dual-screen display height on foldable smartphones
Dynamic Viewport Height (`dvh`) dynamically adjusts its size as mobile browser UI chrome (address bar and toolbars) expands or collapses during scrolling
`dvh` divides viewport height by device pixel ratio for desktop monitors only
`dvh` is static and ignores mobile browser address bars completely
questions.explanation: `dvh` (Dynamic Viewport Height) adapts in real time to mobile browser UI shifts (like address bar show/hide), resolving the dreaded 100vh overflow clipping bug on mobile.

questions.question: What is the effect of applying a negative margin, such as `margin-top: -20px;`, to an element?
options: It pulls the element 20px upward, overlapping any content situated above it in the layout flow
It collapses the height of the element to zero pixels
It creates 20px of transparent white empty space above the element
It rotates the element 180 degrees vertically
questions.explanation: Negative margins pull the element in the direction of the negative value (or pull subsequent siblings toward itself if applied to bottom/right), allowing deliberate overlapping layouts.

questions.question: What is the syntax order for the `box-shadow` property in CSS?
options: box-shadow: inset color offset-y offset-x spread-radius blur-radius;
box-shadow: color blur-radius spread-radius offset-x offset-y;
box-shadow: spread-radius blur-radius offset-y offset-x inset color;
box-shadow: offset-x offset-y blur-radius spread-radius color inset;
questions.explanation: Standard `box-shadow` syntax takes X-offset, Y-offset, optional blur radius, optional spread radius, color, and optional `inset` keyword.

questions.question: How do you create a perfect circle from a square element of `width: 100px; height: 100px;` using CSS?
questions.codeSnippet:
width: 100px;
height: 100px;
options: clip-path: polygon(0 0, 100% 100%);
border-radius: 50%;
shape-outside: circle(100%);
border-radius: 100px 0 100px 0;
questions.explanation: Setting `border-radius: 50%` curves each corner by half the element's dimension, turning equal width and height squares into perfect circles.

questions.question: What does `width: fit-content;` do to an element's dimensions?
options: It forces the element to stretch across the entire screen regardless of parent width
It sets the width to exactly 0px until an image finishes loading
It sizes the element to shrink-wrap its content up to the available width, without stretching to 100% like a normal block
It resizes the font size until all text fits onto a single horizontal line
questions.explanation: `fit-content` allows an element to expand as needed to fit its contents, but caps its maximum width at the available space in its parent container.

questions.question: How does the CSS `clamp()` function work for responsive dimensions (e.g., `width: clamp(300px, 50vw, 800px);`)?
questions.codeSnippet: function work for responsive dimensions (e.g.,
options: It sets a preferred value (`50vw`) that can scale dynamically, but guarantees the value will never drop below `300px` or exceed `800px`
It restricts the element's width to exactly 300px on mobile and 800px on tablet
It calculates the average of the three numbers and sets a fixed pixel width
It rotates through the three values at 1-second animation intervals
questions.explanation: `clamp(MIN, PREFERRED, MAX)` clamps a scalable value between an absolute minimum floor and maximum ceiling, eliminating messy media query breakpoints.

questions.question: What happens when an element with `width: 100%` is given `margin: 20px` inside a parent container under default `content-box`?
options: The margins are ignored completely because width is 100%
The parent container automatically expands to fit the margin without scrolling
The browser automatically reduces the width to 80% to compensate
The element overflows its parent container horizontally by 40px, causing unwanted horizontal scrollbars
questions.explanation: Under `content-box`, `100% width + 40px margin` exceeds the 100% boundary of the parent, spilling out and causing horizontal overflow.

questions.question: Which CSS mathematical function allows combining different measurement units in a single calculation (e.g., subtracting a fixed pixel sidebar from a percentage width)?
options: eval()
sum()
calc() (e.g., width: calc(100% - 250px);)
compute()
questions.explanation: The `calc()` function performs dynamic mathematical operations across mixed units, such as subtracting fixed pixel dimensions (`250px`) from relative percentages (`100%`).

questions.question: Why does vertical margin collapsing not occur between flex items or grid items?
options: Margin collapsing only works when using CSS tables
Browsers convert all margins to padding inside flex containers automatically
Flexbox and Grid items do not support any margin properties
The CSS Flexbox and Grid formatting contexts explicitly establish independent formatting roots that disable standard vertical block margin collapse
questions.explanation: Margins between flex items and grid items never collapse; their margins always stack additively because they operate in flex/grid formatting contexts rather than block formatting contexts.

title: Daily Assessment: CSS Colors, Typography, & Visual Backgrounds
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is the key difference between setting opacity via `opacity: 0.5` versus setting a semi-transparent background via `background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5)`?
options: `opacity: 0.5` only affects text color, leaving backgrounds fully opaque
`rgba()` disables all mouse click events on the element, while `opacity` does not
`opacity: 0.5` makes the target element AND all of its nested child elements semi-transparent, whereas `rgba()` only makes the background color semi-transparent
There is no difference; modern browsers treat them as identical rendering commands
questions.explanation: The `opacity` property affects the entire rendered stacking context including all child text and icons, whereas `rgba()` or `hsla()` only applies alpha transparency to the specific color property.

questions.question: What does the `currentcolor` keyword in CSS represent?
options: It queries the user's desktop wallpaper palette in modern browsers
It returns the default background color of the operating system window
It converts the closest hex color code into a web-safe RGB format
It references the computed value of the element's current `color` property, allowing borders, SVGs, or shadows to match text color dynamically
questions.explanation: `currentcolor` acts as a built-in CSS variable representing the value of the `color` property on that element (or inherited from its parent), commonly used in SVG fills and borders.

questions.question: Why is it considered a best practice to define a 'fallback font stack' (e.g., `font-family: 'Inter', Roboto, -apple-system, sans-serif;`)?
options: It allows the browser to download all four fonts simultaneously to increase rendering speed
If the user's browser fails to load or find the custom primary font, it gracefully falls back to available local system fonts rather than rendering broken characters
It is required by web hosting servers to validate font licensing certificates
It enables multiple languages to display simultaneously inside the same sentence
questions.explanation: A font stack provides an ordered fallback list; if the primary web font fails to load or is unavailable, the browser renders the next available system font.

questions.question: In the `@font-face` rule, what does setting `font-display: swap;` accomplish?
options: It displays a fallback system font immediately while the custom font downloads, then swaps in the custom font once loaded to prevent Invisible Text (FOIT)
It permanently disables custom web fonts on mobile data connections
It alternates between bold and italic fonts on every user click
It blocks the entire webpage rendering until the custom font is 100% downloaded
questions.explanation: `font-display: swap` prevents Flash of Invisible Text (FOIT) by rendering a fallback font immediately and swapping to the custom font once downloaded, improving perceived load performance.

questions.question: Why is setting a unitless `line-height` (e.g., `line-height: 1.5;`) strongly recommended over fixed pixel values (e.g., `line-height: 24px;`) on container elements?
options: Fixed pixel line-heights are completely ignored by modern mobile web browsers
Unitless line-height forces all paragraphs to take up exactly 100% of the viewport height
Unitless line-height converts all lowercase text to capital letters
Unitless `line-height` scales proportionally relative to each child element's individual `font-size`, preventing text collisions when children have larger headings
questions.explanation: When `line-height: 1.5` is inherited, child elements multiply 1.5 by their own font size. A fixed pixel value (e.g., `24px`) inherited by a `36px` heading causes text lines to overlap disastrously.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between `background-size: cover` and `background-size: contain`?
options: `contain` repeats the image 10 times, whereas `cover` only displays it once

`cover` scales the image to completely fill the container (cropping excess edges if aspect ratios differ), while `contain` scales the image so the entire image is visible without cropping (leaving letterboxing if needed)
`cover` compresses image file size, whereas `contain` keeps raw high-resolution data
`contain` only works with SVG vector graphics, while `cover` only works with PNGs
questions.explanation: `cover` guarantees no empty background space in the container by cropping edges as needed; `contain` guarantees the whole image is visible without cropping, potentially leaving uncovered space.

questions.question: Which CSS property creates a fixed 'Parallax' background effect where the background image stays stationary in the viewport while the rest of the page scrolls over it?
options: background-clip: viewport;
background-position: sticky;
background-attachment: fixed;
background-repeat: static;
questions.explanation: `background-attachment: fixed` fixes the background relative to the viewport, creating a classic parallax scrolling effect as content scrolls over the stationary image.

questions.question: Which combination of CSS properties is required to truncate a single line of overflowing text with an ellipsis (`...`)?
options: display: inline; line-clamp: 1; text-wrap: cut;
white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
text-truncate: true; word-break: none;
overflow-wrap: break-word; text-overflow: clip;
questions.explanation: Single-line truncation requires preventing line breaks (`white-space: nowrap`), hiding overflow (`overflow: hidden`), and showing ellipsis (`text-overflow: ellipsis`) within a bounded width container.

questions.question: What CSS standard property controls whether the browser can break words across lines in order to prevent long words or URLs from overflowing its container?
options: hyphen-mode: auto;
overflow-wrap: break-word; (or word-break: break-all;)
text-wrap: force;
letter-spacing: compress;
questions.explanation: `overflow-wrap: break-word` (formerly `word-wrap`) allows unbroken strings like long URLs to break onto new lines when they would otherwise overflow their containing box.

questions.question: What is the numeric equivalent of the `font-weight: bold;` keyword in CSS?
questions.explanation: In the CSS numeric font-weight scale (100–900), `400` represents normal weight, `700` represents bold, and `900` represents black/extra bold.

questions.question: How are multiple background image layers stacked when defined in a single `background` property (e.g., `background: url(top.png), url(bottom.png);`)?
options: The browser blends all layers equally into a single 50% opacity composite
Only the largest file size image is displayed; the other is ignored
The first background image listed is rendered on top (closest to the user), with subsequent layers rendered underneath in descending order
The last background image listed is rendered on top
questions.explanation: Multiple backgrounds are layered from front to back: the first image listed in the comma-separated CSS rule appears on top, closest to the viewer.

questions.question: What is the syntax to create a smooth linear gradient transitioning from purple at the top to orange at the bottom?
options: background-image: gradient-linear(purple -> orange);
background-color: linear(from purple, to orange);
background: radial-direction(purple, orange, 180deg);
background-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, purple, orange);
questions.explanation: Linear gradients use the `linear-gradient(direction, color-stop-1, color-stop-2)` syntax, defaulting to `to bottom` (180deg) if direction is omitted.

questions.question: Which CSS property removes the default underline from hyperlinks (`<a>` tags)?
options: text-decoration: none;
text-underline: hidden;
font-decoration: remove;
link-style: plain;
questions.explanation: `text-decoration: none` removes typographic underlines, overlines, or line-through strokes from text elements.

questions.question: What is the modern CSS space-separated color syntax for an RGB color with 80% opacity?
options: color: rgb(34 197 94) opacity(0.8)
questions.explanation: Modern CSS Color Level 4 syntax allows space-separated RGB/HSL values with an optional slash `/` delimiter preceding alpha transparency (e.g., `rgb(r g b / alpha)`).

questions.question: What does the `text-transform: capitalize;` property do to text?
options: It capitalizes only the very first letter of the entire paragraph sentence
It converts the entire string into all capital uppercase letters
It converts the first letter of every individual word to uppercase while preserving the rest of the letters
It underlines all uppercase acronyms automatically
questions.explanation: `text-transform: capitalize` capitalizes the first character of each word, `uppercase` capitalizes every character, and `lowercase` makes all characters lowercase.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of the OKLCH color space (`oklch(lightness chroma hue)`) over standard RGB/HSL in modern CSS?
questions.codeSnippet: oklch(lightness chroma hue)
options: It is perceptually uniform, meaning identical lightness values appear equally bright to human eyes across all different color hues
It converts all web pages into printable CMYK brochures automatically
It consumes 90% less GPU memory when rendering web animations
It is the only color format supported on iPhone mobile screens
questions.explanation: OKLCH solves HSL's perceptual distortion (where yellow at 50% lightness looks blindingly bright while blue at 50% looks dark) by maintaining true uniform perceptual lightness.

questions.question: How do you apply a multi-line text truncation to clamp a paragraph to exactly 3 visible lines with an ellipsis?
options: max-lines: 3; truncate: multi-line;
line-height: clamp(3); overflow: ellipsis;
display: -webkit-box; -webkit-line-clamp: 3; -webkit-box-orient: vertical; overflow: hidden;
text-lines: 3; text-overflow: ellipsis; overflow: clip;
questions.explanation: Multi-line clamping is achieved via WebKit box properties: `display: -webkit-box`, `-webkit-line-clamp: 3`, `-webkit-box-orient: vertical`, and `overflow: hidden`.

questions.question: What is the effect of `letter-spacing: 0.1em;` on a text heading?
options: It increases the blank space between words while keeping characters tight
It increases the vertical line spacing between rows of text
It sets the width of the font's bounding box to 0.1em
It increases the horizontal tracking space between individual characters by 0.1em
questions.explanation: `letter-spacing` adjusts tracking (the horizontal space between characters), while `word-spacing` adjusts the space between words.

questions.question: Which `background-clip` value allows text to take on the gradient color of the background image underneath it?
options: background-clip: text; (combined with color: transparent;)
background-clip: content-box;
background-clip: font-mask;
background-clip: border-box;
questions.explanation: `background-clip: text` (often `-webkit-background-clip: text`) clips the background graphic to the text character shapes, which when paired with `color: transparent` creates gradient text.

questions.question: What is the difference between `serif` and `sans-serif` generic font families?
options: `sans-serif` fonts cannot display bold or italic font weights

`serif` fonts have small decorative strokes or projections (serifs) at the ends of character strokes (like Times New Roman), while `sans-serif` fonts have clean, straight stroke ends (like Arial/Inter)
`serif` fonts are only used in computer terminal command prompts
`serif` fonts are exclusively designed for mobile touchscreen displays
questions.explanation: Serif typefaces feature small finishing projections/feet at line ends (traditional in print), whereas sans-serif (French for 'without serif') typefaces have clean modern geometric ends.

title: Daily Assessment: Flexbox Architecture & Practical Alignments
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: In CSS Flexbox, which property determines whether the main axis runs horizontally or vertically?
options: flex-wrap
flex-direction
justify-content
align-items
questions.explanation: `flex-direction` establishes the main axis: `row`/`row-reverse` sets a horizontal main axis, while `column`/`column-reverse` sets a vertical main axis.

questions.question: Which `justify-content` value distributes flex items so that the first item is flush against the start edge, the last item is flush against the end edge, and remaining space is split equally between items?
options: center
space-between
space-around
space-evenly
questions.explanation: `space-between` places no space at the outer boundaries, allocating all available free space evenly between adjacent flex items.

questions.question: What is the default value of the `align-items` property on a flex container?
options: center
flex-start
baseline
stretch
questions.explanation: By default, `align-items: stretch` causes flex items to expand along the cross axis to fill the full height (or width in column mode) of the flex container.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between `align-items` and `align-content` in a flex container?
options: `align-items` requires JavaScript, whereas `align-content` is native CSS
`align-content` aligns items along the main axis, while `align-items` aligns along the cross axis
`align-items` aligns individual flex items within their respective line along the cross axis, while `align-content` aligns multi-line flex rows across the entire container when wrapping occurs
`align-content` only works on horizontal rows, while `align-items` only works on vertical columns
questions.explanation: `align-content` manages the distribution of extra space between multiple flex lines (only effective when `flex-wrap: wrap` creates multiple rows/columns).

questions.question: What does setting `flex-shrink: 0;` on a flex item accomplish?
options: It prevents the flex item from shrinking below its initial `flex-basis` size when available space in the container is constrained
It forces the flex item to take up 100% of the container width
It hides the flex item when the viewport width is smaller than 600px
It causes the flex item to expand to fill all remaining positive space
questions.explanation: `flex-shrink: 0` explicitly prohibits an item from shrinking when total flex item widths exceed container capacity (useful for icons, fixed avatars, or sidebars).

questions.question: What is the full expansion of the shorthand rule `flex: 1;`?
options: flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 0; flex-basis: auto;
flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 0%;
flex-grow: 0; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 100px;
flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: auto;
questions.explanation: The shorthand `flex: 1` expands to `flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 0%`, making all items sharing `flex: 1` grow and shrink equally from a base of zero.

questions.question: How can you push a single navigation item (e.g., a 'Login' button or user profile avatar) to the far right edge inside a flex container?
options: Apply `float: right;` to the flex item
Apply `margin-left: auto;` to that specific flex item
Set `align-self: flex-end;` on the flex item
Set `justify-content: flex-end;` on the child element
questions.explanation: In Flexbox, auto margins absorb all remaining free space along the axis; applying `margin-left: auto` to a child pushes it and subsequent items to the far right.

questions.question: Which flex item property allows an individual item to override the container's default `align-items` cross-axis alignment?
options: item-align
justify-self
flex-self
align-self
questions.explanation: `align-self` allows a specific flex item to have its own unique cross-axis alignment (e.g., `align-self: flex-end;` while other items are centered).

questions.question: Why do long unbroken strings or text elements sometimes cause flex items to overflow their container despite having `flex: 1` or `flex-shrink: 1`?
options: Browsers disable flex shrinking whenever fonts larger than 14px are rendered
Flexbox engines automatically convert overflowing text into base64 images
Flex items have a default `min-width: auto;` (minimum content size), which prevents them from shrinking smaller than their inner content width
`flex-shrink` only applies to images and disallows text shrinking
questions.explanation: In Flexbox, items default to `min-width: auto`, meaning the browser won't shrink an item below its content width. Setting `min-width: 0;` on the flex item resolves the overflow issue.

questions.question: What does the `order` property do to flex items, and what is its default value?
options: It determines the z-index stacking context; default value is -1
It sorts items alphabetically by their text content; default value is 'asc'
It renumbers HTML headings dynamically; default value is 1
It reorders visual presentation of items without altering the HTML source order; default value is 0
questions.explanation: The `order` property controls visual rendering sequence (lower/negative numbers appear first, higher numbers last). The default value is `0`.

questions.question: How do you achieve perfect horizontal and vertical centering of a child element inside a flex container?
options: display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;
display: flex; flex-direction: center; margin: 0 auto;
display: flex; align-content: center; text-align: center;
display: flex; justify-items: center; align-self: center;
questions.explanation: Setting `display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;` centers children along both the main axis and cross axis simultaneously.

questions.question: What is the role of the `gap` property in a flexbox layout?
options: It defines the gutter spacing between adjacent flex items without adding extra margin to outer container edges
It limits the maximum number of items allowed in a single flex line
It creates transparent border frames around the entire flex container
It sets the internal padding inside each individual flex item
questions.explanation: `gap` (or `row-gap` and `column-gap`) defines spacing between flex items cleanly, eliminating the need for complex `:last-child` margin negation tricks.

questions.question: What does the `flex-flow` property represent?
options: A property controlling CSS animation fluid transitions in flexbox
A property that forces text to wrap around floated images
A shorthand property combining `flex-direction` and `flex-wrap` (e.g., `flex-flow: row wrap;`)
A property that toggles between flexbox and CSS grid dynamically
questions.explanation: `flex-flow` is shorthand for `flex-direction` and `flex-wrap`, accepting values like `flex-flow: column wrap` or `flex-flow: row nowrap`.

questions.question: When `flex-direction: column` is declared, how do the alignment properties change their axes?
options: All alignment properties are disabled in column mode
`justify-content` controls horizontal alignment, and `align-items` controls vertical alignment
Both `justify-content` and `align-items` control vertical alignment simultaneously
`justify-content` controls vertical alignment (main axis), and `align-items` controls horizontal alignment (cross axis)
questions.explanation: Changing `flex-direction` to `column` rotates the main axis vertically (Y-axis) and the cross axis horizontally (X-axis), swapping the directional impact of `justify-content` and `align-items`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `display: flex` and `display: inline-flex`?
options: There is no functional difference between the two
`display: flex` is mobile-only, whereas `display: inline-flex` is desktop-only
`display: inline-flex` converts all child elements into inline `<span>` tags
`display: flex` creates a block-level flex container that spans 100% width, while `display: inline-flex` creates an inline-level flex container that shrink-wraps to fit its contents
questions.explanation: Similar to `block` vs `inline-block`, `flex` expands to fill available parent width while `inline-flex` only occupies the width required by its children.

questions.question: If three items have `flex-grow: 1`, `flex-grow: 2`, and `flex-grow: 1` respectively, how will 400px of extra free space be distributed among them?
options: Item 1 gets 100px (1/4), Item 2 gets 200px (2/4), and Item 3 gets 100px (1/4)
Item 1 gets 200px, Item 2 gets 100px, and Item 3 gets 100px
Each item gets exactly 133.33px of extra space equally
Item 2 gets all 400px, and Items 1 and 3 receive 0px
questions.explanation: Total grow factor = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. Item 1 receives 1/4 (100px), Item 2 receives 2/4 (200px), and Item 3 receives 1/4 (100px).

questions.question: What is the difference between `flex: auto;` and `flex: none;`?
options: `flex: auto` calculates width based on the user's internet speed
`flex: none` hides all flex items from the screen using `visibility: hidden`
`flex: auto` (`1 1 auto`) allows items to grow and shrink based on their size, while `flex: none` (`0 0 auto`) makes items completely rigid and non-flexible
`flex: none` resets all children to standard CSS table cells
questions.explanation: `flex: none` expands to `0 0 auto` (cannot grow, cannot shrink, sized by width/height/content), whereas `flex: auto` expands to `1 1 auto` (fully flexible).

questions.question: What is the effect of `justify-content: space-evenly;` on flex items?
options: Only even-numbered children receive spacing, while odd children touch each other
The space between any two adjacent items, as well as the space from the edges to the outer items, is exactly identical
Items are stretched to take up equal widths across the row
The space between items is twice the size of the space at the outer edges
questions.explanation: `space-evenly` ensures every gap—including the space between edge items and container boundaries—has the exact same pixel width.

questions.question: What happens to text nodes directly inside a flex container that are not wrapped in an HTML tag?
options: The browser wraps them in an anonymous flex item that participates fully in flex formatting rules
The browser deletes the text nodes during CSSOM compilation
The text nodes escape the flex container and render at the bottom of the `<body>`
The browser displays a console syntax error and stops rendering
questions.explanation: Raw text inside a flex container is automatically encapsulated within an anonymous flex item and sized/aligned according to flex rules.

questions.question: If both `width: 300px;` and `flex-basis: 200px;` are specified on a flex item in a horizontal row, which value takes precedence for initial main-axis sizing?
options: `width: 300px;` always overrides `flex-basis`
The property that was written first in the stylesheet takes precedence
`flex-basis: 200px;` overrides the `width` property on the main axis
The browser averages them and sets width to 250px
questions.explanation: In a flex container, `flex-basis` represents the primary sizing property along the main axis, superseding `width` in row mode or `height` in column mode.

title: Daily Assessment: CSS Grid System & Multi-Column Layouts
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is the foundational architectural difference between CSS Flexbox and CSS Grid?
options: CSS Grid is designed exclusively for mobile screens, while Flexbox is desktop-only
CSS Grid cannot contain images, while Flexbox supports all media types
Flexbox does not support responsive design, while CSS Grid requires JavaScript to render
CSS Flexbox is one-dimensional (handles layouts along a single axis: row OR column), while CSS Grid is two-dimensional (handles rows AND columns simultaneously)
questions.explanation: Flexbox is designed for 1D content distribution (either a row or a column), whereas CSS Grid is a 2D layout system designed to align items along rows and columns simultaneously.

questions.question: What does the fractional unit `1fr` represent in CSS Grid?
options: One share of the remaining available free space in the grid container after fixed tracks are allocated
One fraction of the root font size (equivalent to 16px)
Exactly 100% of the viewport width on full-screen monitors
A fixed measurement equivalent to 1 frame per second animation speed
questions.explanation: The `fr` (fractional) unit divides available remaining space proportionally among tracks after accounting for fixed pixel/content dimensions and gaps.

questions.question: Which CSS Grid template rule generates an intrinsically responsive grid that automatically creates columns of at least 250px and wraps them without needing media queries?
options: grid-template-columns: auto-columns(250px, 100%);
grid-template-columns: responsive(min: 250px, max: 1fr);
grid-template-columns: repeat(all, 250px);
grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
questions.explanation: `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr))` dynamically creates as many 250px+ columns as will fit into the container and stretches them to fill remaining space, creating a zero-media-query responsive grid.

questions.question: What is the key difference between `auto-fill` and `auto-fit` in `repeat(..., minmax(...))` grid definitions?
options: There is no difference; both produce identical track sizes under all conditions
`auto-fit` only works on images, while `auto-fill` works on text cards
`auto-fill` requires an explicit row count, whereas `auto-fit` is automatic
`auto-fill` creates empty phantom tracks if space allows, while `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks to 0px and stretches existing items to fill the container width
questions.explanation: When there are fewer items than available space, `auto-fill` preserves empty grid tracks, whereas `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks and expands current items to occupy full container width.

questions.question: How do you define visual ASCII layout areas in CSS Grid using `grid-template-areas`?
options: grid-template-areas: [header, sidebar, main, footer];
grid-template-areas: "header header" "sidebar main" "footer footer";
grid-template-areas: layout { header; sidebar; main; footer; };
grid-template-areas: area(header) -> area(main) -> area(footer);
questions.explanation: `grid-template-areas` defines named grid cells visually as quoted strings representing rows, mapped to child items using `grid-area: header;`.

questions.question: In CSS Grid, what does a period (`.`) represent inside a `grid-template-areas` string declaration?
options: A decimal separator indicating half-sized fraction tracks
A wildcard character matching any HTML element
A syntax terminator indicating the end of the grid definition
An unnamed, empty grid cell where no named grid area will be placed
questions.explanation: In `grid-template-areas`, a dot `.` denotes an empty, unassigned cell in that specific row and column.

questions.question: What does the line shorthand `grid-column: 1 / 4;` mean for a grid item?
options: The item is visible only on January 4th in calendar widgets
The item starts at grid line 1 and spans across to grid line 4 (covering 3 columns)
The item is placed in row 1, column 4 as a single cell
The item takes up 1/4th (25%) of the total container height
questions.explanation: `grid-column: 1 / 4` specifies `grid-column-start: 1` and `grid-column-end: 4`, spanning 3 grid column tracks across lines 1, 2, 3, and 4.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Explicit Grid and the Implicit Grid in CSS?
options: The Implicit Grid only supports negative pixel values, while the Explicit Grid uses positive values
The Explicit Grid requires JavaScript, whereas the Implicit Grid is pure CSS
The Explicit Grid is defined manually with `grid-template-columns/rows`, while the Implicit Grid is created automatically by the browser to hold extra items that exceed declared tracks
The Explicit Grid is hidden from screen readers, whereas the Implicit Grid is visible
questions.explanation: Tracks defined explicitly via `grid-template-columns/rows` form the explicit grid. When items overflow or are placed beyond those bounds, the browser creates implicit tracks styled via `grid-auto-rows/columns`.

questions.question: Which property controls the packing algorithm in CSS Grid to automatically backfill empty gaps caused by larger grid items?
options: grid-auto-flow: dense;
grid-layout: masonry-auto;
grid-fill: backfill;
grid-pack: compact;
questions.explanation: `grid-auto-flow: dense` (or `row dense`) instructs the placement algorithm to backfill earlier empty spaces in the grid if smaller items appear later in source order.

questions.question: What does the `subgrid` feature (`grid-template-columns: subgrid;`) allow a nested child grid to do?
options: Limit the nested grid to exactly 2 columns on all devices
Automatically convert all grid items into an SVG vector canvas
Inherit and align directly to the grid tracks and line definitions of its parent grid container
Create a separate 3D WebGL coordinate space inside the grid cell
questions.explanation: `subgrid` allows child grid containers to share the track sizing and alignment of their parent grid, ensuring nested elements (like card headers or footers) align across sibling cards.

questions.question: How do you align all grid tracks horizontally inside a grid container when total track widths are smaller than the container?
options: justify-content (e.g., justify-content: center;)
justify-items
align-items
justify-self
questions.explanation: `justify-content` aligns the entire grid track framework along the inline (horizontal) axis inside the grid container.

questions.question: Which property aligns individual content items horizontally inside their respective grid cells across the entire grid?
options: justify-items
align-content
place-content
justify-content
questions.explanation: `justify-items` controls horizontal alignment of all items inside their individual cells (`start`, `end`, `center`, `stretch`), while `justify-self` overrides it for a single item.

questions.question: How can two distinct grid items be made to overlap in CSS Grid without using `position: absolute`?
options: Assign both items to the same overlapping grid row and column coordinates (e.g., both having `grid-area: 1 / 1 / 3 / 3;`) and adjust layering with `z-index`
Set `grid-overlap: enable;` on the parent container
Overlap is impossible in CSS Grid without absolute positioning
Give both elements a negative `grid-gap` value
questions.explanation: Grid items can share identical grid lines or overlapping areas naturally; normal stacking rules and `z-index` dictate which overlapping item renders on top.

questions.question: What does the `minmax(100px, auto)` track sizing function specify?
questions.codeSnippet: minmax(100px, auto)
options: The track will start at 0px and stop expanding at 100px
The track will shrink to 50px on mobile screens
The track will be at least 100px wide/tall, but can expand dynamically to fit larger content as needed
The track will always be exactly 100px and never change
questions.explanation: `minmax(MIN, MAX)` defines a size range: here the track cannot shrink below `100px`, but will expand beyond `100px` if content requires it (`auto`).

questions.question: Which CSS Multi-column property controls how many vertical newspaper-style columns a block of text splits into?
options: grid-template-columns
column-count
column-divisions
text-columns
questions.explanation: The CSS Multi-column Layout property `column-count` defines the exact number of columns text flows through in newspaper style.

questions.question: How can a headline element (`<h2>`) inside a multi-column text layout be made to span across all columns horizontally?
options: grid-column: 1 / -1;
column-break: across;
column-span: all;
colspan="all"
questions.explanation: `column-span: all` allows an element (like a breaking headline or quote) to span across all newspaper columns inside a multi-column container.

questions.question: What is the shorthand syntax for `place-items` in CSS Grid?
options: place-items: <width> <height>;
place-items: <grid-row> <grid-column>;
place-items: <justify-content> <align-content>;
place-items: <align-items> <justify-items>; (e.g., place-items: center;)
questions.explanation: `place-items` is shorthand for `align-items` and `justify-items`. Providing a single value (e.g., `place-items: center;`) centers items both vertically and horizontally in one line.

questions.question: What is the effect of using negative grid line indices (e.g., `grid-column: 1 / -1;`)?
options: `-1` rotates the grid item 180 degrees backwards
`-1` hides the grid item behind the background layer
`-1` references the very last explicit grid line on the opposite edge, allowing an item to span the full width of the explicit grid
`-1` throws a CSS validation error because line numbers must be positive integers
questions.explanation: Negative line numbers count backward from the end of the explicit grid: line `-1` is the last line, `-2` is the second to last line, etc.

questions.question: Which property sets the height of rows created automatically in the implicit grid when items overflow declared rows?
options: grid-template-rows
grid-auto-rows
row-overflow-size
grid-implicit-height
questions.explanation: `grid-auto-rows` specifies the track size for any implicit rows generated automatically when items exceed explicit template rows.

questions.question: What is the unit `max-content` when applied to a grid column track?
options: The track sizes to the narrowest possible width where text wraps at every word
The track sizes to the intrinsic maximum width of its content without soft-wrapping text
The track expands to 100% of the entire viewport monitor width
The track size is capped at 1024px maximum
questions.explanation: `max-content` represents the largest intrinsic size of the content (e.g., a sentence formatted as a single unbroken line without wrapping).

title: Daily Assessment: Positioning: Relative, Absolute, Fixed, Sticky
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is the default value of the CSS `position` property on HTML elements?
options: relative
absolute
initial-flow
static
questions.explanation: By default, elements have `position: static`, meaning they participate in normal document flow and ignore `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`, and `z-index`.

questions.question: How does `position: relative` behave when offset properties like `top: 20px; left: 30px;` are applied?
options: It shifts the element 20px down and 30px right relative to its original position, while preserving its original space in the document layout flow
It scales the element's width and height by 20px and 30px
It pushes all subsequent sibling elements 20px down and 30px right
It removes the element from document flow and positions it relative to the viewport window
questions.explanation: `position: relative` visually shifts the element from its normal position without disturbing surrounding elements, leaving an empty placeholder space where it originally sat.

questions.question: What serves as the 'Containing Block' for an element with `position: absolute;`?
options: The immediate parent element regardless of its CSS positioning property
The nearest ancestor element that has a `position` property other than `static` (e.g., `relative`, `absolute`, `fixed`, or `sticky`)
Always the top-level `<body>` element regardless of parent styles
The nearest element that has `display: flex` or `display: grid`
questions.explanation: An absolutely positioned element searches up the DOM tree for the nearest ancestor with `position` set to anything other than `static`. If none exists, it falls back to the Initial Containing Block (viewport).

questions.question: What is the modern CSS shorthand property to set `top: 0; right: 0; bottom: 0; left: 0;` simultaneously on an absolute overlay?
options: position-all: 0;
offset: 0;
inset: 0;
edges: 0;
questions.explanation: The `inset` shorthand sets all four directional offsets (`top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left`) in a single declaration (e.g., `inset: 0;` for full container overlays).

questions.question: Which classic CSS technique uses absolute positioning and 2D transforms to center an element of unknown dimensions perfectly inside its relative parent?
options: position: relative; align: center; transform: scale(0.5);
position: absolute; top: 50%; left: 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%);
position: absolute; center: true; offset: 50%;
position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; margin: auto;
questions.explanation: `top: 50%; left: 50%` places the element's top-left corner at the parent's center, and `transform: translate(-50%, -50%)` shifts the element back by half its own width and height.

questions.question: What is the key characteristic of an element with `position: fixed`?
options: It is removed from normal flow and positioned relative to the viewport, remaining in the exact same screen position when the page scrolls
It locks into position only after scrolling 500px down the page
It expands to cover 100% of the screen height automatically
It cannot contain any clickable links or form buttons
questions.explanation: `position: fixed` fixes an element relative to the browser viewport coordinate space, remaining pinned on screen during scrolling.

questions.question: Under what circumstance does an element with `position: fixed` stop positioning relative to the viewport window?
options: When the webpage is viewed on a desktop monitor with 4K resolution
When an ancestor element has a CSS `transform`, `perspective`, or `filter` property applied, which establishes a new containing block
When the element contains an image larger than 2MB
When the user switches their browser to dark mode
questions.explanation: CSS specifications state that any ancestor with properties like `transform`, `filter`, or `perspective` creates a new containing block, trapping `fixed` descendants inside that ancestor.

questions.question: How does `position: sticky` operate during user scrolling?
options: It bounces up and down continuously using a CSS spring animation
It stays fixed across the entire page forever, ignoring parent boundaries
It hides the element automatically when the user scrolls down quickly
It behaves like `position: relative` until its containing block scrolls past a specified offset threshold (e.g., `top: 0`), at which point it sticks in place until reaching the end of its parent
questions.explanation: `position: sticky` toggles between relative and fixed positioning based on scroll position, remaining pinned within the boundaries of its immediate parent container.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common reason why `position: sticky; top: 0;` fails to stick when scrolling?
options: The viewport width is greater than 1200px
An ancestor element in the DOM tree has `overflow: hidden`, `overflow: auto`, or `overflow: scroll` applied
The webpage uses HTML5 semantic tags instead of `<div>` tags
The sticky element has a background color defined in hex format
questions.explanation: Any ancestor with `overflow: hidden`, `auto`, or `scroll` breaks `position: sticky` because the scroll context is trapped inside that parent rather than the main document viewport.

questions.question: What does the `z-index` property control in CSS, and on which elements does it work?
options: It controls optical zoom level of images in CSS; it works on `` only
It controls horizontal alignment; it works on all inline text elements
It controls the 3D stacking order along the Z-axis (front-to-back); it only works on positioned elements (non-static) and flex/grid items
It controls font size scaling; it works on headings only
questions.explanation: `z-index` specifies the stacking layer of an element along the Z-axis. It is ignored on elements with default `position: static` (unless they are flex/grid items).

questions.question: Why can't a modal dialog with `z-index: 9999` appear above an element in another container if that modal's parent container has `z-index: 1` and the other element's parent has `z-index: 2`?
options: `z-index` values cannot exceed 1000 in modern web browsers
The browser rounds all z-index numbers down to zero upon page load
Modal dialogs are automatically rendered below all standard HTML text
Because the modal is trapped inside its parent's Stacking Context, and the entire parent context is subordinate to the higher `z-index: 2` context
questions.explanation: Stacking contexts form isolated hierarchies. A child's `z-index` only has meaning within its parent stacking context; it can never escape to out-stack a higher sibling stacking context.

questions.question: Which modern CSS property explicitly creates a new Stacking Context on an element without requiring hacky `position: relative; z-index: 0;` or `opacity: 0.999` styles?
questions.codeSnippet:
position: relative;
z-index: 0;
options: context: separate;
z-context: create;
isolation: isolate;
stacking: new-layer;
questions.explanation: `isolation: isolate` is the standardized CSS property specifically designed to establish a new stacking context cleanly without altering visual rendering.

questions.question: What does `pointer-events: none;` accomplish when applied to a transparent absolute overlay element sitting on top of a form?
options: It allows mouse clicks, hover events, and touches to pass directly through the overlay to interact with the underlying form inputs
It disables the user's physical mouse hardware temporarily
It converts all click events into double-click events
It hides the mouse cursor graphic whenever it hovers over the screen
questions.explanation: `pointer-events: none` makes an element invisible to mouse/touch interactions, allowing clicks to pass through to underlying elements.

questions.question: When percentage values are used on `top`, `bottom`, `left`, and `right` on an absolutely positioned element, what are they calculated relative to?
options: The physical diagonal resolution of the user's monitor
The width and height of the absolutely positioned element itself
The total height of the document body including off-screen scroll area
The width and height of the element's positioned Containing Block (padding box)
questions.explanation: Percentage offsets on positioned elements (`top/bottom: %`, `left/right: %`) resolve relative to the padding box dimensions of the containing block.

questions.question: How do elements with `position: absolute` interact with normal document layout flow?
options: They reserve a transparent blank block equal to their width and height
They automatically float to the left edge of the nearest paragraph
They are completely removed from normal flow; other elements act as if the absolute element does not exist and collapse into its space
They push subsequent elements downward by their exact pixel height
questions.explanation: Out-of-flow positioning (`absolute` and `fixed`) removes the element completely from document flow, so surrounding siblings ignore its geometry entirely.

questions.question: What is the effect of setting both `left: 0;` and `right: 0;` on an absolutely positioned element with `width: auto;`?
options: The element stretches horizontally to span the full width of its containing block (from left edge to right edge)
The element collapses its width to exactly 0px
The browser throws a CSS conflict error and disables the element
The element centers itself horizontally with a fixed 100px width
questions.explanation: When opposite inset properties (`left: 0; right: 0;` or `top: 0; bottom: 0;`) are defined and dimensions are `auto`, the element stretches to fill the distance between the two constraints.

questions.question: Which of the following creates a new Stacking Context in modern CSS?
options: An element with `opacity: 0.95` (any opacity value strictly less than 1)
An element with `display: block` and `margin: 10px`
An element with `text-align: center`
An element with `font-weight: bold`
questions.explanation: Creating a stacking context happens via properties like `opacity < 1`, `transform != none`, `filter != none`, `position: relative/absolute with z-index != auto`, and `isolation: isolate`.

questions.question: In a Sticky Sidebar layout, why is it necessary for the sticky container's parent column to have sufficient height?
options: CSS Grid disables sticky elements inside flex containers
If the parent is not 100vh tall, the browser reloads the webpage
Because a sticky element cannot scroll or stick past the bottom boundary of its immediate parent container
Sticky elements require parent containers to be exactly 5000px tall
questions.explanation: A sticky element can only travel within the boundary of its parent container; if the parent has the same height as the sticky element, it has no room to move and will not stick.

questions.question: What is the stacking behavior of two unpositioned (`position: static`) sibling elements without any z-index?
options: Unpositioned elements can never visually overlap under any circumstances
The element that appears later in the HTML source code renders on top of the earlier element if they overlap
The element with the larger file size renders on top
The earlier element in the HTML source code always renders on top
questions.explanation: In default document stacking, when elements occupy the same space without custom stacking contexts, later elements in source order stack on top of earlier siblings.

questions.question: What is the positioning property value used to create floating action buttons (FABs) pinned to the bottom-right corner of the mobile screen?
options: position: absolute; display: pin;
position: relative; float: bottom-right;
position: static; margin-top: auto; float: right;
position: fixed; bottom: 20px; right: 20px;
questions.explanation: `position: fixed; bottom: 20px; right: 20px;` pins the floating action button to the bottom-right corner of the viewport regardless of page scrolling.

title: Daily Assessment: Media Queries & Responsive UI Design Patterns
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI
lessonTitle: Media Queries & Responsive UI Design Patterns

questions.question: What are the three core technical components of Responsive Web Design (RWD) as originally formulated by Ethan Marcotte?
options: Server-Side Rendering, Microfrontends, and REST APIs
HTML5 Canvas, CSS Transforms, and WebGL
Fluid Grids, Flexible Media (Images/Videos), and CSS Media Queries
JavaScript Frameworks, WebAssembly, and Service Workers
questions.explanation: Ethan Marcotte coined Responsive Web Design based on three pillars: fluid grid layouts, flexible media (scaling images), and media queries.

questions.question: What is the primary philosophy behind 'Mobile-First' responsive CSS design?
options: Creating two completely separate domain websites (e.g., m.example.com and www.example.com)
Building desktop layouts first, then using `max-width` media queries to hide elements on mobile
Writing base styles for small screens first, then using `min-width` media queries to progressively enhance the layout for larger screens
Disabling all CSS animations on mobile devices permanently
questions.explanation: Mobile-first design establishes lightweight baseline styling for mobile viewports, using `@media (min-width: ...)` queries to add complexity as screen real estate increases.

questions.question: Which modern CSS Range syntax is equivalent to the legacy `@media (min-width: 768px) and (max-width: 1024px)` query?
questions.codeSnippet: @media (min-width: 768px) and (max-width: 1024px)
options: @media (768px <= width <= 1024px)
@media (width: [768px, 1024px])
@media (width: between 768px and 1024px)
@media (range: 768px to 1024px)
questions.explanation: CSS Media Queries Level 4 introduced standard mathematical comparison operators (e.g., `@media (768px <= width <= 1024px)`), which is cleaner and less error-prone.

questions.question: Which user preference media query allows developers to style custom Dark Mode color themes based on the operating system setting?
options: @media (theme: dark-mode)
@media (user-style: night)
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)
@media (color-mode: inverted)
questions.explanation: `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` detects if the user has requested a dark theme at the OS or browser level.

questions.question: Why should developers use `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` in modern web applications?
options: To accelerate video playback speed to 2x by default
To improve CPU battery life by automatically pausing background music
To compress GIF animations into WebP format on mobile
To minimize or eliminate non-essential animations and transitions for users with vestibular disorders or motion sensitivity
questions.explanation: `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` respects user accessibility preferences by turning off jarring transitions and parallax effects that trigger motion sickness.

questions.question: What is the difference between `@media (hover: hover)` and `@media (hover: none)`?
options: There is no difference; all mobile smartphones support full hover simulation
`hover: hover` increases button font size when clicked
`hover: hover` targets devices with a precise pointing device that can hover (e.g., desktop mouse), while `hover: none` targets touchscreens where hover is impossible
`hover: none` disables all JavaScript mouse click listeners
questions.explanation: Interaction media queries detect input capabilities: `hover: hover` matches mice/trackpads, whereas `hover: none` with `pointer: coarse` matches finger touchscreens.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between CSS Container Queries (`@container`) and standard Media Queries (`@media`)?
options: Container Queries are deprecated in favor of CSS Flexbox
Media Queries query the dimensions of the entire browser viewport, whereas Container Queries query the size of an individual component's parent container
Media Queries can only resize text, while Container Queries can only resize images
Container Queries only work on Docker container server backends
questions.explanation: Container Queries allow a component (like a card) to adapt based on the width of its parent wrapper rather than the whole screen width, unlocking true modular UI components.

questions.question: What CSS property must be declared on an ancestor element before its children can use `@container` queries?
options: container-type: inline-size; (or container: name / inline-size;)
contain-query: true;
container: enable-query;
display: container-root;
questions.explanation: To query a parent container's width, it must be designated as a containment context using `container-type: inline-size` (or `normal`/`size`).

questions.question: Which CSS rule makes content images responsive so they scale down to fit small containers without exceeding their natural pixel dimensions?
options: img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; }
img { width: 100vw; height: 100vh; }
img { min-width: 100%; resize: both; }
img { scale: auto-fit; object-fit: fill; }
questions.explanation: `max-width: 100%; height: auto;` ensures images shrink gracefully inside narrow containers while maintaining their aspect ratio and never stretching beyond original resolution.

questions.question: Which media type query is used to format pages specifically for paper printing or PDF export (e.g., hiding navigation bars and changing background colors)?
options: @media export-pdf
