@media print
@media paper
@media physical
questions.explanation: `@media print` targets print previews and printer output, allowing developers to hide navbars, force black text on white backgrounds, and control page breaks.

questions.question: How does the `orientation` media feature distinguish between mobile phone orientations?
options: `orientation: landscape` matches when viewport width is greater than height, and `orientation: portrait` matches when height is greater than or equal to width
`orientation: portrait` disables all flexbox column layouts
`orientation: landscape` is only active on smart TV displays
It uses the phone's gyroscope to measure gravitational acceleration in degrees
questions.explanation: `orientation` evaluates the aspect ratio of the viewport: `landscape` when width > height, and `portrait` when height >= width.

questions.question: What is the purpose of using `clamp()` for responsive fluid typography (e.g., `font-size: clamp(1rem, 2.5vw + 0.5rem, 2.5rem);`)?
questions.codeSnippet: for responsive fluid typography (e.g.,
options: It converts all text into uppercase bold font weights
It scales text smoothly with the viewport width without requiring multiple media query breakpoints, while capping minimum and maximum font sizes
It disables custom Google Web Fonts on mobile data networks
It rotates typography 90 degrees in portrait orientation
questions.explanation: `clamp(MIN, VAL, MAX)` creates fluid typography that scales smoothly with the viewport (`vw`), capped by accessible minimum and maximum bounds.

questions.question: In standard responsive UI design, what is a 'Breakpoint'?
options: A JavaScript error that pauses browser script execution
A specific viewport width threshold (e.g., 640px, 768px, 1024px) at which the page layout transitions using media queries
An HTML tag that forces a line break inside a paragraph
The point where an image file size exceeds the network bandwidth limit
questions.explanation: A breakpoint is the viewport width where media queries trigger layout modifications (e.g., switching from single-column mobile to multi-column desktop).

questions.question: How do you hide an element on mobile screens (< 768px) and display it as a flex container on desktop screens (>= 768px) using mobile-first CSS?
options: .element { display: flex; } @media (max-width: 768px) { .element { display: hide; } }
.element { visibility: collapse; display: desktop-only; }
@media (screen: desktop) { .element { visible: flex; } }
.element { display: none; } @media (min-width: 768px) { .element { display: flex; } }
questions.explanation: In mobile-first design: write `.element { display: none; }` as baseline, then override with `display: flex;` inside `@media (min-width: 768px)`.

questions.question: Which media query detects whether a user's device has a high pixel density screen (such as Apple Retina displays)?
options: @media (gpu-render: retina)
@media (pixel-density: ultra)
@media (screen-quality: 4k)
@media (-webkit-min-device-pixel-ratio: 2), (min-resolution: 192dpi)
questions.explanation: `min-resolution: 192dpi` (or `-webkit-min-device-pixel-ratio: 2`) targets high-density Retina screens to serve 2x high-resolution bitmap assets.

questions.question: What is the recommended responsive UX pattern for handling large data tables on narrow mobile screens?
options: Deleting 80% of the table data rows automatically on mobile
Shrinking the font size to 2px so all columns fit onto a single screen
Wrapping the `<table>` in an overflow container (`overflow-x: auto;`) or transforming rows into stacked vertical card blocks via CSS
Disabling scrolling completely and displaying an error message
questions.explanation: Large tables should either be wrapped in a smooth horizontal scroll container (`overflow-x: auto`) or restructured into stacked cards on mobile screens for usability.

questions.question: What is an 'Off-Canvas' navigation pattern commonly used in responsive mobile web apps?
options: A dropdown menu that only works when the user disconnects from the internet
A navigation sidebar hidden off-screen (e.g., `transform: translateX(-100%)`) that slides smoothly into view when a hamburger icon is tapped
A menu rendered on a separate physical external computer monitor
A navigation bar that renders exclusively on HTML `<canvas>` elements
questions.explanation: An off-canvas menu is positioned outside the viewport (`translateX(-100%)`) and animated into view upon clicking a hamburger toggle button.

questions.question: Which media feature query detects if a user has requested high contrast in their system accessibility settings?
options: @media (prefers-contrast: more)
@media (contrast-mode: high)
@media (accessibility: max-contrast)
@media (high-contrast: active)
questions.explanation: `@media (prefers-contrast: more)` allows developers to enhance border outlines, increase font weights, and boost color contrast for visually impaired users.

questions.question: What does the `@media (display-mode: standalone)` query detect?
options: Whether the user has connected dual monitors to their computer
Whether the webpage is embedded inside a third-party `<iframe>`
Whether the computer is operating without an active internet connection
Whether the web application is running as an installed Progressive Web App (PWA) in its own dedicated window without browser URL chrome
questions.explanation: `display-mode: standalone` targets PWAs launched from home screens or desktops, allowing custom title bars and app-like UI styling.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of using CSS container query units (such as `cqw` and `cqh`) over viewport units (`vw` and `vh`)?
options: `cqw` replaces all need for HTML and JavaScript in modern browsers
`cqw` increases the download speed of web pages over 5G networks
`cqw` calculates dimensions based on the user's battery percentage
`cqw` (Container Query Width) is relative to the parent container's width, allowing components to scale fluidly regardless of where they are placed in the layout
questions.explanation: `1cqw` equals 1% of the query container's width, enabling modular components (like cards or widgets) to size fluidly whether placed in a narrow sidebar or a wide main area.

title: Daily Assessment: Bootstrap 5 Grid System & Responsive Utilities
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What was one of the most notable architectural changes introduced in Bootstrap 5 compared to Bootstrap 4?
options: Replacing all HTML5 tags with React JSX components
Completely dropping the jQuery dependency in favor of modern vanilla JavaScript
Removing the 12-column grid system in favor of table layouts
Requiring all stylesheets to be written in Python
questions.explanation: Bootstrap 5 eliminated the dependency on jQuery, rewritten completely in native vanilla JavaScript with improved performance and smaller bundle sizes.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between `.container` and `.container-fluid` in Bootstrap 5?
options: `.container` has a fixed responsive max-width at each breakpoint tier, while `.container-fluid` always spans 100% width across all viewport sizes
`.container-fluid` converts all child elements into SVG vector graphics
`.container` automatically removes all margin and padding gutters
`.container-fluid` only works on desktop monitors, while `.container` is mobile-only
questions.explanation: `.container` adjusts max-width at each breakpoint (`sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`, `xxl`), while `.container-fluid` continuously occupies 100% width across all viewports.

questions.question: What are the 6 standard responsive breakpoint tiers in Bootstrap 5?
options: mobile (<480px), tablet (≥480px), desktop (≥1024px), ultra (≥2048px)
questions.explanation: Bootstrap 5 features 6 responsive tiers: `xs` (default <576px), `sm` (576px), `md` (768px), `lg` (992px), `xl` (1200px), and the new `xxl` (1400px).

questions.question: In the Bootstrap 5 12-column grid system, what is the mandatory parent-child hierarchy rule?
options: Columns must be placed directly inside `<main>` without `.container` or `.row`
Containers (`.container`) wrap Rows (`.row`), and Rows must be the immediate parents of Columns (`.col-*`)
Rows can be placed directly inside other Rows without any columns
Columns must wrap Rows, which in turn wrap Containers
questions.explanation: Bootstrap's grid hierarchy strictly requires `.container` (or `.container-fluid`) -> `.row` -> `.col-*` so margins, paddings, and negative row margins calculate correctly.

questions.question: How do you create a column layout that stacks vertically as 100% width on mobile screens, splits into 2 equal columns on tablets (≥768px), and 4 equal columns on desktops (≥992px)?
options: col-1 col-md-2 col-lg-4
col-xs-12 col-tab-6 col-desk-4
col-12 col-md-6 col-lg-3
col-full col-tablet-half col-desktop-quarter
questions.explanation: In a 12-column grid: `col-12` = 100% width, `col-md-6` = 6/12 (50% or 2 per row), and `col-lg-3` = 3/12 (25% or 4 per row).

questions.question: What does the `.col-auto` class do on a grid column in Bootstrap 5?
options: It randomly assigns a column width between 1 and 12
It sizes the column to fit the natural intrinsic width of its inner content
It hides the column automatically when other columns are clicked
It automatically expands the column to 100% width on all screens
questions.explanation: `.col-auto` sets column width based on content size (`width: auto`), allowing adjacent columns with `.col` to fill the remaining available space.

questions.question: Which utility class is used to shift a column 3 grid columns to the right on medium screens (≥768px)?
options: offset-md-3
col-skip-3
push-md-3
shift-md-3
questions.explanation: `.offset-md-3` applies `margin-left: 25%` (3/12 columns) at the `md` breakpoint to offset the column horizontally.

questions.question: Which Bootstrap 5 gutter classes set a horizontal column gutter of size 3 and vertical row gutter of size 4 on a `.row`?
options: gx-3 gy-4
gap-x-3 gap-y-4
gutter-x-3 gutter-y-4
gutter-h3 gutter-v4
questions.explanation: Bootstrap 5 uses `.gx-*` for horizontal gutters (column padding/negative row margins) and `.gy-*` for vertical row gutters between stacked items.

title: Daily Assessment: JS Setup, Variables (var, let, const), & Data Types

questions.question: What is the primary difference in scoping between `var` and `let`/`const` in JavaScript?
options: `var` is strictly asynchronous, while `let` and `const` execute synchronously
`let` and `const` can be redeclared multiple times in the same scope, but `var` cannot
`var` is block-scoped, while `let` and `const` are module-scoped only
`var` is function-scoped (or globally scoped if outside a function), while `let` and `const` are block-scoped (confined to `{}` blocks)
questions.explanation: `var` declarations ignore curly brace `{}` blocks (like `if`, `for`) and attach to the enclosing function or global window, whereas `let` and `const` strictly respect block scope.

questions.question: What happens when you access a `let` or `const` variable before its line of declaration in code?
options: The variable returns `null` automatically
The variable returns `undefined` without throwing any errors
The browser reloads the webpage
A `ReferenceError` is thrown because the variable is trapped in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
questions.explanation: While `let` and `const` declarations are hoisted, they remain uninitialized in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) from block start until declaration, throwing a `ReferenceError` if accessed early.

questions.question: Why does `const user = { name: 'Alice' }; user.name = 'Bob';` execute successfully without error?
questions.codeSnippet:
const user = { name: 'Alice' };
user.name = 'Bob';
options: JavaScript automatically converts `const` objects to `let` when properties change
Strings are mutable reference types in JavaScript
`const` prevents reassignment of the variable identifier binding, but the underlying object stored in heap memory remains mutable
The `name` property is a built-in primitive that bypasses `const` constraints
questions.explanation: `const` creates an immutable variable binding (you cannot do `user = {}`), but does not make the object value itself immutable; object properties can still be modified.

questions.question: Which of the following lists all 7 primitive data types defined in modern ECMAScript?
options: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint
number, text, flag, null, undefined, pointer, struct
string, number, boolean, array, object, function, null
integer, float, char, string, boolean, list, dict
questions.explanation: JavaScript has exactly 7 primitive types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, and bigint. Arrays, functions, and plain objects are all reference objects.

questions.question: What is the historical quirk returned by `typeof null` in JavaScript?
options: "object"
"undefined"
"primitive"
"null"
questions.explanation: Due to a legacy bug in JavaScript's original 1995 implementation where type tags stored `000` for objects and `null` was represented as a NULL pointer (all zeros), `typeof null` returns `"object"`.

questions.question: What does the expression `typeof NaN` evaluate to in JavaScript?
options: "number"
"NaN"
"error"
"undefined"
questions.explanation: `NaN` stands for 'Not-a-Number', but in the IEEE 754 floating-point specification and JavaScript type system, its official data type is `number`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Number.isNaN(value)` and the global `isNaN(value)` function?
questions.codeSnippet: Number.isNaN(value)
options: There is no difference; both are interchangeable synonyms
`Number.isNaN()` checks if the value is strictly `NaN` without type coercion, whereas global `isNaN()` coerces non-numeric values to numbers first
`Number.isNaN()` converts strings to floats automatically
Global `isNaN()` only works in Node.js, while `Number.isNaN()` is browser-only
questions.explanation: Global `isNaN('hello')` coerces `'hello'` to `NaN` and returns `true`, while `Number.isNaN('hello')` does not coerce and correctly returns `false` because `'hello'` is a string.

questions.question: Why does `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` evaluate to `false` in JavaScript?
options: Strict equality `===` only compares integer numbers in JavaScript
Binary floating-point arithmetic (IEEE 754) cannot represent certain base-10 decimal fractions with exact precision, resulting in `0.30000000000000004`
The `+` operator automatically concatenates decimal numbers as strings
JavaScript does not support mathematical addition of decimal numbers
questions.explanation: Like most languages using IEEE 754 double-precision floats, binary representation of fractions like 0.1 and 0.2 produces rounding approximations, making `0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004`.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the `BigInt` data type introduced in ES2020?
options: To represent complex numbers with real and imaginary coordinates
To store high-resolution bitmap images directly in variable memory
To safely represent and perform arithmetic on integers larger than `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` ($2^{53} - 1$)
To accelerate mathematical calculations by offloading them to GPU cores
questions.explanation: `BigInt` allows working with arbitrarily large integers beyond JavaScript's safe integer limit ($9,007,199,254,740,991$), designated with an `n` suffix (e.g., `9007199254740995n`).

questions.question: What unique property is guaranteed when creating a `Symbol` in JavaScript (e.g., `const s1 = Symbol('id'); const s2 = Symbol('id');`)?
questions.codeSnippet: in JavaScript (e.g.,
options: Symbols can only store integer numbers between 0 and 255
Every Symbol is guaranteed to be completely unique and immutable; `s1 === s2` evaluates to `false`
Symbols automatically expose all private class properties to the global window
`s1 === s2` evaluates to `true` because their description strings match
questions.explanation: `Symbol()` creates an entirely unique token every time it is called, even if provided the same descriptive string, preventing property collision on objects.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding string immutability in JavaScript?
options: Characters in strings can be modified in-place using index assignment: `str[0] = 'X'`
Strings can only contain alphanumeric ASCII characters
Strings stored in `let` variables are mutable, while `const` strings are immutable
Strings cannot be modified in-place; methods like `.replace()`, `.slice()`, and `.toUpperCase()` always return a brand new string
questions.explanation: All primitive values in JavaScript (including strings) are immutable; assigning `str[0] = 'X'` fails silently (or throws an error in strict mode), and methods return new string copies.

questions.question: What are the 8 falsy values that evaluate to `false` in a boolean context in JavaScript?
options: false, 0, "null", "undefined", [], () => {}
false, 0, "0", [], {}, null, undefined, NaN
false, -1, "false", null, undefined, NaN, Infinity
false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN
questions.explanation: In JavaScript, exactly 8 values are falsy: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n` (BigInt zero), `""` (empty string), `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`. Note that `[]`, `{}`, and `"0"` are truthy!

questions.question: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined` in JavaScript?
options: `undefined` indicates a variable has been declared but not assigned a value, while `null` is an intentional assignment representing the absence of an object value
`undefined` only exists inside functions, while `null` is global only
There is no difference; both evaluate to strict equality: `null === undefined`
`null` is a primitive type, whereas `undefined` is a complex object type
questions.explanation: `undefined` is the default uninitialized state of variables and missing return values, whereas `null` is an explicit, deliberate assignment indicating 'empty/no value'.

questions.question: What happens when you enable Strict Mode by placing `"use strict";` at the beginning of a script or function?
options: It compiles the JavaScript code into WebAssembly ahead of time
It converts all JavaScript variables into statically-typed TypeScript types
It prevents accidental global variable creation, throws errors on silent failures (like assigning to read-only properties), and disables `with` statements
It forces all asynchronous functions to execute synchronously
questions.explanation: `"use strict";` catches common coding errors by eliminating silent bugs, prohibiting undeclared variables, throwing errors on invalid property deletions, and securing `this`.

questions.question: How does JavaScript memory allocation handle Primitives versus Reference Objects?
options: Objects are stored on the Stack, while Primitives are stored on the Heap
Primitives are fixed-size values stored directly on the Call Stack, while Objects are stored on the Heap with memory address references kept on the Stack
Both Primitives and Objects are stored in the browser's IndexedDB database
JavaScript does not use Stack or Heap memory models
questions.explanation: Primitive data types have fixed sizes stored directly on the Stack. Dynamic, variable-size data (Objects, Arrays) reside in Heap memory, referenced by stack pointers.

questions.question: What is the result of `parseInt('42px', 10)` versus `Number('42px')`?
questions.codeSnippet: parseInt('42px', 10)
options: `parseInt` returns `NaN`, while `Number` returns `42`
`parseInt('42px', 10)` parses leading digits and returns `42`, while `Number('42px')` fails on non-numeric characters and returns `NaN`
Both expressions return `42`
Both expressions return `NaN`
questions.explanation: `parseInt()` parses characters sequentially until it encounters an invalid character, returning `42`. `Number()` attempts full type coercion, failing and returning `NaN` on `'42px'`.

questions.question: What is a Tagged Template Literal in JavaScript (e.g., `myTag`Hello ${name}` `)?
options: A CSS preprocessor syntax used in Sass
A regular expression pattern used to sanitize SQL queries
An HTML template tag (`<template>`) placed inside JavaScript
A syntax that allows parsing a template literal with a custom function, receiving an array of raw strings and interpolated expression arguments
questions.explanation: Tagged templates pass the string fragments and evaluated expressions to a function (e.g., `function myTag(strings, ...values)`), widely used in libraries like styled-components.

questions.question: What does the expression `Boolean([])` evaluate to in JavaScript?
options: true (All objects, including empty arrays and empty objects, are truthy)
undefined
false (Because the array contains zero elements)
NaN
questions.explanation: In JavaScript, all objects (including empty arrays `[]` and empty plain objects `{}`) are truthy; only the 8 specific falsy primitives evaluate to `false`.

questions.question: Which string method extracts a portion of a string from index `start` up to (but not including) index `end` without modifying the original string?
questions.codeSnippet: up to (but not including) index
options: str.splice(start, end)
str.pop(start, end)
str.slice(start, end)
str.cut(start, end)
questions.explanation: `str.slice(start, end)` extracts a substring up to `end` index and supports negative indices. `splice()` is an array method that mutates arrays.

questions.question: What is the Garbage Collection mechanism predominantly used by modern JavaScript engines like V8?
options: Immediate deletion of variables upon function definition
Strict reference counting without cycle detection
Mark-and-Sweep algorithm (tracing reachable objects from global roots and freeing unreachable memory)
Manual `free()` and `malloc()` memory pointer commands
questions.explanation: Modern JS engines use generational Mark-and-Sweep garbage collection, tracing memory roots (globals, active execution contexts) and sweeping unreachable objects to resolve circular reference leaks.

title: Daily Assessment: Operators, Expressions, and Conditional Statements
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is the output of the expressions `'5' + 3` and `'5' - 3` in JavaScript?
options: `'53'` (string concatenation) and `2` (arithmetic subtraction with numeric coercion)
`NaN` and `2`
questions.explanation: The `+` operator triggers string concatenation if either operand is a string (`'5' + 3 = '53'`). The `-` operator only exists for arithmetic, forcing numeric coercion (`5 - 3 = 2`).

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between abstract equality (`==`) and strict equality (`===`)?
options: `==` performs implicit type coercion before comparison, whereas `===` requires both type AND value to be strictly identical without coercion
`==` is used for objects, while `===` is used for numbers only
`==` is faster than `===` because it skips type validation
`===` converts both operands to strings before comparing
questions.explanation: Strict equality (`===`) checks both data type and value without coercion. Abstract equality (`==`) coerces operands following complex type conversion rules before comparing.

questions.question: What does the Nullish Coalescing Operator (`??`) do in an expression `const port = userPort ?? 3000;`?
options: It returns `3000` only if `userPort` is strictly `null` or `undefined`, preserving valid falsy values like `0`, `""`, or `false`
It throws an error if `userPort` is a string
It returns `3000` whenever `userPort` is any falsy value (including `0` or `""`)
It checks if `userPort` equals the integer `3000`
questions.explanation: `??` only falls back when the left operand is nullish (`null` or `undefined`). In contrast, `||` falls back on any falsy value (which wrongly overwrites `userPort = 0`).

questions.question: How does the Optional Chaining Operator (`?.`) prevent runtime crashes when accessing deeply nested properties (e.g., `user?.address?.city`)?
options: It catches the error and restarts JavaScript execution from the beginning of the file
It automatically creates empty object nodes `{}` in memory for missing properties
It forces the browser to fetch missing properties from the backend API
If any reference in the chain evaluates to `null` or `undefined`, expression evaluation short-circuits and immediately returns `undefined` instead of throwing a `TypeError`
questions.explanation: Optional chaining (`?.`) short-circuits gracefully upon reaching `null` or `undefined`, returning `undefined` instead of throwing `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`.

questions.question: What is the return value of the short-circuit expression `"Hello" && 0 && "World"`?
options: 0 (Logical AND short-circuits and returns the first falsy operand it encounters)
"World"
false
"Hello"
questions.explanation: Logical AND (`&&`) evaluates left to right: it checks `'Hello'` (truthy), moves to `0` (falsy), short-circuits immediately, and returns the actual value `0`.

questions.question: What is the return value of the expression `false || "" || "Default Value"`?
options: false
true
"Default Value" (Logical OR returns the first truthy value found, or the last value if all are falsy)
questions.explanation: Logical OR (`||`) scans left to right: `false` is falsy, `""` is falsy, so it reaches and returns the truthy value `'Default Value'`.

questions.question: What does the double NOT operator `!!value` accomplish in JavaScript?
options: It reverses the polarity of a binary bitwise byte
It explicitly casts/converts any truthy or falsy value into a pure primitive boolean (`true` or `false`)
It creates an asynchronous promise that rejects immediately
It multiplies a numeric value by negative one twice
questions.explanation: The first `!` inverts the value to an opposite boolean, and the second `!` inverts it back, providing a concise way to cast any variable to a boolean.

questions.question: What is the syntax of the Ternary Operator in JavaScript?
options: if (condition) -> expressionIfTrue else expressionIfFalse
condition ? (expressionIfFalse) : (expressionIfTrue)
condition : expressionIfTrue ? expressionIfFalse
condition ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse
questions.explanation: The ternary operator is the only JavaScript operator taking 3 operands: `condition ? ifTrue : ifFalse`, returning the evaluated branch expression.

questions.question: What happens in a `switch` statement if a matching `case` block omits the `break` statement?
options: The JavaScript engine throws a syntax compilation error and halts
Execution falls through to execute subsequent `case` blocks sequentially regardless of whether their case conditions match (Case Fallthrough)
The `default` clause is executed immediately
The `switch` statement loops indefinitely in an infinite cycle
questions.explanation: Without a `break` statement, execution continues downwards through subsequent `case` statements (fallthrough), executing their code until a `break` or `switch` end is reached.

questions.question: What comparison algorithm is used internally by the `switch (x)` statement to match `case y:` clauses?
options: Strict Equality comparison (`x === y`)
Object.is() equivalence
String conversion equality (`String(x) === String(y)`)
Abstract Equality comparison (`x == y`)
questions.explanation: `switch` statements strictly compare evaluated expressions against case clauses using `===` (e.g., `switch('5')` will NOT match `case 5:`).

questions.question: What is the 'Guard Clause' pattern in function control flow?
options: Enforcing private variable encapsulation via closures
Using cryptographic hash checks before variable assignment
Checking for invalid inputs or edge conditions at the very beginning of a function and returning early to avoid nested `if-else` blocks
Wrapping every function body in a `try-catch` block
questions.explanation: Guard clauses handle errors, invalid states, or base cases upfront with early `return` statements, keeping the main happy-path logic flat and readable.

questions.question: What is the result of the comparisons `null == undefined` and `null === undefined`?
questions.codeSnippet: null == undefined
options: `true` for both comparisons
`false` for `==`, and `true` for `===`
`false` for both comparisons
`true` for abstract equality (`==`), but `false` for strict equality (`===`)
questions.explanation: Under abstract equality rules, `null == undefined` is explicitly defined to return `true`. Under strict equality, their types differ (`object` vs `undefined`), so `null === undefined` is `false`.

questions.question: Why does `NaN === NaN` evaluate to `false` in JavaScript?
options: Because `NaN` is a dynamic function rather than a value
`NaN === NaN` actually evaluates to `true` in modern ES6+
According to IEEE 754 specifications, `NaN` is not equal to any value, including itself; `Number.isNaN()` or `Object.is()` must be used to test for `NaN`
Because `===` converts `NaN` to zero before checking
questions.explanation: IEEE 754 specifies that `NaN` represents an invalid numerical result and cannot equal anything (even another `NaN`). Use `Number.isNaN(x)` or `Object.is(NaN, NaN)`.

questions.question: What does the Logical OR Assignment operator `x ||= y` do?
options: It assigns `y` to `x` only if `x` is currently falsy (`x || (x = y)`)
It performs bitwise OR assignment on 32-bit integers
It compares `x` and `y` and returns a boolean value
It assigns `y` to `x` only if `x` is strictly `null`
questions.explanation: Logical assignment `x ||= y` evaluates `x`, and if `x` is falsy, assigns `x = y` (useful for setting default configurations).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `finally` block in a `try...catch...finally` construct?
options: To suppress all runtime errors without logging to the console
To execute only when no errors occur in the `try` block
To execute cleanup code guaranteed to run regardless of whether an exception was thrown or caught in the `try`/`catch` blocks
To restart the `try` block if an error occurred
questions.explanation: The `finally` block always executes after `try` and `catch` finish (even if `try` or `catch` contains a `return` statement), commonly used to close file handles or reset loading states.

questions.question: What is the difference between post-increment (`x++`) and pre-increment (`++x`) when assigned to a variable?
options: There is no functional difference in return value between them
`x++` is valid in loops only, while `++x` is for arithmetic expressions
`x++` returns the original value before incrementing, while `++x` increments the value first and returns the updated value
`++x` multiplies `x` by 2, while `x++` adds 1
questions.explanation: If `let x = 5; let y = x++;`, `y` becomes 5 and `x` becomes 6. If `let y = ++x;`, `x` becomes 6 and `y` becomes 6.

questions.question: What does the `instanceof` operator test in JavaScript?
options: Whether a function returns a Promise object
Whether an object's prototype chain contains the `.prototype` property of a constructor function or class
Whether a variable has been declared in local scope
Whether two objects have identical memory addresses
questions.explanation: `obj instanceof ClassName` traverses `obj`'s prototype chain to see if `ClassName.prototype` appears anywhere in the chain.

questions.question: What does the `in` operator test in the expression `'name' in user`?
options: Whether the string `'name'` is a substring inside the `user` string
Whether the specified property name exists as a direct or inherited property in the target object
Whether the `user` array contains an element with value `'name'`
Whether the `user` variable is an instance of a Map collection
questions.explanation: The `in` operator returns `true` if the specified property key exists in the object or anywhere in its prototype chain.

questions.question: How can you manually trigger a custom runtime error in JavaScript control flow?
options: System.err('Invalid input parameter');
error.raise('Invalid input parameter');
console.error('Invalid input parameter');
throw new Error('Invalid input parameter');
questions.explanation: The `throw` statement accompanied by an `Error` object instance (`throw new Error(...)`) halts execution and transfers control to the nearest `catch` block.

questions.question: What is the result of evaluating `[1, 2] == '1,2'` in JavaScript?
options: `undefined`
`false` (Because an array can never equal a string)
`true` (The array is coerced to a string via `.toString()` before abstract equality comparison)
TypeError: Invalid comparison operands
questions.explanation: When comparing an object/array to a string with `==`, JavaScript converts the object to a primitive via `[1, 2].toString()` which produces `'1,2'`, making `'1,2' == '1,2'` evaluate to `true`.

title: Daily Assessment: Loops: for, while, forEach, & Iterations
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is the classic closure output issue when using `var` inside a `for` loop with `setTimeout` (e.g., `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100); }`)?
options: It logs `3, 3, 3` because `var` is function-scoped and all timer callbacks share the exact same mutated `i` variable
It logs `0, 1, 2` as expected
It throws a `ReferenceError`
It logs `undefined, undefined, undefined`
questions.explanation: Because `var` is function-scoped, a single shared `i` variable is hoisted. By the time `setTimeout` callbacks run after the loop completes, `i` has incremented to 3. Replacing `var` with block-scoped `let` logs `0, 1, 2`.

questions.question: How does a `do...while` loop differ fundamentally from a standard `while` loop?
options: A `while` loop guarantees at least one execution, while `do...while` does not
A `do...while` loop tests its exit condition AFTER executing the body, guaranteeing that the loop body runs at least once
A `do...while` loop runs asynchronously in the background
A `do...while` loop only iterates through object properties
questions.explanation: `while` is a pre-test loop (checks condition before entering), while `do...while` is a post-test loop that always executes its block at least once before evaluating the condition.

questions.question: What is the difference in behavior between `break` and `continue` statements inside a loop?
options: `continue` restarts the loop from index 0
`break` immediately terminates the entire loop, whereas `continue` skips the remainder of the current iteration and jumps to the next cycle
`break` only works in `switch` statements and is illegal inside loops
`continue` terminates the loop, while `break` pauses for 1 second
questions.explanation: `break` exits the enclosing loop completely, while `continue` aborts the current pass and advances to the loop's next increment/condition check.

questions.question: Why is the `for...in` statement generally discouraged for iterating over standard Array elements?
options: It iterates over all enumerable property keys (including non-integer keys and inherited prototype properties) as strings, with no guaranteed index order
`for...in` throws a fatal TypeError when applied to arrays with more than 10 items
`for...in` deletes array elements as it reads them
`for...in` is deprecated in ES6 and removed from modern browsers
questions.explanation: `for...in` is designed for inspecting object keys. On arrays, it returns indices as strings (`"0"`, `"1"`), iterates over prototype properties if extended, and does not guarantee numerical order. Use `for...of` or `for` instead.

questions.question: What does the `for...of` statement iterate over in JavaScript?
options: The property key names of plain JavaScript objects
The private methods of ECMAScript classes
The values of iterable collections such as Arrays, Strings, Maps, Sets, and NodeLists
Only CSS class selectors in the DOM tree
questions.explanation: `for...of` invokes the collection's `[Symbol.iterator]` method, directly yielding each value in sequence across iterable data structures.

questions.question: What is a major limitation of `Array.prototype.forEach()` compared to a standard `for` or `for...of` loop?
options: `forEach` mutates the original array automatically
`forEach` can only process arrays with fewer than 100 elements
You cannot use `break` or `continue` statements to terminate early, and it cannot properly await asynchronous promises sequentially
`forEach` cannot access the index of each array item
questions.explanation: `forEach` always runs its callback for every element; `break` or `continue` syntax is invalid inside `forEach`, and passing an `async` callback causes all promises to fire concurrently without awaiting.

questions.question: How do you iterate over both the keys and values of a plain object using `for...of`?
options: for (const key, value in myObject) { ... }
for (const [key, value] of myObject) { ... }
for (const item of Object.items(myObject)) { ... }
for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(myObject)) { ... }
questions.explanation: Plain objects are not iterable directly with `for...of`, but `Object.entries(myObject)` returns an array of `[key, value]` pairs that can be cleanly unpacked.

questions.question: What is a Labeled Statement in JavaScript and what is its primary use case?
options: Adding accessibility labels to HTML form inputs dynamically
Prefixing a loop with an identifier label (e.g., `outerLoop: for (...)`) to allow `break outerLoop;` or `continue outerLoop;` from within deeply nested inner loops
Renaming variables in minified production bundles
Creating named bookmarks in browser history
questions.explanation: Labels (e.g., `topLoop: for (...)`) give nested loops a name, enabling a `break topLoop;` inside an inner loop to break out of multiple nested loops simultaneously.

questions.question: What is the underlying protocol required for any custom object to work with the `for...of` loop or spread operator (`...`)?
options: The object must implement the Iterable protocol by having a `[Symbol.iterator]` method that returns an Iterator with a `.next()` method
The object must be declared using the `class` keyword
The object must have a numeric `.length` property and `id` property
The object must inherit directly from `Array.prototype`
questions.explanation: The Iterable protocol requires an object to have a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method returning an iterator object with a `.next()` method that yields `{ value, done }`.

questions.question: What happens when a Generator Function (`function*`) encounters a `yield` keyword during execution?
options: It throws an asynchronous rejection to the event loop
It pauses function execution and sends the yielded value back to the caller, retaining its entire local state until `.next()` is called again
It terminates the function permanently and clears all memory variables
It restarts the generator from line 1
questions.explanation: Generators pause execution at each `yield`, returning `{ value, done: false }` to the iterator consumer, and resume right where they stopped on the next `.next()` invocation.

questions.question: What common bug occurs when mutating an array using `.splice()` inside a forward-counting `for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++)` loop?
options: The browser crashes due to a stack overflow error
The array length permanently becomes `Infinity`
Removing an item shifts remaining elements left, causing the loop to skip evaluating the element immediately following the deleted item
All remaining array numbers are converted to negative values
questions.explanation: When removing an element at index `i`, subsequent elements shift down by 1. Since `i` increments to `i + 1` next, the element that moved into index `i` is skipped. Iterating backwards (`for (let i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)`) prevents this.

questions.question: What is the essential component of any recursive function to prevent an infinite call stack loop?
options: An explicit `while (true)` wrapper statement
A `try-catch` error suppression block
A Base Case (a condition that terminates recursion and returns a value without making further recursive calls)
A `setTimeout` delay of at least 10 milliseconds
questions.explanation: Recursive functions must have at least one base case that returns a concrete result without self-calling; without it, the function triggers maximum call stack size exceeded (`RangeError`).

questions.question: What is the Big-O time complexity of two nested loops iterating over an array of length $N$ (e.g., `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) for (let j = 0; j < n; j++)`)?
options: $O(N^2)$ (Quadratic time complexity)
$O(N)$ (Linear time complexity)
$O(1)$ (Constant time complexity)
$O(\log N)$ (Logarithmic time complexity)
questions.explanation: When an outer loop runs $N$ times and an inner loop runs $N$ times for each outer pass, total operations equal $N \times N = N^2$, resulting in $O(N^2)$ quadratic complexity.

questions.question: How do you iterate asynchronously through streams or async generators sequentially in modern ES2018+ JavaScript?
options: while.await (asyncIterable.hasNext()) { ... }
for await (const item of asyncIterable) { ... }
for (await item of asyncIterable) { ... }
async for (const item in asyncIterable) { ... }
questions.explanation: The `for await...of` loop pauses execution on each iteration until the asynchronous promise returned by the async iterable resolves.

questions.question: What is the result of running `for (const key of Object.keys({ a: 1, b: 2 }))`?
questions.codeSnippet: for (const key of Object.keys({ a: 1, b: 2 }))
options: It throws a TypeError because objects cannot have keys
It iterates through `['a', 1]` and `['b', 2]` arrays
It iterates through the values `1` and `2`
It iterates through the strings `'a'` and `'b'`
questions.explanation: `Object.keys()` returns an array of an object's own enumerable string property names (here `['a', 'b']`).

questions.question: Which loop construct is best suited when the exact number of iterations is unknown in advance, but depends on an external runtime condition being met?
options: Array.prototype.forEach()
switch (condition)
for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++)
while (condition) { ... }
questions.explanation: `while` loops excel when looping depends on dynamic conditions (e.g., reading until end of file, waiting for user input, polling status) rather than a fixed count.

questions.question: What will happen if a `while` loop has a condition that never becomes false and contains no `break` or `return`?
options: An Infinite Loop occurs, blocking the JavaScript single-threaded event loop and freezing the browser tab / CPU thread
The browser offloads the loop to a background web worker automatically
The JavaScript engine automatically terminates the loop after 1000 iterations
The loop converts itself into an asynchronous Promise
questions.explanation: Because JavaScript execution is single-threaded, a synchronous infinite loop starves the event loop, causing the browser tab to hang and become unresponsive.

questions.question: In `Array.prototype.forEach((element, index, array) => ...)`, what does the second argument `index` represent?
options: The number of remaining unprocessed items
The memory pointer address of the element
The total length of the array
The numerical 0-based index of the current element being processed in the array
questions.explanation: The callback passed to `forEach` receives `(currentValue, index, array)`, where `index` is the integer position of that element.

questions.question: What is the output of `for (const char of 'JS') console.log(char);`?
questions.codeSnippet: for (const char of 'JS') console.log(char);
options: It throws a TypeError because strings are not iterable
It logs `'JS'` once as a single string
It logs `'J'` on the first iteration and `'S'` on the second iteration
It logs `0` and `1`
questions.explanation: Strings are primitive iterables in JavaScript; iterating over a string with `for...of` yields each individual character (and correctly handles Unicode code points).

questions.question: How can you optimize a traditional `for` loop over an array so it doesn't recompute the `.length` property on every single iteration?
options: Use `for (let i = 0; i != null; i++)`
Set `arr.length = Infinity` before the loop
Wrap the loop inside `eval()`
Cache the length in the initialization clause: `for (let i = 0, len = arr.length; i < len; i++)`
questions.explanation: Caching `len = arr.length` evaluates the array length once upfront rather than querying the property on each iteration (a micro-optimization in tight performance loops).

title: Daily Assessment: Function Declarations, Expressions, & Arrow Functions
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: How does hoisting differ between Function Declarations (`function foo(){}`) and Function Expressions (`const foo = function(){}`)?
questions.codeSnippet: function foo(){}
options: Function Expressions are hoisted with their body, while Function Declarations cannot be called before definition
Neither Function Declarations nor Function Expressions participate in hoisting
Function Declarations are hoisted along with their entire function body, whereas Function Expressions are hoisted as variable bindings only (trapped in TDZ or initialized to `undefined`)
Both forms are hoisted identically with full function body execution
questions.explanation: Function declarations are fully hoisted with implementation, allowing them to be invoked anywhere in the enclosing scope. Function expressions follow standard variable hoisting rules (`let`/`const` remain uninitialized in TDZ).

questions.question: How do Arrow Functions handle the `this` context compared to traditional `function` declarations?
options: Arrow functions bind `this` to the global `window` object in all cases
Arrow functions allow dynamic rebinding of `this` via `.bind()` and `.call()`
Arrow functions do not have their own `this`; they lexically inherit `this` from the enclosing outer execution context
Arrow functions automatically bind `this` to the nearest HTML DOM element
questions.explanation: Arrow functions have lexical `this` scoping, meaning they capture `this` from the enclosing scope at definition time and cannot be rebound using `.bind()`, `.call()`, or `.apply()`.

questions.question: Why can't Arrow Functions be used as Constructor Functions with the `new` keyword?
options: Arrow functions can only return primitive numbers and strings
Arrow functions require at least 3 parameters to construct an object
Arrow functions are strictly asynchronous and cannot return synchronous instances
Arrow functions lack an internal `[[Construct]]` method and do not possess a `.prototype` property
questions.explanation: Arrow functions do not have a `prototype` property or internal construct mechanism; invoking `new (() => {})` throws a `TypeError: ... is not a constructor`.

questions.question: What is a Closure in JavaScript?
options: A function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment, allowing it to access outer variables even after the outer function has finished executing
A method used to close open WebSocket connections and database pools
A built-in encryption algorithm for securing localStorage data
An automated syntax error thrown when curly braces `{}` are unmatched
questions.explanation: A closure gives a function access to its outer scope variables even after the outer function has returned and popped off the call stack, enabling data privacy and stateful factories.

questions.question: How do Rest Parameters (`...args`) differ from the legacy `arguments` object inside a function?
options: `...args` produces a genuine JavaScript Array containing only excess arguments, while `arguments` is an array-like object containing all passed arguments and lacking array methods like `.map()`
`...args` is limited to a maximum of 3 arguments
`arguments` is a true Array, while `...args` is a linked list
`...args` only works in Node.js, while `arguments` is browser-only
questions.explanation: Rest parameters (`...args`) produce a real `Array` instance (supporting `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.reduce()`), whereas `arguments` is an array-like object missing prototype array methods.

questions.question: How do you implicitly return an object literal from an arrow function without syntax ambiguity?
options: Use double curly braces: `const create = () => {{ a: 1 }};`
Wrap the object literal in parentheses: `const create = () => ({ a: 1 });`
Use brackets: `const create = () => [{ a: 1 }];`
Prefix with return keyword without braces: `const create = () => return { a: 1 };`
questions.explanation: Without parentheses, JavaScript treats `{}` as a function body block rather than an object literal. Wrapping in `({ a: 1 })` enables concise implicit object returns.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE)?
options: To create a private execution scope immediately upon definition, preventing variables from leaking into the global namespace
To force a function to run on a background Web Worker thread
To pause JavaScript execution until the DOM is fully loaded
To compile JavaScript code into native machine assembly
questions.explanation: IIFEs (`(function(){ ... })()`) create an isolated local scope, historically used in module patterns to avoid polluting the global window object.

questions.question: What is the difference between `.call()` and `.apply()` when explicitly setting a function's `this` context?
options: `.apply()` permanently binds `this`, while `.call()` does not
`.call()` accepts arguments individually as a comma-separated list, while `.apply()` accepts arguments as a single array
`.call()` is asynchronous, while `.apply()` is synchronous
`.call()` works only on arrow functions, while `.apply()` works on regular functions
questions.explanation: Both immediately invoke the function with a custom `this` value: `fn.call(context, arg1, arg2)` vs `fn.apply(context, [arg1, arg2])` (remember: Apply = Array, Call = Comma).

questions.question: What does the `.bind()` method return when called on a function?
options: A boolean indicating if the binding was successful
The evaluated return value of the immediately executed function
An exact clone of the global `window` object
A brand new function with its `this` context and optional initial parameters permanently bound
questions.explanation: Unlike `call` and `apply` which invoke immediately, `fn.bind(thisArg)` returns a new bound function that can be executed later with the locked `this` context.

questions.question: What defines a 'Pure Function' in functional programming?
options: A function that executes in under 1 millisecond
Given the same arguments, it always returns the exact same result and produces zero observable side effects (e.g., modifying globals or mutating arguments)
A function that does not use any `if-else` conditional statements
A function that contains no comments or whitespace
questions.explanation: Pure functions are deterministic (same input $\rightarrow$ same output) and have no side effects (no network calls, DOM mutation, or variable reassignments outside scope).

questions.question: What is a Higher-Order Function (HOF)?
options: A function that takes one or more functions as arguments, or returns a function as its result
A function that has a higher mathematical execution priority
A function that can only be invoked by administrators
A function declared inside the global scope of the document
questions.explanation: In JavaScript, functions are first-class citizens; functions that accept callback functions (e.g., `.map()`, `addEventListener`) or return new functions are Higher-Order Functions.

questions.question: What is Function Currying?
options: Converting synchronous code into asynchronous Promise chains
Combining two strings into a single formatted URL slug
Encrypting function source code to prevent reverse engineering
A technique of translating a function that takes multiple arguments into a sequence of nested functions that each take a single argument: $f(a, b, c) \rightarrow f(a)(b)(c)$
questions.explanation: Currying transforms a multi-argument function into unary functions called sequentially (e.g., `const add = a => b => a + b; add(2)(3) // 5`).

questions.question: Why is defining an object method as an Arrow Function generally an anti-pattern (e.g., `const obj = { val: 42, getVal: () => this.val };`)?
questions.codeSnippet: const obj = { val: 42, getVal: () => this.val };
options: `this` inside the arrow function resolves to the outer lexical scope (`window` or `undefined`) rather than the calling object `obj`, causing `obj.getVal()` to return `undefined`
Object methods must have names longer than 5 characters
Arrow functions cannot return numbers or boolean values
Arrow functions in objects cause memory leaks during garbage collection
questions.explanation: Because arrow functions do not have dynamic `this` binding, `this` does not refer to `obj`, but to the enclosing scope (usually `window` or `{}` in Node module scope).

questions.question: What does the `fn.length` property represent on a JavaScript function?
options: The number of times the function has been called during runtime
The byte size of the function in heap memory
The number of formal parameters declared before the first parameter with a default value or rest parameter
The total number of lines of source code in the function body
questions.explanation: `fn.length` indicates the function's arity—the number of expected formal arguments, excluding rest parameters (`...args`) and parameters with default values.

questions.question: When are Default Function Parameter values evaluated in JavaScript (e.g., `function getItem(id = getDefaultId())`)?
questions.codeSnippet: function getItem(id = getDefaultId())
options: Every 5 seconds in a background interval timer
At parse/compile time when the script is first loaded into the V8 engine
At call time, only when the function is invoked with an omitted argument or with `undefined`
Whenever the function is invoked with `null`
questions.explanation: Default parameters evaluate at runtime call time; if the argument is `null`, `null` is passed and the default is NOT used. The default triggers only for `undefined` or omitted arguments.

questions.question: What is the output of invoking `(function(a){ return (function(){ return a; })(); })(10);`?
options: ReferenceError: a is not defined
10 (The inner function forms a closure over parameter `a` of the outer function)
undefined
null
questions.explanation: The inner immediately-invoked function retains access to `a` via the scope chain and closure, returning `10`.

questions.question: What is Partial Application in functional programming?
options: Executing a function partially and pausing it indefinitely without returning
Fixing a number of arguments to a function, producing another function of smaller arity
Catching errors in half of the try-catch blocks
Deploying only 50% of an application's microservices to production
questions.explanation: Partial application takes a function of $N$ arguments and pre-applies $M$ arguments ($M < N$), returning a function that accepts the remaining $N - M$ arguments (e.g., using `fn.bind(null, arg1)`).

questions.question: What happens when a function without an explicit `return` statement completes execution?
options: It returns `null`
It returns `0`
It throws an unhandled error
It returns `undefined` by default
questions.explanation: In JavaScript, any function that finishes executing without encountering a `return <value>` statement implicitly returns `undefined`.

questions.question: How does the `this` keyword behave in a standalone regular function call in Strict Mode (`"use strict"; function show(){ console.log(this); } show();`)?
questions.codeSnippet: keyword behave in a standalone regular function call in Strict Mode (
options: `this` points to the global `window` object
`this` points to an empty object `{}`
`this` points to the `show` function itself
`this` is `undefined`
questions.explanation: In non-strict mode, standalone calls default `this` to the global object (`window`). In Strict Mode, `this` remains `undefined` to prevent accidental global modifications.

questions.question: What is a Memoization higher-order function designed to do?
options: Record audio notes during user typing sessions
Compress JavaScript code to reduce HTTP transfer size
Cache the results of expensive function calls based on input arguments to return cached outputs on repeated identical inputs
Limit the maximum call stack depth to 10 frames
questions.explanation: Memoization stores function results in a lookup table (e.g., an object or `Map`); if the function is called again with the same arguments, the cached result is returned immediately ($O(1)$).

questions.question: Which of the following array methods mutates the original array in-place rather than returning a new array?
options: splice()
map()
filter()
slice()
questions.explanation: `splice()`, `push()`, `pop()`, `shift()`, `unshift()`, `sort()`, and `reverse()` mutate the array in-place. Methods like `slice()`, `map()`, and `filter()` return new arrays.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of `Array.prototype.map()`?
options: To sort elements alphabetically in ascending order
To transform every element in an array by calling a provided callback function and returning a new array of the exact same length
To filter out unwanted elements based on a condition
To reduce an array into a single accumulated primitive value
questions.explanation: `.map()` applies a transformation callback to each element and produces a new array with the same number of elements containing the returned values.

questions.question: What is the return value of `Array.prototype.filter()` when no elements satisfy the predicate condition?
questions.codeSnippet: Array.prototype.filter()
options: An empty array `[]`
undefined
null
questions.explanation: `.filter()` always returns an array containing all matching elements; if none match, it returns an empty array `[]` (which is truthy).

questions.question: What are the 4 arguments passed to the callback function of `Array.prototype.reduce((acc, cur, idx, arr) => ...)`?
options: Accumulator (`acc`), Current Element (`cur`), Current Index (`idx`), and Source Array (`arr`)
Target, Source, Prototype, and Context
Previous Element, Next Element, Total Count, and Result
Key, Value, Map, and Scope
questions.explanation: The `reduce` reducer callback receives `(accumulator, currentValue, currentIndex, array)`, updating the accumulator value across iterations.

questions.question: What happens if you call `.reduce()` on an empty array without providing an initial value argument?
options: It returns `undefined` without error
It returns an empty array `[]`
It throws a `TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value`
It returns `0` automatically
questions.explanation: If no initial value is provided, `reduce` uses the first element as initial accumulator. On an empty array, there is no first element, causing a fatal `TypeError`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Array.prototype.find()` and `Array.prototype.filter()`?
questions.codeSnippet: Array.prototype.find()
options: `find()` returns the very first matching element value (or `undefined`), while `filter()` returns an array of all matching elements
There is no difference; both return arrays
`find()` mutates the array, while `filter()` is immutable
`filter()` returns the index of the element, while `find()` returns the value
questions.explanation: `find()` short-circuits on the first match and returns that single item directly. `filter()` iterates through the entire array and collects all matching items in a new array.

questions.question: What is the output of `[10, 2, 5, 1].sort()` in standard JavaScript without a custom comparator function?
options: `[10, 5, 2, 1]` (Descending numerical order)
`[10, 2, 5, 1]` (No sorting occurs)
`[1, 10, 2, 5]` (Elements are converted to strings and sorted in lexicographical/alphabetical Unicode order)
`[1, 2, 5, 10]` (Correct numerical ascending order)
questions.explanation: By default, `.sort()` converts elements to strings, sorting `'10'` before `'2'` because `'1'` precedes `'2'`. Numerical sorting requires a comparator: `.sort((a, b) => a - b)`.

questions.question: How does `[NaN].includes(NaN)` compare to `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)`?
options: Both return `true`
`[NaN].includes(NaN)` returns `true`, while `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` returns `-1`
Both return `-1`
`includes` returns `false`, while `indexOf` returns `0`
questions.explanation: `indexOf()` uses Strict Equality (`===`), and since `NaN !== NaN`, it fails to find `NaN` (-1). `includes()` uses the SameValueZero algorithm and correctly detects `NaN`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Array.prototype.some()` and `Array.prototype.every()`?
questions.codeSnippet: Array.prototype.some()
options: `every()` returns an array, while `some()` returns a boolean
`some()` mutates the array, while `every()` does not
`some()` only checks even numbers, while `every()` checks odd numbers
`some()` returns `true` if AT LEAST ONE element passes the test, while `every()` returns `true` only if ALL elements pass the test
questions.explanation: `some()` checks for existential condition ($exists$) and short-circuits on the first truthy value. `every()` checks universal condition ($ orall$) and short-circuits on the first falsy value.

questions.question: What does `[1, [2, [3, 4]]].flat(2)` return?
options: [1, 2, 3, 4] (Flattens nested arrays up to a depth of 2)
questions.explanation: `.flat(depth)` recursively flattens sub-arrays up to the specified depth; depth 2 completely flattens a 2-level deeply nested array into `[1, 2, 3, 4]`.

questions.question: What does `Array.prototype.flatMap()` do?
options: It sorts and filters an array simultaneously
It converts a 2D array into an HTML table
It maps each element using a mapping function, then flattens the resulting array by a depth of 1 in a single efficient pass
It compresses array data into a zip file
questions.explanation: `arr.flatMap(fn)` is equivalent to `arr.map(fn).flat(1)`, efficiently transforming and unwrapping arrays in one operation.

questions.question: How do modern ES2023 immutable array methods like `.toSorted()` and `.toReversed()` differ from `.sort()` and `.reverse()`?
options: They execute asynchronously using Web Workers
They convert array values into strings permanently
They sort arrays in reverse order only
They return a brand new sorted/reversed copy of the array without mutating the original source array
questions.explanation: ES2023 introduced non-mutating equivalents: `toSorted()`, `toReversed()`, `toSpliced()`, and `with()`, allowing functional manipulation without mutating source data.

questions.question: What is the modern, concise idiom to remove duplicate primitive values from an array `[1, 2, 2, 3, 1]`?
options: array.filter(Boolean)
[...new Set(array)]
Array.unique(array)
array.deduplicate()
questions.explanation: Passing an array into a `Set` strips all duplicates because Set values must be unique; spreading back into an array `[...new Set(array)]` yields `[1, 2, 3]`.

questions.question: How can you generate an array of numbers from 0 to 9 in a single line using `Array.from()`?
options: new Array(10).range();
Array.generate(0, 10);
Array.from(10);
Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) => i);
questions.explanation: `Array.from({ length: 10 }, (v, i) => i)` creates an array of length 10 and executes the map callback for each index, generating `[0, 1, 2, ..., 9]`.

questions.question: How do iteration methods like `.forEach()` and `.map()` treat 'sparse' array holes (e.g., `const arr = [1, , 3];`)?
questions.codeSnippet: treat 'sparse' array holes (e.g.,
options: They throw a `ReferenceError` on empty slots
They stop loop execution immediately upon hitting a hole
They skip empty holes entirely without executing the callback on unassigned indices
They convert empty holes into `undefined` and execute the callback
questions.explanation: Array prototype methods (like `forEach`, `map`, `filter`) skip unassigned sparse holes, only invoking the callback for indices that actually exist on the array.

questions.question: What is the modern standard ECMAScript method to group array elements by a categorical key (e.g., grouping users by role)?
options: users.groupBy('role')
users.categorize(user => user.role)
Array.group(users, 'role')
Object.groupBy(users, user => user.role)
questions.explanation: `Object.groupBy(items, callback)` (standardized in ES2024) groups items into an object whose keys are the return values of the callback function.

questions.question: How can you safely create a true Deep Clone of a nested multi-dimensional array in modern JavaScript?
options: myArray.slice()
structuredClone(myArray)
Array.from(myArray)
[...myArray]
questions.explanation: Spread `[...arr]` and `.slice()` only perform a shallow copy (nested arrays still share references). `structuredClone()` recursively creates a true deep copy.

questions.question: What does the expression `['a', 'b', 'c'].slice(1, 3)` return?
options: ['b', 'c'] (Extracts elements from index 1 up to, but not including, index 3)
questions.explanation: `slice(start, end)` extracts items starting at index 1 (`'b'`) up to index 3 (exclusive), returning `['b', 'c']` without modifying the original array.

questions.question: How do you find the maximum numeric value in an array `[12, 45, 8, 99]` using `reduce`?
options: arr.reduce((max, cur) => max + cur, 0)
arr.reduce((max, cur) => cur > max ? cur : max, arr[0])
arr.reduce((max, cur) => cur < max ? cur : max)
arr.reduce(Math.sum)
questions.explanation: The reducer compares the accumulator `max` with each `cur` element, carrying forward the higher value across the array to find `99`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Array.of(7)` and `new Array(7)`?
options: `Array.of(7)` throws an error because it requires at least 2 arguments
`Array.of(7)` creates 7 empty slots, while `new Array(7)` creates `[7]`
`Array.of(7)` creates an array with one element `[7]`, whereas `new Array(7)` creates an empty array with length 7 and 7 sparse holes
Both expressions create the exact same array `[7]`
questions.explanation: `new Array(7)` creates a sparse array with `length = 7` and no elements. `Array.of(7)` avoids this single-number constructor trap and returns `[7]`.

title: Daily Assessment: Object Manipulation & Higher-Order Functions

questions.question: What is the difference between accessing object properties using Dot Notation (`obj.prop`) versus Bracket Notation (`obj[prop]`)?
options: Dot notation creates a new property if it does not exist, while bracket notation does not
Bracket notation only works for arrays, not plain objects
Dot notation is asynchronous, while bracket notation is synchronous
Bracket notation allows dynamic property evaluation, variables as keys, and keys containing spaces or special characters; dot notation only accepts static valid identifiers
questions.explanation: Bracket notation `obj[expression]` dynamically evaluates the expression inside brackets (e.g., `obj['user-age']` or `obj[myVar]`), whereas dot notation requires a static identifier.

questions.question: What does the Computed Property Name syntax accomplish in an object literal (e.g., `const key = 'role'; const user = { [key]: 'admin' };`)?
questions.codeSnippet:
const key = 'role';
const user = { [key]: 'admin' };
options: It marks the property as private and non-enumerable
It converts the property value into an encrypted hash
It dynamically evaluates the expression inside brackets `[]` and uses the resulting value as the object's property name
It binds a getter function to the property automatically
questions.explanation: Computed property names allow dynamic keys inside object literals without needing a secondary assignment (`obj[key] = 'admin'`).

questions.question: How does Object Destructuring with property renaming work (e.g., renaming `id` to `userId`)?
options: const { id: userId } = user;
const { userId = id } = user;
const { id as userId } = user;
const { id -> userId } = user;
questions.explanation: The syntax `const { propertyName: newVariableName } = object;` unpacks `propertyName` and assigns its value to `newVariableName`.

questions.question: What is the key limitation of copying nested objects using the Spread Operator (`const clone = { ...original };`)?
questions.codeSnippet: const clone = { ...original };
options: It converts the object into an array automatically
It fails and throws a runtime error if the object has more than 5 properties
It removes all string properties from the clone
It creates a Shallow Copy only; nested child objects and arrays are copied by reference and still share memory with the original object
questions.explanation: Object spread `{ ...obj }` only copies top-level properties. If a property is a nested object (`user.address`), the clone only receives a copy of the pointer address.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between `Object.freeze()` and `Object.seal()`?
questions.codeSnippet: Object.freeze()
options: `Object.freeze()` makes an object completely immutable (cannot add, delete, or modify existing properties), while `Object.seal()` prevents adding/deleting properties but allows modifying existing writable properties
There is no difference; they are exact aliases
`Object.seal()` converts all properties to functions, while `freeze` does not
`Object.freeze()` only works on arrays, while `Object.seal()` works on objects
questions.explanation: `Object.freeze()` sets `writable: false` and `configurable: false` on all properties. `Object.seal()` sets `configurable: false` (no add/delete) but leaves `writable: true` (existing values can change).

questions.question: Why should developers use `Object.hasOwn(obj, 'prop')` instead of `obj.hasOwnProperty('prop')` in modern JavaScript?
questions.codeSnippet: Object.hasOwn(obj, 'prop')
options: `Object.hasOwn()` also checks prototype chain properties
`Object.hasOwn()` runs 100x faster by compiling directly to GPU shaders
`obj.hasOwnProperty()` is deprecated and removed from modern browsers
`Object.hasOwn()` is safe to use on objects created without a prototype (e.g., `Object.create(null)`) or objects where `hasOwnProperty` has been overridden
questions.explanation: Calling `obj.hasOwnProperty()` on an object created via `Object.create(null)` crashes with a `TypeError`. ES2022's `Object.hasOwn(obj, prop)` safely handles all objects.

questions.question: What does `Object.fromEntries()` do?
questions.codeSnippet: Object.fromEntries()
options: It transforms a list of key-value pairs (such as a 2D array `[['a', 1], ['b', 2]]` or a `Map`) into a plain JavaScript object
It checks if an object contains any entries
It extracts all values from an object into a single array
It deletes all non-enumerable properties from an object
questions.explanation: `Object.fromEntries()` is the inverse of `Object.entries()`, turning array pairs or Maps back into plain `{ a: 1, b: 2 }` objects.

questions.question: In property descriptors via `Object.defineProperty()`, what does setting `enumerable: false` do?
questions.codeSnippet: Object.defineProperty()
options: The property becomes read-only and cannot be modified
The property throws an error whenever accessed
The property will not show up in `for...in` loops, `Object.keys()`, or `JSON.stringify()`, but remains accessible via direct property lookup
The property is deleted from memory permanently
questions.explanation: Non-enumerable properties are hidden from general iteration (`for...in`, `Object.keys`, `Object.entries`) while remaining directly readable and usable.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a JavaScript `Map` and a plain Object (`{}`)?
options: `Map` cannot be iterated using loops, while plain objects can
`Map` allows keys of ANY data type (including functions, objects, and numbers), preserves insertion order, and has an $O(1)$ `.size` property
Plain objects can only hold up to 100 properties, while `Map` has no limit
Plain objects encrypt their property keys, while `Map` stores plain text
questions.explanation: A `Map` supports keys of any type (e.g., objects as keys), maintains precise insertion order, has `.size`, and avoids default prototype key collisions.

questions.question: How does a `WeakMap` differ from a standard `Map` in terms of memory management?
options: `WeakMap` deletes all stored data after 60 seconds automatically
`WeakMap` keys must be Objects, and references to keys are held 'weakly', allowing them to be garbage-collected if no other references exist elsewhere
`WeakMap` cannot store values; it only stores keys
`WeakMap` consumes more memory because it creates duplicate backups
questions.explanation: In `WeakMap`, object keys do not prevent garbage collection, making `WeakMap` ideal for private state storage and DOM node caching without causing memory leaks.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Debounce function and a Throttle function?
options: Debounce delays execution until a certain time has elapsed since the LAST call, while Throttle guarantees execution at fixed maximum regular intervals
Throttle cancels all future calls, while Debounce accelerates execution
There is no difference; they are interchangeable terms
Debounce is for mouse clicks, while Throttle is exclusively for audio volume
questions.explanation: Debouncing waits for user activity to stop (ideal for search autocomplete typing); Throttling limits continuous triggers to once every $N$ milliseconds (ideal for scroll/resize events).

questions.question: What is Function Composition in JavaScript (e.g., `compose(f, g)(x)`)?
options: Combining two strings into a single CSS class name
Passing the output of one function as the input to the next function, evaluated from right to left: $f(g(x))$
Inheriting properties from multiple parent prototype classes
Executing two asynchronous functions in parallel using `Promise.all`
questions.explanation: Composition combines mathematical functions such that $(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$, cleanly separating small, reusable transformation steps.

questions.question: What is the Prototype Chain lookup mechanism in JavaScript when accessing `obj.prop`?
options: JavaScript creates the missing property automatically with value `null`
JavaScript queries the backend database for missing properties
JavaScript checks `obj` for the property; if not found, it traverses up `obj.__proto__` through successive prototypes until found or reaching `null`
JavaScript searches all active variables in global scope before checking the object
questions.explanation: Property lookup inspects the object instance, then delegates upward through its prototype chain (`Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`) until reaching `Object.prototype`, ending at `null`.

questions.question: How do you create an object that has NO prototype whatsoever (a truly dictionary-like object with no `toString` or `hasOwnProperty` methods)?
options: Object.create(null)
Object.freeze({})
new Object(null)
const obj = {}; obj.prototype = null;
questions.explanation: `Object.create(null)` creates a clean object without inheriting from `Object.prototype`, preventing prototype pollution attacks and prototype key conflicts in dictionary maps.

questions.question: What does `structuredClone(obj)` handle that `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` fails to support?
questions.codeSnippet: structuredClone(obj)
options: HTML5 video playback controls
CSS stylesheets and media queries
SQL database connection credentials
Circular references, `Date` objects, `Map`, `Set`, `RegExp`, `ArrayBuffer`, and `BigInt` data types
questions.explanation: `structuredClone()` natively supports complex structures (circular references, Maps, Sets, Dates, BigInts), whereas JSON serialization drops Dates into strings, deletes `undefined`/Functions/Symbols, and crashes on BigInt/circular references.

questions.question: What is the role of Getters (`get`) and Setters (`set`) in JavaScript objects?
options: They allow an object to send HTTP GET and POST requests automatically
They convert synchronous functions into Web Worker threads
They define accessor properties that execute functions behind the scenes when reading or assigning a property value
They restrict an object to holding only string data
questions.explanation: Getters and setters bind an object property to a function, enabling computed properties, data encapsulation, and input validation upon assignment.

questions.question: What is the result of spreading two objects with identical keys: `const result = { ...{ a: 1, b: 2 }, ...{ b: 99, c: 3 } };`?
options: TypeError: Duplicate object keys
{ a: 1, b: 99, c: 3 } (The last spread object overrides conflicting keys from earlier objects)
questions.explanation: When spreading objects, property conflicts resolve in favor of the rightmost object; `{ b: 99 }` overrides `{ b: 2 }`, resulting in `{ a: 1, b: 99, c: 3 }`.

questions.question: What does `Object.values(obj)` return?
questions.codeSnippet: Object.values(obj)
options: A string summary of the object's constructor
A set of the object's property names
An array containing all of the object's own enumerable property values in standard iteration order
A boolean indicating if the object has values
questions.explanation: `Object.values()` returns an array of the values corresponding to an object's own enumerable string-keyed properties.

questions.question: What is a 'Set' collection in JavaScript and what is its most defining characteristic?
options: A fixed-size array that cannot grow or shrink
A collection of values where each value must be unique; duplicate values are automatically discarded
A key-value map where keys must be functions
An array that only stores negative floating point numbers
questions.explanation: `Set` stores unique values of any type, providing fast $O(1)$ membership checks with `.has()` and automatic deduplication.

questions.question: Why is `Object.freeze()` described as a 'Shallow Freeze'?
questions.codeSnippet: Object.freeze()
options: Because it only works inside the browser Developer Console
Because it only freezes immediate top-level properties; nested child objects remain completely mutable unless recursively frozen
Because it only freezes numbers and leaves strings mutable
Because the freeze effect automatically expires after 10 minutes
questions.explanation: `Object.freeze()` only locks the direct surface properties of an object. If a property references another object (`obj.nested.x = 10`), the nested object can still be modified unless deeply frozen.
