questions.question: What is the return value of `document.getElementById('nonExistentId')` when no matching element exists in the DOM?
questions.codeSnippet: document.getElementById('nonExistentId')
options: null
Throws a `NotFoundError`
undefined
Empty NodeList `[]`
questions.explanation: `document.getElementById()` and `document.querySelector()` return `null` if no element matching the ID/selector exists in the document.

questions.question: What is the key difference in behavior between `document.querySelectorAll('.card')` and `document.getElementsByClassName('card')`?
questions.codeSnippet: document.querySelectorAll('.card')
options: `querySelectorAll` is synchronous, while `getElementsByClassName` is asynchronous
`querySelectorAll` mutates the DOM, while `getElementsByClassName` does not
`getElementsByClassName` supports CSS pseudo-selectors, while `querySelectorAll` does not
`querySelectorAll` returns a static (non-live) `NodeList`, while `getElementsByClassName` returns a live `HTMLCollection` that automatically updates when DOM elements change
questions.explanation: A live `HTMLCollection` reflects DOM mutations immediately in memory, whereas a static `NodeList` returned by `querySelectorAll()` is a snapshot of elements at the moment of query execution.

questions.question: Consider the code: `element.innerHTML = 'User & Admin';`. What will `element.textContent` evaluate to?
questions.codeSnippet: element.innerHTML = 'User & Admin';
options: "User & Admin"
"User & Admin"
"User & Admin"
"User & Admin"
questions.explanation: `textContent` extracts the raw text content of all descendants without HTML tags, decoding HTML entities like `&` into literal `&` characters.

questions.question: Which `classList` method toggles a CSS class: adding it if absent, and removing it if already present?
options: element.classList.switch('active')
element.classList.flip('active')
element.classList.toggle('active')
element.classList.change('active')
questions.explanation: `.classList.toggle(className)` adds the class if it does not exist on the element, or removes it if it does exist, returning a boolean indicating its new presence.

questions.question: How do you correctly set a CSS custom property (variable) on an element using JavaScript?
options: element.style.primaryColor = '#3b82f6';
element.style['--primary-color'] = '#3b82f6';
element.style.setProperty('--primary-color', '#3b82f6');
element.setAttribute('css-var', '--primary-color: #3b82f6');
questions.explanation: CSS custom properties (variables) must be set using the standard `style.setProperty(propertyName, value)` method because kebab-case `--var` syntax is not accessible via direct camelCase property assignment.

questions.question: Given `<button id="btn" data-user-role="admin" data-action-id="105"></button>`, how do you access the `data-user-role` attribute via JavaScript dataset?
questions.codeSnippet: <button id="btn" data-user-role="admin" data-action-id="105"></button>
options: btn.dataset.userRole
btn.dataset['data-user-role']
btn.data.userRole
btn.dataset.user_role
questions.explanation: The HTML `data-*` attributes are mapped to JavaScript's `dataset` object by converting hyphenated attribute names into camelCase (`data-user-role` $\rightarrow$ `dataset.userRole`).

questions.question: What is the difference between `element.childNodes` and `element.children`?
options: `childNodes` only works on `<div>` tags
`children` includes text nodes, while `childNodes` excludes them
There is no difference; both return identical HTMLCollections
`childNodes` includes all child nodes (Element nodes, Text nodes, and Comment nodes), while `children` includes ONLY Element nodes (`Node.ELEMENT_NODE`)
questions.explanation: `element.childNodes` returns a NodeList containing whitespace text nodes, comments, and elements. `element.children` returns an HTMLCollection containing strictly HTML element tags.

questions.question:
Where does `element.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', '

New

')` insert the new HTML markup?
questions.codeSnippet:
element.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', '

New

')
options: Inside the element, as its very last child node
After the element itself as a following sibling
Inside the element, as its very first child node
Before the element itself as a preceding sibling
questions.explanation: The positions for `insertAdjacentHTML` are: `beforebegin` (before element), `afterbegin` (inside, first child), `beforeend` (inside, last child), and `afterend` (after element).

questions.question: Why is creating elements using `document.createDocumentFragment()` considered best practice when adding 1,000 items to the DOM?
questions.codeSnippet: document.createDocumentFragment()
options: It automatically encrypts text nodes to prevent XSS attacks
It renders the items asynchronously on a Web Worker thread
It creates a lightweight in-memory container that batches all DOM nodes, triggering only a single Reflow and Repaint when appended to the document
It compresses the HTML tags into binary code before appending
questions.explanation: Appending elements one-by-one triggers repeated browser reflows and repaints. Appending all elements to a `DocumentFragment` first and then inserting the fragment into the DOM incurs only one reflow.

questions.question: What does `element.cloneNode(true)` do compared to `element.cloneNode(false)`?
questions.codeSnippet: element.cloneNode(true)
options: `cloneNode(true)` clones event listeners, while `cloneNode(false)` does not
`cloneNode(true)` performs a deep clone copying the element, its attributes, and all child descendant nodes, while `cloneNode(false)` clones only the parent element shell
`cloneNode(true)` creates an exact shallow copy with shared child references
`cloneNode(false)` deletes the original element from the DOM
questions.explanation: The boolean parameter controls recursion: `true` clones the entire subtree (all descendants and text), while `false` (or omitted) clones only the single element and its attributes (without attached event listeners).

questions.question: What information is returned by `element.getBoundingClientRect()`?
questions.codeSnippet: element.getBoundingClientRect()
options: The boundary dimensions of the user's physical monitor display
The total number of CSS classes attached to the element
The exact GPS coordinates of the client computer
A `DOMRect` object with the element's `width`, `height`, and floating-point pixel positions (`top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left`, `x`, `y`) relative to the viewport
questions.explanation: `getBoundingClientRect()` returns size and position coordinates relative to the top-left of the current browser viewport.

questions.question: What is the difference between `node.remove()` and `parent.removeChild(node)`?
questions.codeSnippet: parent.removeChild(node)
options: `node.remove()` only works in Node.js, while `removeChild` is for browsers
`removeChild()` is deprecated and removed from modern browsers
`node.remove()` deletes the element from memory permanently, while `removeChild` keeps it cached in localStorage
`node.remove()` can be called directly on the element without referencing its parent, while `removeChild()` must be called on the explicit parent node
questions.explanation: Modern DOM Level 4 introduced `element.remove()` allowing an element to remove itself directly (`el.remove()`), superseding the verbose `el.parentNode.removeChild(el)`.

questions.question: What does `element.closest('.card')` do?
questions.codeSnippet: element.closest('.card')
options: It measures the pixel distance between `element` and the nearest `.card`
It traverses upward through the element and its ancestors in the DOM tree, returning the first ancestor that matches the selector `.card` (or `null`)
It queries all child elements inside `element` matching `.card`
It finds the closest sibling element to the right
questions.explanation: `element.closest(selector)` searches up the ancestor chain starting from the element itself, returning the closest matching element or `null`.

questions.question: Which of the following operations is notorious for triggering forced synchronous layout (layout thrashing / reflow) inside a loop?
options: Alternating between writing to DOM styles (`el.style.width = ...`) and reading geometry properties (`el.offsetWidth`) in every iteration
Calling `console.log()` inside a loop
Pushing items into a JavaScript array
Using `const` instead of `let` in variable assignments
questions.explanation: Reading geometry (like `offsetWidth`, `clientHeight`) forces the browser to immediately recalculate layout if styles were mutated in the same frame, causing severe layout thrashing.

questions.question: How do you smoothly scroll the webpage so that a specific element `#pricing` is centered in the viewport?
options: window.scroll({ element: '#pricing', transition: 500 });
document.querySelector('#pricing').scrollToView('center');
window.scrollToElement('#pricing', 'smooth');
document.querySelector('#pricing').scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'center' });
questions.explanation: `element.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'center' })` provides native smooth scrolling alignment to the vertical center of the viewport.

questions.question: What is the most concise modern method to remove all child nodes from a container element `parent`?
options: parent.deleteAll();
parent.replaceChildren();
parent.childNodes.clear();
parent.empty();
questions.explanation: `parent.replaceChildren()` (without arguments) empties all children from an element in a single operation, faster and cleaner than `parent.innerHTML = ''`.

questions.question: Why is setting `element.innerHTML = userInput;` dangerous when `userInput` comes from untrusted user input?
options: It prevents search engines from indexing the website
It crashes the V8 JavaScript compiler due to syntax overflow
It creates a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability by allowing malicious `` scripts to execute in the victim's browser
It deletes all cookies stored on the backend server
questions.explanation: Assigning unescaped user strings directly to `innerHTML` exposes the application to XSS attacks. Safe alternatives include `element.textContent` or sanitizing with DOMPurify.

questions.question: What does `element.matches('button.primary:not([disabled])')` return?
questions.codeSnippet: element.matches('button.primary:not([disabled])')
options: The index of the element in the DOM tree
A boolean `true` if the element would be selected by the specified CSS selector, or `false` otherwise
A new cloned DOM node matching the criteria
An array of all matching child elements
questions.explanation: `element.matches(selector)` tests whether the element matches a CSS selector string, returning `true` or `false`.

questions.question: How do you replace an existing DOM element `oldNode` with a `newNode` directly in modern DOM API?
options: oldNode.changeTo(newNode);
oldNode.replaceWith(newNode);
oldNode.swap(newNode);
document.replace(oldNode, newNode);
questions.explanation: The `ChildNode.replaceWith()` method replaces an element in its parent's children list with one or more replacement nodes directly.

questions.question: What is the result of running `element.setAttribute('disabled', 'false')` on an HTML button?
questions.codeSnippet: element.setAttribute('disabled', 'false')
options: The button becomes disabled (because `disabled` is a boolean attribute whose presence alone disables the button, regardless of value string)
The button is enabled because the value is `'false'`
The browser throws a TypeError
The attribute is removed from the DOM
questions.explanation: In HTML, boolean attributes (like `disabled`, `readonly`, `checked`) are active whenever the attribute exists; `setAttribute('disabled', 'false')` still adds the attribute, disabling the button. To enable it, use `removeAttribute('disabled')` or `btn.disabled = false`.

title: Daily Assessment: Event Listeners, Bubbling, and Delegation Patterns
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI
lessonTitle: Event Listeners, Bubbling, and Delegation Patterns

questions.question:
Why does the following attempt to remove an event listener fail? 
`btn.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('Hi')); btn.removeEventListener('click', () => console.log('Hi'));`
questions.codeSnippet:
btn.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('Hi'));
btn.removeEventListener('click', () => console.log('Hi'));
options: Event listeners cannot be removed once attached in modern JavaScript
`removeEventListener` requires passing the string name of the event handler function
The arrow function in `removeEventListener` creates a brand new function reference in memory, which does not match the reference registered in `addEventListener`
`removeEventListener` only works for mouse hover events, not click events
questions.explanation: `removeEventListener()` requires the exact same function reference that was passed to `addEventListener()`. Passing a new inline anonymous function creates a different memory reference that fails to match.

questions.question: What are the three sequential phases of DOM Event Propagation when a user clicks on an element?
options: 1. Trigger Phase -> 2. Execution Phase -> 3. Termination Phase
1. Bubbling Phase -> 2. Target Phase -> 3. Capturing Phase
1. DOM Phase -> 2. CSSOM Phase -> 3. Render Phase
1. Capturing Phase (Window down to target) -> 2. Target Phase -> 3. Bubbling Phase (Target up to Window)
questions.explanation: DOM events originate at `window` and travel downward through ancestors during Capturing, trigger at the target, and bubble back upward through ancestors during Bubbling.

questions.question: How do you register an event listener to execute specifically during the Capturing Phase rather than the default Bubbling Phase?
options: Set `event.phase = 'capture'` inside the handler
Pass `'capture'` as the event type name: `btn.addEventListener('capture:click', fn)`
Pass `{ capture: true }` (or boolean `true`) as the third argument to `addEventListener`
Wrap the handler function inside `requestAnimationFrame`
questions.explanation: By default, `addEventListener` listens in the bubbling phase (`capture: false`). Setting `{ capture: true }` (or `true`) intercepts the event on its way down during the capture phase.

questions.question: What is the difference between `event.stopPropagation()` and `event.stopImmediatePropagation()`?
questions.codeSnippet: event.stopPropagation()
options: There is no difference; both are identical aliases
`stopPropagation()` prevents the event from traveling further up/down the DOM tree, while `stopImmediatePropagation()` also prevents other listeners attached to the SAME element from executing
`stopImmediatePropagation()` prevents default browser actions like link navigation, while `stopPropagation` does not
`stopPropagation()` deletes the event from browser history permanently
questions.explanation: If multiple listeners are registered on the same element, `stopPropagation()` allows sibling listeners on that element to finish, whereas `stopImmediatePropagation()` stops sibling listeners on that element immediately as well.

questions.question: What is the primary architectural benefit of the 'Event Delegation' pattern (e.g., listening for item clicks on a parent `<ul>` container)?
options: It converts click events into touch events on mobile devices
It bypasses all browser CORS restrictions on network requests
It improves memory efficiency by using a single event listener and automatically handles events for dynamically added child elements without reattaching listeners
It accelerates CSS animation frame rates to 120 FPS
questions.explanation: Event delegation leverages bubbling by placing a single listener on a common parent. It catches events from existing and future dynamically added children while saving memory.

questions.question: In an event handler attached to a parent container, what is the difference between `event.target` and `event.currentTarget`?
options: `event.target` is the actual innermost element that was clicked, while `event.currentTarget` is the element to which the event listener was attached
`event.target` is only defined in the capture phase, while `event.currentTarget` is in bubbling
There is no difference; they always point to the exact same DOM node
`event.currentTarget` is always the global `window` object
questions.explanation: When clicking a `<span>` inside a `<button>` with a listener on `<div class="container">`: `e.target` is the `<span>`, and `e.currentTarget` (or `this` in regular functions) is the `<div>`.

questions.question: How do you configure an event listener so that it automatically unregisters and removes itself after executing exactly once?
options: element.addEventListener('click:once', handler);
element.addSingleListener('click', handler);
element.addEventListener('click', handler, { single: true });
element.addEventListener('click', handler, { once: true });
questions.explanation: The `{ once: true }` option invokes the listener once and then automatically removes it, eliminating manual `removeEventListener()` cleanup code.

questions.question: Why should developers set `{ passive: true }` on touch and scroll event listeners (e.g., `window.addEventListener('scroll', fn, { passive: true })`)?
questions.codeSnippet: { passive: true }
options: It reduces the frequency of scroll events to 1 per second
It informs the browser that the handler will never call `event.preventDefault()`, allowing the browser to scroll the page smoothly without waiting for JavaScript execution
It disables mouse clicks while scrolling is active
It pauses scrolling whenever CPU utilization exceeds 80%
questions.explanation: Without `{ passive: true }`, scrolling can stutter because the browser must wait for the JS thread to finish to check if `preventDefault()` is called. Passive listeners guarantee smooth scrolling performance.

questions.question: How do you dispatch a custom event named `'cartUpdated'` carrying data `{ itemCount: 5 }` to other components in the application?
options: element.triggerEvent('cartUpdated', { itemCount: 5 });
element.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('cartUpdated', { detail: { itemCount: 5 }, bubbles: true }));
window.emit('cartUpdated', { detail: 5 });
document.sendEvent(new Event('cartUpdated', { count: 5 }));
questions.explanation: Custom events are created with `new CustomEvent(name, { detail: data, bubbles: true })` and fired via `element.dispatchEvent(customEvent)`.

questions.question: Which keyboard event property provides the human-readable character generated by the keypress (e.g., `'Enter'`, `'a'`, `'Escape'`) regardless of keyboard layout?
options: event.keyCode
event.key
event.which
event.charNumber
questions.explanation: `event.key` is the modern standard property returning key characters (e.g., `'Enter'`, `'ArrowUp'`, `'Escape'`). Legacy `keyCode` and `which` are deprecated.

questions.question: What is the difference between the mouse events `mouseenter` and `mouseover`?
options: `mouseenter` is triggered only on mouse click, while `mouseover` is on hover
There is no difference; both bubble identically
`mouseover` only works for touchscreens, while `mouseenter` is for mouse only
`mouseenter` does NOT bubble and only fires when entering the element itself, while `mouseover` bubbles up the DOM tree and fires when entering any child element
questions.explanation: `mouseenter` / `mouseleave` do not bubble (preventing jittery firing when moving across child boundaries), whereas `mouseover` / `mouseout` bubble continuously.

questions.question: What is the key difference between the `DOMContentLoaded` event and the `window.onload` (load) event?
options: `DOMContentLoaded` is only supported in Internet Explorer
`window.onload` fires before `DOMContentLoaded`
`window.onload` only fires when the user clicks on the page
`DOMContentLoaded` fires as soon as the HTML document is fully parsed and DOM tree is built, while `window.onload` waits for all external resources (images, stylesheets, frames) to finish loading
questions.explanation: `DOMContentLoaded` triggers early when HTML parsing is complete (ideal for initializing UI scripts), whereas `window.load` fires later after all external images, fonts, and sub-resources finish downloading.

questions.question: How can you cleanly cancel multiple event listeners simultaneously using modern `AbortController`?
options: Call `window.clearAllListeners()`
Pass `{ signal: controller.signal }` to all `addEventListener` calls, then invoke `controller.abort()` when teardown is required
Delete the parent DOM node and recreate it
Set `document.events.enabled = false`
questions.explanation: Passing an `AbortSignal` (`{ signal: controller.signal }`) allows canceling single or grouped event listeners instantly by calling `controller.abort()`.

questions.question: What does `event.preventDefault()` do when called inside an anchor tag (`<a>`) click event listener?
questions.codeSnippet: event.preventDefault()
options: It prevents the browser from navigating to the URL specified in the anchor's `href` attribute
It prevents other click listeners from executing on the same anchor
It deletes the `href` attribute from the anchor element in the DOM
It closes the current browser tab immediately
questions.explanation: `event.preventDefault()` stops the default browser action associated with that event (e.g., preventing page navigation on links, form submission refreshes, or context menu popups).

questions.question: What is the value of `this` inside an event listener callback written as an Arrow Function: `btn.addEventListener('click', (e) => { console.log(this); });`?
questions.codeSnippet: inside an event listener callback written as an Arrow Function:
options: The outer lexical scope (usually the global `window` object or enclosing class instance)
The `<button>` element that was clicked
`null`
The `MouseEvent` object itself
questions.explanation: Because arrow functions have lexical `this`, `this` does NOT point to the event target button (`e.currentTarget`), but inherits `this` from where the listener was defined.

questions.question: What is the difference between `input` and `change` events on an `<input type="text">` element?
questions.codeSnippet: <input type="text">
options: `input` only works on numbers, while `change` is for text
`change` fires on every keystroke, while `input` fires only when pressing Enter
`input` fires synchronously on every keystroke or character insertion, while `change` fires only after the input loses focus (`blur`) and its value has changed
There is no difference; both fire synchronously on every character change
questions.explanation: The `input` event updates in real time on every character typed or pasted; `change` commits only when the user commits the change by blurring (clicking away) or pressing Enter.

questions.question: Which event must have `event.preventDefault()` called inside its handler to allow an element to act as a valid Drop Target for Drag-and-Drop operations?
questions.codeSnippet: event.preventDefault()
options: dragstart
dragend
dragleave
dragover
questions.explanation: By default, browsers disallow dropping elements onto other elements. Calling `event.preventDefault()` inside the `dragover` event listener marks that element as a valid drop target.

questions.question: Which pair of focus events bubble up the DOM tree and can therefore be used with Event Delegation?
options: focus and blur
focusstart and focusend
focusin and focusout
active and inactive
questions.explanation: Standard `focus` and `blur` events do NOT bubble. Their counterpart events `focusin` and `focusout` do bubble, enabling form-wide focus delegation on parent containers.

questions.question: How do you detect if the user held down the 'Shift' key while clicking a button?
options: Check if `event.shiftKey === true` inside the click handler
Listen for a separate `keydown` event simultaneously
Check `event.key === 'Shift'` in the click handler
Check `document.isShiftPressed()`
questions.explanation: Mouse events expose boolean modifier flags: `event.shiftKey`, `event.ctrlKey`, `event.altKey`, and `event.metaKey` (Command on Mac / Windows key).

questions.question: What will happen if an event handler attached to an element throws an uncaught runtime error?
options: The error is logged to the console, but the event continues bubbling up the DOM tree to subsequent ancestor handlers
The browser immediately terminates all JavaScript execution on the page
The event propagation is automatically cancelled and halted
The browser reloads the webpage automatically
questions.explanation: An uncaught exception in an event listener halts execution of that specific handler, but does not abort the browser's event propagation pipeline to remaining listeners.

title: Daily Assessment: Form Validation & Dynamic HTML Creation
courseName: Python Full Stack + DSA with AI

questions.question: What is the standard JavaScript technique to prevent a web form from causing a full page refresh upon submission?
options: form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => { e.preventDefault(); });
form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => { e.stopPageReload(); });
form.addEventListener('submit', () => { return false; });
form.setAttribute('refresh', 'false');
questions.explanation: Forms naturally submit via HTTP GET/POST and reload the page. Calling `e.preventDefault()` inside the `'submit'` event handler intercepts submission for AJAX/Fetch handling.

questions.question: How can you extract all named inputs from a `<form id="myForm">` into a plain JavaScript key-value object in a single line?
questions.codeSnippet: <form id="myForm">
options: const data = JSON.parse(myForm.values);
const data = Array.from(myForm.inputs);
const data = myForm.toJSON();
const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(myForm));
questions.explanation: `new FormData(form)` extracts all input names and values, and `Object.fromEntries()` transforms the iterable FormData entries into a clean `{ username: 'Alice', email: '...' }` object.

questions.question: What does the Constraint Validation method `input.checkValidity()` return?
questions.codeSnippet: input.checkValidity()
options: The sanitized value of the input field
An array of failed validation rules
A boolean `true` if the input satisfies all its HTML5 validation constraints (e.g., `required`, `pattern`, `minlength`), or `false` otherwise
A string containing the validation error message
questions.explanation: `checkValidity()` evaluates validity constraints, returning `true` or `false` and firing an `'invalid'` event on the element if validation fails.

questions.question: What is the difference between `input.checkValidity()` and `input.reportValidity()`?
questions.codeSnippet: input.checkValidity()
options: `checkValidity()` only works on password fields, while `reportValidity()` is for emails
`reportValidity()` submits the form to the server automatically
There is no difference; both are exact synonyms
`reportValidity()` checks validity AND triggers the browser's native popup tooltip error message to the user, while `checkValidity()` only returns a boolean silently
questions.explanation: `reportValidity()` evaluates constraints, returns a boolean, and actively shows the browser's native validation popup balloon on the invalid field.

questions.question: How do you set a custom validation error message on an `<input id="email">` element that prevents form submission?
questions.codeSnippet: <input id="email">
options: emailInput.setAttribute('error-msg', 'Please enter an official corporate email address');
emailInput.customError = 'Please enter an official corporate email address';
emailInput.setCustomValidity('Please enter an official corporate email address');
emailInput.validationMessage = 'Please enter an official corporate email address';
questions.explanation: `setCustomValidity(message)` sets a custom error string. Passing a non-empty string marks the field invalid; passing `''` (empty string) clears the custom error and marks it valid.

questions.question: Which property on `input.validity` is `true` when an input with `required` is submitted with an empty value?
options: input.validity.badInput
input.validity.typeMismatch
input.validity.patternMismatch
input.validity.valueMissing
questions.explanation: `ValidityState.valueMissing` is `true` if the element has the `required` attribute but contains no value upon validation check.

questions.question: Which JavaScript regular expression test correctly validates that a username contains only 3 to 16 alphanumeric characters and underscores?
options: /^[a-z]{3-16}/.test(username)
/^[a-zA-Z0-9_]{3,16}$/.test(username)
/^[a-zA-Z0-9_]3,16$/.test(username)
/^[a-zA-Z0-9_]*/.test(username)
questions.explanation: `^` anchors to start, `[a-zA-Z0-9_]` specifies allowed characters, `{3,16}` enforces 3 to 16 repetitions, and `$` anchors to string end.

questions.question: How do you clone and instantiate the contents of an HTML `<template id="cardTpl">` element in JavaScript?
questions.codeSnippet: <template id="cardTpl">
options: const clone = document.querySelector('#cardTpl').content.cloneNode(true);
const clone = document.querySelector('#cardTpl').innerHTML.render();
const clone = document.importNode('#cardTpl');
const clone = document.querySelector('#cardTpl').clone();
questions.explanation: HTML `<template>` elements contain an inactive `DocumentFragment` in `.content`. Cloning `.content.cloneNode(true)` creates an active DOM instance ready for population.

questions.question: How do you implement a Show/Hide password toggle functionality on `<input type="password" id="pwd">`?
questions.codeSnippet: <input type="password" id="pwd">
options: pwd.style.visibility = pwd.style.visibility === 'hidden' ? 'visible' : 'hidden';
pwd.setAttribute('secure', pwd.getAttribute('secure') === 'true' ? 'false' : 'true');
pwd.type = pwd.type === 'password' ? 'text' : 'password';
pwd.mask = !pwd.mask;
questions.explanation: Toggling the `type` property between `'password'` (masked with dots) and `'text'` (visible plain text) seamlessly toggles password visibility.

questions.question: How can you collect all selected checkbox values with `name="hobby"` into an array of strings?
options: const hobbies = document.getElementsByName('hobby').values();
const hobbies = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('input[name="hobby"]:checked')).map(cb => cb.value);
const hobbies = form.formData.getAllChecked('hobby');
const hobbies = document.querySelectorAll('input[name="hobby"]').checkedValues();
questions.explanation: `querySelectorAll('input[name="hobby"]:checked')` selects only checked checkboxes; `Array.from(...).map(cb => cb.value)` extracts their values into an array.

questions.question: How do you read a user-selected image file from `` and preview it in an `` element using `FileReader`?
questions.codeSnippet: <input type="file" id="avatar">
options: previewImg.src = FileReader.read(avatar.value);
const reader = new FileReader(); reader.onload = (e) => { previewImg.src = e.target.result; }; reader.readAsDataURL(avatar.files[0]);
previewImg.src = avatar.files[0].path;
const reader = new FileReader(avatar.files[0]); previewImg.src = reader.toURL();
questions.explanation: `FileReader.readAsDataURL(file)` asynchronously converts the file into a base64 Data URL, which triggers the `onload` handler where `e.target.result` is assigned to `img.src`.

questions.question: How do you dynamically populate a child 'City' dropdown (`<select id="citySelect">`) based on a selected country code?
questions.codeSnippet: <select id="citySelect">
options: citySelect.options = cities[countryCode];
citySelect.bindDataset(cities[countryCode]);
citySelect.addItems(cities[countryCode]);
citySelect.replaceChildren(...cities[countryCode].map(c => new Option(c.name, c.id)));
questions.explanation: Using `new Option(text, value)` creates standard `<option>` elements, and `citySelect.replaceChildren(...)` replaces existing options with the new city options in one clean call.

questions.question: How do you implement a real-time character counter for a `<textarea maxlength="200" id="bio">`?
questions.codeSnippet: <textarea maxlength="200" id="bio">
options: bio.addEventListener('input', () => { counter.textContent = `${bio.maxLength - bio.value.length} characters left`; });
bio.onchange = () => { counter.textContent = 200 - bio.textLength; };
bio.addEventListener('select', () => { counter.text = bio.maxLength; });
bio.addEventListener('keydown', () => { counter.textContent = bio.value.length; });
questions.explanation: Listening to the `'input'` event ensures the counter updates on every keystroke, backspace, and clipboard paste in real time by evaluating `bio.maxLength - bio.value.length`.

questions.question: What is the effect of calling `form.reset()` in JavaScript?
options: It deletes the entire `<form>` element and its inputs from the DOM tree
It restores all form controls to their initial default values specified in HTML markup and clears user inputs
It submits the form to the server with empty values
It clears the browser's entire cookie and cache storage

questions.question: Why should a submit button be disabled (`submitBtn.disabled = true;`) immediately after form submission begins in an async web app?

To prevent the browser from timing out the network connection
To encrypt the user's password before sending to the backend
Because HTTP POST requests disallow enabled buttons in request payloads

questions.question: How do you extract a dropped file from a Drag-and-Drop drop zone event in JavaScript?

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'novalidate' boolean attribute when applied to `<form novalidate>`?

It prevents the server from validating passwords on backend databases
It disables browser built-in HTML5 validation balloon popups so developers can handle validation entirely via custom JavaScript UI
It allows users to bypass HTTPS encryption
questions.explanation: Adding `novalidate` prevents native browser validation tooltip balloons from popping up, allowing custom JS validation error messages and styling to take over.

questions.question: Which debounced search input technique ensures an API search query is sent only after the user stops typing for 300ms?
options: searchInput.addEventListener('change', () => fetchResults());
searchInput.debounce(300, fetchResults);
let timer; searchInput.addEventListener('input', (e) => { clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => fetchResults(e.target.value), 300); });
searchInput.addEventListener('input', (e) => { setTimeout(() => fetchResults(e.target.value), 300); });

questions.question: How do you dynamically create and display a temporary notification banner that automatically fades out and removes itself after 3 seconds?
options: const toast = new Toast('Notification'); toast.display(3000);
const toast = document.createElement('div'); toast.className = 'toast'; document.body.appendChild(toast); setTimeout(() => toast.remove(), 3000);
document.alert('Notification', { duration: 3000 });
window.showBanner('Notification', 3000);

questions.question: What is Progressive Enhancement in web form engineering?
options: Translating the form into multiple languages using AI ahead of time
Gradually increasing the font size of form inputs as the user types
Requiring users to complete a CAPTCHA on every single input field
Ensuring the form works fundamentally with basic HTML POST submission if JavaScript fails or is disabled, and enhancing with AJAX/Fetch validation when JavaScript is available

questions.question: How do ES Modules (ESM) handle exported variable bindings compared to CommonJS (`require()`)?

ES Modules export live bindings (mutations in the exporting module are reflected dynamically in importers), while CommonJS exports static value copies
CommonJS exports live bindings, while ES Modules export frozen snapshots
ES Modules do not allow exporting variables, only classes
questions.explanation: ESM exports live bindings (if an exported variable changes inside the module, imported references see the updated value in real time). CommonJS copies the value at require time.

questions.question: What is the difference between Named Exports and Default Exports in ES Modules?

questions.question: What does the dynamic import syntax `import('./analytics.js')` return?

An HTML `<script>` DOM element
A Promise that resolves to the module namespace object containing all exports
A boolean indicating if the file was found on the server

questions.question: What feature did ES2022 standardize regarding `await` in top-level module code?

questions.question: How do you unpack a property using a dynamic variable name via destructuring?

questions.question: Why does `"use strict";` not need to be declared inside an ES Module file (`<script type="module">`)?

questions.question: What is the output of `const obj = { a: 1, b: 2 }; const { a, ...rest } = obj; console.log(rest);`?
options: undefined

questions.question: Which of the following is true about how ES Modules are loaded in HTML documents (`<script type="module" src="app.js">`)?

questions.question: What is the result of using the spread operator with `Math.max()` on an array `const numbers = [4, 18, 3, 92, 11];`?

questions.question: What happens if an ES Module has circular dependencies (e.g., module A imports module B, and module B imports module A)?

title: Daily Assessment: Promises, Async/Await, and Fetch API Integration

lessonTitle: Promises, Async/Await, and Fetch API Integration

questions.question: What is the exact console output sequence of the following asynchronous JavaScript code?
questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (`1, 4`). Promise `.then()` callbacks enter the Microtask Queue and execute before the Macrotask Queue (`3`). `setTimeout` enters the Macrotask Queue and executes last (`2`).

questions.question: What are the three possible mutual lifecycle states of a JavaScript `Promise`?
options: `active`, `paused`, `stopped`
`waiting`, `completed`, `failed`
`pending`, `fulfilled`, `rejected`
`initialized`, `resolved`, `terminated`
questions.explanation: A Promise starts in `pending` and transitions immutably to either `fulfilled` (with a value) or `rejected` (with an error reason).

questions.question: What happens when you return a plain value (e.g., `return 42;`) from inside a `.then()` callback in a Promise chain?
options: The returned value is ignored and `undefined` is passed to the next `.then()`
The `.then()` method returns a new Promise that immediately resolves to the returned value (`42`)
It throws a `TypeError: Cannot return non-promise from .then`
The Promise chain terminates immediately
questions.explanation: Any value returned from a `.then()` handler is automatically wrapped in `Promise.resolve(value)`, allowing seamless method chaining.

questions.question: How does `Promise.all([p1, p2, p3])` behave if `p2` rejects with an error while `p1` and `p3` are still pending?
questions.codeSnippet: Promise.all([p1, p2, p3])
options: It converts the error into an empty object `{}`
It returns `[p1_result, null, p3_result]`
It rejects immediately with `p2`'s rejection error (fail-fast behavior), ignoring the results of other pending promises
It waits for `p1` and `p3` to complete and ignores `p2`'s error
questions.explanation: `Promise.all()` is all-or-nothing: if any single promise rejects, the entire `Promise.all()` immediately rejects with that first rejection reason.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of `Promise.allSettled([p1, p2, p3])` over `Promise.all()`?
questions.codeSnippet: Promise.allSettled([p1, p2, p3])
options: It runs promises on multi-threaded GPU cores

It never short-circuits on rejection; it waits for ALL promises to settle and returns an array of objects describing each outcome (`{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }`)
It retries failed promises up to 5 times automatically
It only works with HTTP GET requests
questions.explanation: `Promise.allSettled()` guarantees all asynchronous tasks finish, giving detailed reports for every promise regardless of success or failure.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Promise.race()` and `Promise.any()`?
options: There is no difference; both are exact aliases
`Promise.any()` returns all values, while `Promise.race()` returns one
`Promise.race()` only works with timers, while `Promise.any()` is for fetch
`Promise.race()` settles with the first settled promise (whether fulfilled OR rejected), while `Promise.any()` settles with the first FULFILLED promise (ignoring rejections until all fail)
questions.explanation: `Promise.race()` takes the very first result (even if it's an error). `Promise.any()` seeks the first success; if all reject, it rejects with an `AggregateError`.

questions.question: Why does the following Fetch API code fail to catch HTTP 404 and 500 errors in the `.catch()` block?
options: The `fetch()` Promise only rejects on network failures or blocked requests; HTTP error statuses (404, 500) resolve normally and require checking `response.ok` manually
The URL must end in `.json` for errors to trigger `.catch()`
HTTP 404 is considered a successful response by all web protocols
`fetch()` does not support `.catch()` method chaining
questions.explanation: `fetch()` treats HTTP 4xx and 5xx responses as successful HTTP communications. Developers must inspect `if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.statusText);` to trigger catch blocks.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to send a JSON payload in an HTTP POST request using the Fetch API?
options: fetch(url, { method: 'POST', data: data });
fetch.post(url, JSON.toPayload(data));
fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify(data) });
fetch(url, { bodyType: 'json', payload: data });
questions.explanation: Standard Fetch POST requires setting `method: 'POST'`, providing `headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }`, and passing a stringified payload to `body`.

questions.question: How do you implement a 5-second request timeout for a `fetch()` call using `AbortController`?
options: fetch(url).setTimeout(5000);
const c = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { cancelAfter: 5000 });
fetch(url, { timeout: 5000 });
const c = new AbortController(); setTimeout(() => c.abort(), 5000); fetch(url, { signal: c.signal });
questions.explanation: Binding `signal: controller.signal` to `fetch()` allows aborting the pending HTTP request when `controller.abort()` is called via `setTimeout`.

questions.question: What does an `async` function always return in JavaScript?
options: A Promise (wrapping the returned value in `Promise.resolve` or rejections in `Promise.reject`)
A callback function
A generator iterator object
The raw synchronous value directly
questions.explanation: Functions declared with `async` always return a Promise, even if you write `return 42;` (which returns `Promise.resolve(42)`).

questions.question: What is the difference in execution between sequential `await` and `Promise.all()` in the following code?
questions.codeSnippet:
// Approach A: const u = await getU(); const p = await getP();
// Approach B: const [u, p] = await Promise.all([getU(), getP()]);
options: Approach A executes requests sequentially in series (total time = A + B), while Approach B executes both requests concurrently in parallel (total time = max(A, B))
Approach A is faster because it uses less network bandwidth
Approach B is invalid syntax in modern JavaScript
Both approaches take identical execution time
questions.explanation: Awaiting promises sequentially forces `getP()` to wait until `getU()` finishes. Using `Promise.all()` starts both requests concurrently in parallel, slashing total wait time.

questions.question: How do you handle errors properly in an `async/await` function?
options: Use `.catch()` on every variable name
Async functions cannot throw errors
Wrap the `await` expressions in a `try...catch` block
Set `window.errorHandling = 'async';`
questions.explanation: Rejected promises awaited inside an `async` function throw exceptions, which can be cleanly intercepted using standard synchronous-like `try...catch` blocks.

questions.question: What is Microtask Queue Starvation in JavaScript?
options: When the browser runs out of cookies
A CPU hardware bug on mobile smartphones
A memory leak caused by unclosed IndexedDB connections
Continuously scheduling microtasks (e.g., recursive `Promise.resolve().then(...)` or `queueMicrotask`) without returning control, starving macrotasks, UI rendering, and user input
questions.explanation: The event loop processes all pending microtasks before rendering or checking macrotasks; an unending chain of microtasks starves the event loop and locks up UI rendering.

questions.question: What happens if an `async` function throws an unhandled exception?
options: The returned Promise is rejected with the thrown error
The error is converted into an empty string
The function returns `null` silently
The browser terminates JavaScript execution across all tabs
questions.explanation: Throwing inside an `async` function (e.g., `throw new Error('fail');`) causes the function's returned Promise to reject with that error.

questions.question: Which Response method is used to extract the binary image or file payload from a Fetch request?
options: response.blob() (or response.arrayBuffer())
response.image()
response.toFile()
response.binary()
questions.explanation: `response.blob()` resolves to a `Blob` object representing raw binary data (ideal for images, PDFs, or media downloads).

questions.question: What is the output of the following code?
options: Promise { 'Result' }
"Result"
TypeError: test(...).then is not a function
undefined
questions.explanation: `test()` returns a Promise resolving to `'Result'`; `.then()` receives the resolved string `'Result'`.

questions.question: What global event listener captures unhandled Promise rejections in modern web browsers?
options: document.onreject = handler;
window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', event => { console.log(event.reason); });
window.addEventListener('promiseerror', handler);
window.addEventListener('async:error', handler);
questions.explanation: The `unhandledrejection` event fires on `window` whenever a Promise rejects without an attached `.catch()` handler.

questions.question: What does `queueMicrotask(() => { ... })` do?
questions.codeSnippet: queueMicrotask(() => { ... })
options: It creates a background Web Worker thread
It schedules a function to run 1 hour in the future
It queues a task to be processed on the backend server
It explicitly enqueues a callback into the Microtask Queue, executing it immediately after the current synchronous script and before rendering or macrotasks
questions.explanation: `queueMicrotask()` provides a standardized API to schedule microtask callbacks with higher priority than `setTimeout(fn, 0)` without Promise instantiation overhead.

questions.question: What is the return value of `Promise.resolve(5).then(x => x * 2).then(x => { throw new Error('err'); }).catch(e => 100).then(x => x + 1)`?
questions.codeSnippet:
Promise.resolve(5)
  .then(x => x * 2)
  .then(x => { throw new Error('err'); })
  .catch(e => 100)
  .then(x => x + 1);
options: UnhandledPromiseRejection
101 (The `.catch()` handler catches the error, recovers by returning 100, and passes 100 to the next `.then()` which computes 100 + 1)
NaN
questions.explanation: Errors skip intermediate `.then()` handlers until reaching `.catch()`. The `.catch()` returns `100` (recovering the chain), which flows into the subsequent `.then(x => x + 1)` to yield `101`.

questions.question: Why should `await` NOT be used inside a traditional `Array.prototype.forEach()` loop?
options: `forEach` throws a syntax error if `await` is inside its callback
`forEach` can only process synchronous integers
`forEach` converts all promises into numbers automatically
`forEach` does not wait for async callback promises to resolve, running all iterations concurrently without waiting and ignoring returned promises
questions.explanation: `forEach` is synchronous and ignores the Promises returned by async callbacks. For sequential async loops, use `for (const item of array)` with `await`.

questions.question: Which of the following represents a valid JSON string according to RFC 8259 specifications?
options: {"name": "Alice", "date": new Date()}
{"name": "Alice", "age": 25, "active": true, "roles": ["admin"]}
{ 'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25, }
{ name: "Alice", age: 25 }
questions.explanation: JSON strictly requires double quotes around property keys and string values, prohibits trailing commas, and disallows JavaScript expressions/constructors like `new Date()`.

questions.question: What happens when `JSON.stringify()` encounters an object containing a function, `undefined`, and a Symbol property?
questions.codeSnippet: JSON.stringify()
options: It omits all three properties from the serialized JSON string output
It converts all three into empty strings `""`
It converts the function into executable text and keeps undefined
It throws a fatal `TypeError`
questions.explanation: `JSON.stringify()` omits functions, `undefined`, and Symbols when serializing objects (or converts them to `null` if encountered inside an array).

questions.question: How can you safely format a JSON string with 2-space indentation for human readability?
options: JSON.stringify(data, 'indent: 2');
JSON.stringify(data).indent(2);
JSON.stringify(data, null, 2);
JSON.format(data, 2);
questions.explanation: The third argument of `JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space)` controls whitespace indentation (passing `2` formats with 2 spaces).

questions.question: How do you parse a JSON string containing an ISO date string (e.g., `'{"createdAt": "2026-09-11T12:00:00Z"}'`) and automatically restore it as a real JavaScript `Date` object?
options: Set `JSON.parseDates = true;` before parsing
Use `JSON.parse(jsonStr, { parseDates: true });`
JSON parses dates automatically without extra code
Use a reviver function: `JSON.parse(jsonStr, (key, value) => key === 'createdAt' ? new Date(value) : value);`
questions.explanation: The reviver callback in `JSON.parse(text, reviver)` transforms each key-value pair during parsing, allowing strings matching date patterns to be instantiated as `Date` objects.

questions.question: Why should `JSON.parse()` almost always be wrapped in a `try...catch` block when processing API responses or localStorage data?
options: Because invalid, malformed, or empty JSON strings throw a fatal `SyntaxError` that will crash the application if uncaught
Because `try...catch` accelerates JSON parsing speed by 50%
Because valid JSON is automatically deleted from memory unless caught
Because `JSON.parse()` triggers network requests behind the scenes
questions.explanation: Malformed JSON (or empty strings) causes `JSON.parse()` to throw a synchronous `SyntaxError: Unexpected token...`, making `try-catch` error handling essential.

questions.question: If an object has a custom `.toJSON()` method defined, how does `JSON.stringify()` treat that object?
options: It calls the `.toJSON()` method and serializes whatever value `.toJSON()` returns instead of serializing the raw object
It ignores the `.toJSON()` method completely
It throws a TypeError for conflicting methods
It deletes the object from the DOM
questions.explanation: If an object defines a `toJSON()` method, `JSON.stringify()` delegates serialization to that method (which is how `Date.prototype.toJSON()` formats ISO date strings).

questions.question: When uploading a file using Fetch and `FormData`, why is it an anti-pattern to manually set `headers: { 'Content-Type': 'multipart/form-data' }`?
options: Manually setting the header omits the required `boundary` parameter string, causing the backend server to fail to parse the multipart payload
Because `FormData` is encrypted with SSL automatically
Because `FormData` only works with `Content-Type: application/json`
Because browsers reject all POST requests with custom headers
questions.explanation: When passing `body: new FormData()`, the browser automatically sets `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary...`. Manually setting it strips the boundary delimiter, breaking server parsing.

questions.question: What is an 'Optimistic UI Update' pattern in web API applications?
options: Disabling all error logging in production builds
Assuming the user's internet connection will never fail
Immediately updating the frontend UI as if the API mutation succeeded, and only reverting the change if the backend request subsequently fails
Displaying positive smiley face icons when forms submit
questions.explanation: Optimistic UI provides instant responsiveness (e.g., liking a post instantly toggles the heart icon), rolling back to the previous state with an error toast only if the network call rejects.

questions.question: How do you implement an API retry mechanism with Exponential Backoff in JavaScript?
options: Set `fetch(url, { retry: 'exponential' })`
Reload the entire browser window repeatedly until status is 200
Catch the error, wait for a progressively doubling delay (`Math.pow(2, attempt) * 1000ms`), and recursively re-call the fetch function up to max attempts
Send 100 requests simultaneously in a `while (true)` loop
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff delays retries by $2^{\text{attempt}} \times \text{baseDelay}$, preventing client retries from overwhelming recovering servers.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the HTTP `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header in REST API integration?
questions.codeSnippet: Authorization: Bearer <token>
options: To specify which web browser model is sending the request
To authenticate the client by passing a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) or OAuth access token with each protected request
To authorize the server to charge the user's credit card
To bypass HTTPS encryption requirements on public Wi-Fi
questions.explanation: The `Authorization: Bearer <JWT>` header transmits authentication credentials securely on each API call for token-based authorization.

questions.question: What should an application do when an API responds with HTTP Status Code `401 Unauthorized`?
options: Display a 500 Internal Server Error page
Retry the exact same request 50 times in a loop
Attempt to refresh the access token using a refresh token, or redirect the user to the Login page to re-authenticate
Delete all HTML elements from the webpage
questions.explanation: `401 Unauthorized` indicates missing or expired authentication; modern apps intercept 401s, request a new token via refresh endpoint, and retry the original call.

questions.question: What is the difference between Polling and Server-Sent Events (SSE) for receiving live data updates from a backend?
options: Polling is full-duplex, while SSE is bidirectional
SSE only works in Node.js backends
Polling does not consume any network bandwidth
Polling repeatedly sends periodic HTTP requests on a timer, while SSE maintains a single persistent unidirectional HTTP connection streaming events from server to client
questions.explanation: Short/long polling incurs repeated HTTP overhead. Server-Sent Events (`EventSource`) establishes a persistent, low-overhead HTTP stream where the server pushes real-time updates.

questions.question: How can you read a Streaming API response (such as an LLM AI text generation stream) chunk-by-chunk using the Fetch API?
options: const stream = response.json(); while (stream.hasData()) { console.log(stream.next()); }
const reader = response.body.getReader(); const decoder = new TextDecoder(); while (true) { const { value, done } = await reader.read(); if (done) break; console.log(decoder.decode(value)); }
response.stream().forEach(chunk => console.log(chunk));
response.on('data', chunk => console.log(chunk));
questions.explanation: `response.body.getReader()` accesses the `ReadableStream` reader, allowing asynchronous decoding of streaming binary chunks (`Uint8Array`) using `TextDecoder` in real time.

questions.question: How do you cache an API response in `localStorage` with a 1-hour expiration timestamp?
options: Set `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` on `localStorage`
Store an object `{ data: apiResult, expiry: Date.now() + 3600000 }` stringified, and compare `Date.now() > item.expiry` before reading
localStorage.cache(url, apiResult, '1h');
localStorage.setItem(url, apiResult, { ttl: 3600 });
questions.explanation: `localStorage` has no native TTL; storing a wrapper object with an `expiry` timestamp allows checking if the cache is stale before making network requests.

questions.question: What causes a CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) error in the browser when making a `fetch()` request to an API?
options: The JavaScript code contains syntax errors in the JSON payload
The client computer does not have an active SSL certificate installed
The user's monitor refresh rate is lower than 60Hz
The server did not return an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header matching the client's origin protocol, domain, or port
questions.explanation: Browsers enforce the Same-Origin Policy; cross-origin requests are blocked unless the server explicitly sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` or `https://myclient.com`.

questions.question: What is the recommended method to build an Infinite Scroll pagination loader in pure JavaScript?
options: Load all 1,000,000 database records upfront on initial page load
Use `setInterval` polling every 500ms
Attach a synchronous `scroll` listener that recalculates document height every millisecond
Use an `IntersectionObserver` observing a sentinel element at the bottom of the feed to trigger fetching the next page when scrolled into view
questions.explanation: `IntersectionObserver` efficiently triggers page fetching when a target footer sentinel enters the viewport, avoiding scroll event layout thrashing.

questions.question: What does the `Accept: application/json` request header communicate to an API server?
options: It enables client-side database caching
It informs the server that the client expects and can process a response formatted in JSON
It informs the server of the data format contained in the request body
It forces the server to accept all uploaded files
questions.explanation: `Accept` specifies desired response MIME types (`application/json`), whereas `Content-Type` describes the MIME type of the sent request payload.

questions.question: How do you safely render dynamic text from an external API into a DOM container to prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)?
options: document.write(apiData.title);
cardTitle.eval(apiData.title);
cardTitle.textContent = apiData.title; (or sanitize with DOMPurify before assigning to innerHTML)
cardTitle.innerHTML = apiData.title;
questions.explanation: Using `element.textContent` treats API strings strictly as text without HTML parsing, neutralizing any injected `<script>` or `onerror` tags.

questions.question: What HTTP Status Code is standard for a successful `DELETE` request that returns no content in the response body?
options: 204 No Content
202 Accepted
201 Created
200 OK
questions.explanation: Status code `204 No Content` indicates the server successfully fulfilled the request and there is no additional content to send in the response payload.

questions.question: What is the output of `JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: undefined, c: null, d: NaN })`?
questions.codeSnippet: JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: undefined, c: null, d: NaN })
options: TypeError: NaN cannot be serialized
"{"a":1,"b":undefined,"c":null,"d":NaN}"
"{"a":1,"c":null,"d":null}"
questions.explanation: `undefined` properties are omitted, `null` remains `null`, and `NaN` (as well as `Infinity`) is converted to `null` in JSON serialization.

questions.question: What is the output of the following Python division operations?
questions.explanation: `7 / 2` performs true floating-point division (3.5). `7 // 2` performs floor division rounding towards negative infinity (3). `-7 // 2` evaluates to -3.5, which floors down to -4.

questions.question:
Consider the following code evaluating reference equality (`is`) versus value equality (`==`): 
What is the output?
questions.codeSnippet:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
c = [1, 2, 3]
print(a is b, a is c, a == c)
options: True True True
False False True
True False False
True False True
questions.explanation: `a is b` is `True` because `b` references the exact same list object in memory (`id(a) == id(b)`). `a is c` is `False` because `c` is a newly created list with a distinct memory address. `a == c` is `True` because their contents are identical.

questions.question: What is the output of the string slice operations below?
questions.codeSnippet:
s = 'Python'
print(s[::-1], s[1:5:2])
options: nohtyP yhn
nohtyP yto
Python yto
nohtyP yh
questions.explanation: `s[::-1]` reverses the string ('nohtyP'). `s[1:5:2]` starts at index 1 ('y'), stops before index 5 ('n'), and steps by 2, picking indices 1 ('y') and 3 ('h') to produce 'yh'.

questions.question: What will the following `for...else` loop output?
options: Loop Finished
0 1 2 Loop Finished
No output is printed
SyntaxError: else cannot be attached to a for loop
questions.explanation: In Python, the `else` clause of a `for` or `while` loop executes if and only if the loop completes all iterations normally without encountering a `break` statement.

questions.question: What does the expression `list(range(10, 2, -3))` evaluate to in Python?
questions.explanation: `range(start=10, stop=2, step=-3)` starts at 10, decrements by 3 (10, 7, 4), and stops before reaching 2, yielding `[10, 7, 4]`.

questions.question: What is the result of the short-circuit boolean expression `'apple' and 0 or 'banana'` in Python?
options: True
'banana'
'apple'
questions.explanation: Evaluation proceeds left to right: `'apple' and 0` evaluates `'apple'` (truthy) and returns the second operand `0`. Then `0 or 'banana'` evaluates `0` (falsy) and returns the truthy operand `'banana'`.

questions.question: How does Python evaluate chained comparison operators like `1 < x < 10`?
options: Chained comparisons are illegal and raise a SyntaxError in Python
It converts all operands into floating-point numbers before comparison
It evaluates `(1 < x)` to a boolean, then compares `True < 10` or `False < 10`
It translates to `(1 < x) and (x < 10)`, evaluating the middle expression `x` only once
questions.explanation: Python natively supports mathematical chained comparisons: `a < b < c` is evaluated as `a < b and b < c`, with `b` evaluated only once for efficiency and side-effect prevention.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between Python's type system and statically typed languages like C++ or Java?
options: Python does not support data types in memory
Python variables must have explicit type declarations before assignment
Python is dynamically typed (variable types are bound to values at runtime rather than fixed to variable names) and strongly typed (implicit incompatible type coercion like `1 + '2'` is forbidden)
Python is weakly typed and converts strings to integers automatically in all operations
questions.explanation: Python is dynamically typed (variables are untyped references to typed objects in heap memory) and strongly typed (`'5' + 2` raises a `TypeError` rather than coercing silently).

questions.question: What does the Walrus Operator (`:=`) introduced in Python 3.8 allow developers to do?
options: Perform fast parallel multi-threading operations
Compare two complex numbers for geometric distance
Assign values to variables within an expression (e.g., `if (n := len(items)) > 5:`)
Declare immutable constants at the module level
questions.explanation: The walrus operator `:=` is the assignment expression operator, allowing variable assignment and evaluation within conditions, comprehensions, and while loops.

questions.question: What is the Small Integer Caching mechanism in CPython?
options: Negative integers are stored in local CPU registers only
Integers larger than 256 are automatically compressed into 8-bit bytes
Integers between 0 and 100 cannot be modified in loops
CPython pre-allocates and caches singleton integer objects in the range `[-5, 256]` in memory, so all references to these numbers share the exact same object identity (`is`)
questions.explanation: CPython maintains an array of integer objects for values from -5 to 256. Any variable assigned an integer in this range references the shared global singleton in memory.

questions.question: What is the output of the following Structural Pattern Matching (`match...case`) code?
questions.codeSnippet:
point = (0, 5)
match point:
    case (0, 0):
        print('Origin')
    case (0, y):
        print(f'Y-axis at {y}')
    case (x, 0):
        print(f'X-axis at {x}')
    case _:
        print('Somewhere else')
options: Y-axis at 5
Somewhere else
Y-axis at 0
Origin
questions.explanation: Structural pattern matching matches the tuple `(0, 5)` against `case (0, y):`, binding `y = 5` and executing the second case block.

questions.question: What happens when you call `'hello'.index('z')` versus `'hello'.find('z')`?
options: `.find('z')` returns `-1`, while `.index('z')` raises a `ValueError: substring not found`
`.find('z')` returns `None`, while `.index('z')` returns `0`
Both methods raise a `ValueError`
Both methods return `-1`
questions.explanation: In Python string methods, `.find()` returns `-1` on missing substrings (ideal for `if s.find(...) != -1`), whereas `.index()` raises a `ValueError`.

questions.question: What is the role of the Python Virtual Machine (PVM) and `__pycache__` folder?
options: Python compiles source code (`.py`) into platform-independent Bytecode (`.pyc` stored in `__pycache__`), which is then executed by the CPython interpreter (PVM)
The PVM translates Python directly into C++ source files
`__pycache__` stores temporary browser cookies and session tokens
The PVM compiles Python into native x86 machine binaries ahead of time
questions.explanation: CPython compiles `.py` source into bytecode instructions (`.pyc` cached in `__pycache__` to speed up future imports) and executes them on the Python Virtual Machine.

questions.question: What will `rest` contain after unpacking `a, b, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`?
questions.explanation: Extended iterable unpacking with `*rest` captures all remaining unassigned elements into a new Python list `[3, 4, 5]`.

questions.question: Why does `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` evaluate to `False` in Python, and how should floating-point numbers be accurately compared?
options: Python converts all decimal arithmetic to fractions automatically
IEEE 754 binary floating-point representation has rounding inaccuracies; use `math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)` or the `decimal.Decimal` module for precision
Because `0.1` and `0.2` are converted to integers; use `round()` only
Python does not support floating point arithmetic; use `float.compare()`
questions.explanation: Due to binary floating-point precision limits, `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. The standard library provides `math.isclose()` for tolerant floating-point comparison.

questions.question: What does the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in CPython do?
options: It prevents unauthorized users from modifying Python packages in site-packages
It is a mutex that prevents multiple native OS threads from executing Python bytecodes simultaneously, ensuring CPython memory management thread safety
It locks Python scripts to a single computer hardware MAC address
It disables file read/write access during database transactions
questions.explanation: The GIL ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time within a single process, making multi-processing (rather than multi-threading) necessary for CPU-bound parallelism.

questions.question: What does `int('1010', 2)` evaluate to in Python?
options: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10
10 (Parses the string '1010' as a base-2 binary integer)
questions.explanation: The second argument to `int(string, base)` specifies the numeric base (radix). Base 2 parses binary `'1010'` as $1\times8 + 0\times4 + 1\times2 + 0\times1 = 10$.

questions.question: What will `bool('False')` evaluate to in Python?
options: True (Because any non-empty string is truthy in Python)
TypeError: Cannot convert text to boolean
False (Because the string spells the word 'False')
None
questions.explanation: In Python, `bool(string)` tests if the string is non-empty. Only the empty string `""` evaluates to `False`; any non-empty string (including `'False'` or `'0'`) evaluates to `True`.

questions.question: How do you format a floating-point number `num = 123.4567` to 2 decimal places using Python f-strings?
options: f"{round(num, 2):f}"
f"{num:.2f}"
f"{num:2d}"
f"{num.toPrecision(2)}"
questions.explanation: The format specifier `:.2f` in f-strings formats floating-point numbers to fixed 2 decimal places, producing `'123.46'`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `pass` and `continue` in a Python `for` loop?
options: `pass` terminates the loop completely, while `continue` skips to the next item
There is no difference; both statements are identical

`pass` is a null statement placeholder that does nothing and continues execution of the current iteration, while `continue` immediately skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next cycle
`continue` is used only in `try-except` blocks, while `pass` is for loops
questions.explanation: `pass` is an executable no-op used when syntax requires a statement block. `continue` alters control flow by skipping the remainder of the loop body for that iteration.
